papers.title: Federated Learning for Cross-Regional Epidemic Forecasting with Asynchronous Outbreaks
papers.abstract: Objective: Epidemic outbreaks are often asynchronous across regions, yet collaborative forecasting is hampered by privacy laws and heterogeneous public health interventions. We developed and evaluated, as a proof of concept, a federated learning (FL) framework for cross-regional COVID-19 forecasting under asynchronous outbreaks among Guangdong, Macau, and Portugal, while maintaining data sovereignty. Methods: Using daily case data from WHO and China CDC for the three regions, whose outbreaks were asynchronous and interventions heterogeneous, we trained Long Short-Term Memory networks via FL for short-term forecasting, benchmarked against localized and centralized training using Root Mean Square Error, Mean Absolute Error, and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error. All experiments used the Flower FL framework with consistent hyperparameters across sites. Publicly available, aggregated case-count data were used so that the centralized benchmark could be computed as a reference. Results: The dataset comprised 1,233 daily observations (411 days) of new confirmed COVID-19 cases from November 24, 2021, to January 8, 2023. The earlier Omicron wave in Portugal supplied transmission dynamics that improved forecasts in the later-onset regions of Macau and Guangdong. The FL model achieved a normalized Root Mean Square Error of 0.028, an 88.3% improvement over the local model (0.240) and comparable to the centralized model, with network overhead mainly determined by model size and aggregation rounds. Conclusion: FL achieved short-term forecasting accuracy close to centralized training while maintaining data residency, with acceptable overhead. Leveraging asynchronous outbreaks across regions may offer a practical path to privacy-preserving collaborative forecasting, though prospective validation is required.

papers.title: Communication-Learning Co-Design for Pinching-Antenna-Assisted Federated Learning in Heterogeneous Wireless Networks
papers.abstract: Wireless federated learning (FL) suffers from two coupled bottlenecks: statistical heterogeneity across clients and communication-constrained model synchronization over unreliable wireless links. Instead of focusing on algorithmic design and/or wireless resource optimization, this paper provides a systematic study of pinching antenna (PA)-empowered FL for heterogeneous wireless networks and develops a unified communication-and-learning framework. Specifically, we integrate a segmented waveguide-enabled pinching antenna (SWAN) architecture with a heterogeneity-robust FL algorithm based on client variance reduction and dual quantization, so as to jointly mitigate communication bottlenecks and client drift. On this basis, we further develop a two-stage SWAN-assisted downlink protocol and formulate fairness-oriented uplink optimization problems for PA positioning, bandwidth allocation, and quantization design. Efficient solution frameworks are then derived for the resulting downlink and uplink optimization problems. Experimental results show the superiority of the proposed design in convergence speed and final accuracy under non-independent and identically distributed data and communication bottlenecks.

papers.title: Gradient Inversion through Linear and Affine Subspace Constraints
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a machine-learning model without directly sharing their local datasets. However, as prior works have shown, the gradients exchanged during training may reveal sensitive information about client data. Most existing attacks usually optimize dummy inputs to match the true client gradients (Gradient Inversion Attacks), while some attempt to reconstruct them based on the observation that aggregate gradients from a fully connected (FC) layer are a linear combination of its inputs. In this work, we extend this observation by showing that aggregate gradients from an FC layer with the correct scaling are actually an affine combination of its inputs. We evaluate a gradient inversion attack that leverages either known linear-subspace information or its affine-subspace counterpart at each FC layer to improve reconstruction accuracy. Our results show that subspace-based methods can substantially improve reconstruction quality over the chosen baselines in certain settings. We further demonstrate that moderate overestimation of the batch size can generally improve or preserve reconstruction quality, even when the true batch size is unknown. We additionally examine reconstruction under gradient perturbations introduced by a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, providing insight into the effectiveness of the considered formulations under noisy conditions.

papers.title: FedVP: Federated Learning across Heterogeneous Models by Pooling Locally Trained Verifiers
papers.abstract: Conventional federated learning relies on the shared model backbone to aggregate client updates, limiting collaboration among institutions that deploy large language models (LLMs) from different families and at different scales. We propose Federated Verifier Pool (FEDVP), a new federated learning paradigm that enables heterogeneous clients to collaborate through shared verification rather than parameter aggregation. Each client trains a verifier using local data and responses generated by its chosen LLM backbone. The server pools these independently trained verifiers and combines their judgments to select answers without merging model parameters. This allows both LLM backbones and verifiers to differ in architecture and size, while keeping the LLM backbones frozen and deriving collaborative gains from improved answer selection. We evaluate FEDVP across five public medical question-answering datasets treated as federated clients, using Qwen and LLaMA backbones ranging from 3B to 14B parameters. FEDVP consistently improves performance across all five clients and outperforms the strongest conventional federated baselines by 1.46-5.79 percentage points in mean accuracy.

papers.title: Data-Efficient Unlearning-Based Backdoor Detection in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Detecting backdoor attacks in federated learning (FL) is challenging because malicious clients can manipulate the global model while preserving main-task performance. Static model-update statistics may therefore fail to clearly distinguish malicious from benign clients. Unlearning-based detectors instead probe client models through loss ascent on clean server data, but detection performance degrades with scarce proxy data. We propose Screening via Unlearning Response Analysis (SURA), a data-efficient detector. SURA reuses the same small clean proxy across multiple train-mode loss-ascent steps, strengthening client responses without additional clean data. For federated vision models with batch normalization (BN), repeated probing also changes BN running statistics and can confound endpoint measurements. SURA addresses this by restoring the shared pre-probe BN state only at readout while preserving the parameter changes induced by probing. This separates repeated probing from response measurement and removes BN drift and the interaction between parameter and BN-state changes from the readout. Across six backdoor attacks, SURA uses only 10 clean server images, outperforms methods under the same data budget, and approaches the robustness obtained with much larger proxy sets.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Log Mining-Based Anomaly and Threat Detection: A Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Computer systems produce a large number of logs every day. Cyberattacks often leave some signs in these logs. Traditional tools use fixed rules to find attacks, but they may miss new attacks and cannot easily handle large amounts of data. AI uses a different approach. It learns what normal log activity looks like and detects unusual activity. This paper discusses five main AI approaches. Machine learning methods such as Decision Trees and XGBoost are fast and easy to understand. Deep learning methods such as LSTM and Autoencoders learn patterns from log sequences. Transformers and LLMs can understand complex log patterns. Graph Neural Networks connect related events to detect multi-step attacks. Explainable and Federated Learning help make AI results easier to understand and support secure learning.The paper explains the strengths and limitations of these methods and compares them based on accuracy, false alarms, speed, cost, and understandability. It also discusses common problems, such as limited attack data and changing log formats, and suggests areas for future research.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: ExclaveFL: Verifiable Claims for Federated Learning using Exclaves
papers.abstract: In federated learning (FL), data providers jointly train a machine learning model without sharing training data. This makes it challenging to provide verifiable claims about the trained model, e.g., related to the employed training data, data sanitization, or training algorithm—a malicious data provider can simply deviate from the correct training protocol without detection. Prior FL training systems have used trusted execution environments (TEEs) to protect the training computation, relying on the confidentiality and integrity of TEEs. TEE confidentiality, however, has been shown to be vulnerable to various attacks, e.g., via side channels. We describe ExclaveFL , a system for training FL models that establishes verifiable claims about models through fine-grained runtime attestation proofs. Since such proofs only require integrity, ExclaveFL generates them using exclaves , which are integrity-only execution environments without software-managed secrets, making them immune to data leakage attacks. ExclaveFL uses exclaves to attest data transformations during FL training, and the runtime attestation proofs then form an attested dataflow graph of the entire training computation. The graph is checked by an auditor to ensure that the trained model satisfies claims, e.g., about the use of data sanitization by data providers or aggregation by the model provider. Since exclaves require minor yet proprietary firmware changes, we evaluate a variant with similar performance but slightly weaker security guarantees on existing AMD SEV-SNP hardware. We show that ExclaveFL introduces less than 12% overhead compared to unprotected FL model training.

papers.title: Data auditing and quality assurance in a federated learning consortium: getting the best of both worlds from cross-institutional and in-house data quality inspection
papers.abstract: Introduction Rare and heterogeneous disease research increasingly relies on privacy-enhancing technologies such as federated learning (FL) to enable cross-institutional collaboration across fragmented datasets. However, data quality assurance in FL can be limited, because individual-level data are not directly accessible to researchers. While schema-dependent inspection offers a partial solution, it requires standardised schemas or resource-intensive frameworks, hindering scalability and collaboration. To address these challenges, we implemented two complementary dashboards and evaluated their interplay. Methodology We adapted a recognised data quality control framework for re-use of electronic health record (EHR) data using breast cancer records from Centre Léon Bérard into two dashboards: (1) an in-house dashboard for intra-clinic quality assessment, and (2) a federated dashboard for inter-clinic quality assessment. To evaluate detection capabilities, artificial inconsistencies were introduced into distributed datasets mirroring the in-house source. Results The in-house dashboard provided granularity and reliability, pinpointing individual-level inconsistencies, while the federated dashboard enabled cross-institutional pattern detection–trade-offs inherent to their designs. The federated system revealed ecosystem-wide trends inaccessible to single-institution tools, whereas the in-house dashboard provided local validation and thoroughness. Discussion Our findings confirm a complementary relationship: FL dashboards provide scalable, collaborative oversight but may require additional quality checks, while in-house tools ensure thoroughness at the cost of scalability. A combined model seemingly offers the optimal balance, accommodating both institution-specific needs and collaborative research requirements in evolving, multi-institutional ecosystems.
papers.venue: Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics

papers.title: Federated learning reconciles data sovereignty with collaborative energy-transition modelling across the Global South: a public-data benchmark anchored in Indonesia
papers.abstract: Abstract Meeting Paris-aligned trajectories in the Global South requires rapid, data-intensive coordination of where and how low-carbon energy infrastructure is built, yet the underlying data are fragmented across sovereign jurisdictions reluctant to pool sensitive energy, land and infrastructure information. Wealthy blocs are answering their own version of this problem with shared or sovereign compute at extraordinary cost — a €10-billion European network of publicly funded ‘AI Factories’ and a US$500-billion private buildout in the United States — scales no developing country can replicate alone. Federated learning (FL), in which institutions jointly train a shared model by exchanging model parameters rather than raw data, offers an alternative technical foundation, but its value for cross-country energy modelling in developing regions has not been quantified. Treating 44 Global South countries (16,404 operating facilities) in the Global Energy Monitor Global Integrated Power Tracker as sovereign data silos, we benchmarked four training regimes on a geospatial renewable-versus-fossil classification task. Federated averaging matched centralized pooling of all raw data to three decimal places (AUC 0.895 versus 0.895) while no record left its country of origin, and personalized FL exceeded isolated national training (0.910 versus 0.905; two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.048), with the advantage larger on average among data-poor silos and widening as training data were artificially restricted. Independent replication on the 2021 WRI Global Power Plant Database (31 silos, 6,545 plants) reproduces the sovereignty result, though there the personalization advantage is statistically indistinguishable from zero. A high-capacity gradient-boosted model trained on pooled data outperforms every federated configuration tested (0.960 versus 0.815 trained locally), a gap driven by training-set volume rather than implicit country identification: the median silo holds 63 training facilities against 11,479 pooled. Aggregation therefore has large and rising value with model capacity, no country's own data suffice for the most capable methods, and extending federation to such models is the decisive next step. These results provide a quantitative foundation for federated architectures — national AI Labs coupled to shared, renewably powered training infrastructure under parity governance — as coordination infrastructure for Global South energy transitions, with Indonesia as the natural first national pilot.
papers.venue: Research Square

papers.title: A Communication-Aware Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for UAV-Swarm Relay Deployment via 3D Trajectory Control
papers.abstract: **A Communication-Aware Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for UAV-Swarm Relay Deployment via 3D Trajectory Control** **Shanshan He** Department of Communication Engineering, Jilin University, Changchun 130012, China **Abstract:** Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms can restore communication after infrastructure failure and extend low-altitude Internet of Things (IoT) services, but trajectory decisions interact with access links, backhaul bottlenecks, data queues, battery use, service fairness, and flight constraints. This paper formulates these couplings as a communication-aware constrained Markov game and implements a lightweight communication-aware multi-agent dueling double DQN (CA-MAD3QN). The implemented learner controls only discrete three-dimensional UAV motion; user association, bandwidth, access power, and the MEC term are fixed or rule based and are not claimed as learned optimization variables. Backhaul capacity is propagated to every user through an explicit service-scaling factor before queue evolution. The revised numerical study compares CA-MAD3QN with discrete MAPPO, vanilla DQN, one-step mod-el-predictive optimization, greedy tracking, and static deployment over three independent training seeds and reports 95% confidence intervals. Under the stress setting, CA-MAD3QN achieves an episode utility of 85.36 ± 28.94 (95% CI); the evidence does not establish universal superiority over the competitive baselines, so no such claim is made. In the two-UAV testbed, an exact joint-action projection eliminates modeled realized violations; disabling that projection for the same trained policy yields 0.863 violations per slot on average. Preliminary small-scale tests with two to four UAVs show increasing aggregate throughput but also expose projection and training-variance limitations. The results are therefore pre-sented as an auditable proof of concept rather than hardware validation. **Keywords:** UAV Swarm; Communication Relay; Three-Dimensional Trajectory Optimization; Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning; Mobile Edge Computing; Safety Projection; Federated Learning **Citation:** He S. A Communication-Aware Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework for UAV-Swarm Relay Deployment via 3D Trajectory Control. Engineering and Computing Insights. Published online November 10, 2026:22-35. doi:10.67728/eci.2026.003

papers.title: Corrigendum to: Federated Learning: An Approach for Managing Data Privacy and Security in Collaborative Learning
papers.abstract: Following publication of the article entitled “Federated Learning: An Approach for Managing Data Privacy and Security in Collaborative Learning” [1], certain phrases and expressions were identified that were unclear or inconsistent with established scientific terminology. To ensure accuracy and clarity of the published record, these expressions have been corrected using appropriate terminology that more accurately conveys the intended scientific meaning. These corrections are limited to the wording and terminology of the affected passages and do not alter the data, results, scientific interpretations, or conclusions of the article. The specific corrections are provided below: Section 3.6.1, Paragraph 1 Original text: With the rise of big data technology in recent years, technologies such as deep learning, reinforcement learning, visualization, and others have been widely deployed and have achieved substantial success in fields such natural language processing, picture recognition, and video detection. Corrected text: With the rise of big data technology in recent years, technologies such as deep learning, reinforcement learning, visualization, and others have been widely deployed and have achieved substantial success in fields such as natural language processing, image classification, and video analysis. The original article has been updated accordingly. This Corrigendum is published to ensure transparency and accuracy of the scholarly record. The corrected version of the article is available online at: https://www.benthamscience.com/article/145773 The authors regret these errors and apologise for any inconvenience they may have caused.
papers.venue: Recent Advances in Electrical & Electronic Engineering (Formerly Recent Patents on Electrical & Electronic Engineering)

papers.title: FedRD: Towards Memory-Efficient Federated Learning on Mobile Devices via Fragmentation-Aware Memory Management
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables multiple devices to collaboratively train a global model while preserving data privacy. However, the substantial memory requirements during local training pose a significant challenge for deploying FL on resource-constrained mobile devices in real-world scenarios. This paper introduces FedRD, a memory-efficient FL framework that well trades off model performance and training efficiency through hierarchical management. Specifically, FedRD features the following core techniques. First, a Memory Budget Predictor is designed to well estimate the available memory under fluctuating workloads in highly dynamic environments. With the memory budget, a Memory-aware Participant Selector is designed to select the participating devices for each training round through jointly evaluating the memory, computation, and statistical utility in order to well balance the model performance and training efficiency. Finally, we develop a memory-efficient training engine that enables local training under strict memory budgets by reshaping allocation workloads from both spatial and temporal perspectives, effectively mitigating memory fragmentation. Extensive experiments are conducted to evaluate FedRD on both simulation testbed and off-the-shelf mobile devices. The experiment results demonstrate that FedRD significantly outperforms the baselines, achieving up to 41% higher model accuracy while reducing wall-clock time by 9 × across varying memory budgets.

papers.title: Beyond-Birthday-Bound Stream Ciphers for Constrained IoT: A Focused Review
papers.abstract: Constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices often need to protect large volumes of operational data over extended periods, while frequent key refreshment may be impractical due to limited computational resources, energy constraints, and communication overhead. However, conventional single-call counter-mode constructions and lightweight authenticated-encryption schemes remain subject to the birthday bound, which limits secure data processing under a key to approximately O(2^n/2), irrespective of key length. This limitation motivates the investigation of beyond-birthday-bound stream ciphers for resource-constrained deployments. This review synthesizes the literature on BBB stream ciphers for constrained IoT, with particular emphasis on sum-of-permutations (SoP) constructions instantiated with the NIST-standardized Ascon-p12 permutation. Through a structured literature synthesis, we classify existing BBB constructions, compare their security models and bounds with birthday-bound alternatives, and examine available evidence concerning implementation performance, fault resistance, side-channel leakage, quantum security, and authenticated-encryption (AEAD) composition. The findings indicate that SoP-CTR offers a promising single-master-key approach to BBB security, but its practical deployment readiness remains insufficiently established. In particular, implementation benchmarks are concentrated on Cortex-M4 and x86-64 platforms; the fault and side-channel behavior of two-branch permutation structures remains inadequately characterized; formal security analyses in the quantum random oracle model (QROM) are limited; and the reviewed literature does not establish a proven cipher-specific AEAD composition using a lightweight tweakable message authentication code (MAC). The review also identifies potential applications of BBB stream ciphers in AI-enabled IoT and edge computing, particularly for protecting sensor-data communications and federated learning model updates. However, direct evaluations in these application settings remain lacking. To address these gaps, we propose a conceptual four-dimensional evaluation framework covering cross-architecture benchmarking, hardware hardening, formal quantum analysis, and AEAD composition with physical leakage assessment. This framework provides a structured basis for future research and deployment-oriented evaluation rather than presenting an empirically validated solution.
papers.venue: Journal of Future Artificial Intelligence and Technologies

papers.title: FedEAGD: Trajectory-Guided Drift-Aware Distillation for Personalized Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Abstract Personalized federated learning (PFL) aims to balance shared knowledge with client-specific adaptation under heterogeneous data. However, data that are not independently and identically distributed (non-IID), together with partial client participation, can cause shared representations to vary across communication rounds, hindering knowledge transfer. Existing methods mainly address heterogeneity through model personalization or historical knowledge transfer, while sample-level temporal representation changes remain underexplored. We propose FedEAGD, a trajectory-guided PFL framework that uses a client-specific exponential moving average (EMA) teacher to summarize shared-model history. The discrepancy between each sample's current and historical shared representations quantifies temporal drift and adaptively determines the strength of historical distillation. Progressive gated residual fusion (PGRF) introduces personalized information according to a stage-wise schedule. Representation anchoring and residual decoupling regularize this process, while post-aggregation calibration and late-stage server smoothing coordinate local adaptation with global model updates. Only the shared feature extractor is communicated, while personalized components remain local. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and DomainNet evaluate FedEAGD under varying data heterogeneity, client participation rates, and federation sizes. On CIFAR-100 with a Dirichlet concentration parameter of $\alpha=0.1$, FedEAGD achieves 63.05\% accuracy, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 5.96 percentage points.
papers.venue: Research Square

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Of Things (Aiot): A Review Of Architectures, Learning Techniques And Applications Of Iot With AI
papers.abstract: Abstract—The Internet of Things (IoT) connects sensors, cameras, smartphones and machines to the internet so that they can collect and exchange data, while Artificial Intelligence (AI) analyses that data to recognize patterns and make decisions. Their combination, often called the Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT), enables systems that monitor, control and manage activities with minimal human involvement. This paper reviews AIoT from the perspectives of architecture, intelligence and application. It explains layered IoT architectures, communication protocols and context-aware computing, then surveys machine learning and deep learning for IoT data analytics, including streaming analytics, anomaly detection and edge-based inference, as well as federated learning for privacy. Applications in smart homes, smart cities, healthcare, agriculture and industrial IoT are reviewed. Security threats such as large IoT botnets are discussed as a key concern. A five-layer AIoT architecture comprising perception, connectivity, edge intelligence, cloud analytics and application layers is proposed, along with research gaps, objectives, a comparison of learning approaches and an analysis of challenges in interoperability, energy, privacy and security. The review concludes that AIoT can greatly improve automation, accuracy and productivity when built with security and privacy in mind.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Robust and Communication-Efficient Personalized Federated Learning for False Power Consumption Detection in Heterogeneous Smart Grids
papers.abstract: Detecting false power consumption data injection (FDI) attacks requires utilities to collaborate without sharing consumers’ raw data. Federated learning (FL) enables such collaboration. However, conventional FL exchanges complete models in every round and loses accuracy when the utilities’ data are not independent and identically distributed (non-IID). It also produces a shared detector that a malicious participant can exploit to craft evasion attacks. This paper proposes a personalized federated learning (PFL) approach in which utilities jointly train convolutional feature-extraction layers while keeping their classification layers local. Adversarial examples are incorporated into local training to improve resistance to evasion. The approach requires a single model per utility and no public dataset at the server. We evaluate it on the Ausgrid and Irish Smart Energy Trial datasets, with utilities that differ in both consumption patterns and attack characteristics. Compared with conventional FL, the proposed approach reduces the data exchanged per round and utility from 306.63 KB to 3.50 KB. With adversarial training, it improves accuracy by up to 23.75 and 29.82 percentage points on Ausgrid and ISET, respectively, and lowers the success rates of the evaluated FGSM and BIM attacks. These results show that personalization can ease the accuracy–robustness trade-off while substantially reducing communication costs.
papers.venue: Energies

papers.title: Explainable AI-based disease diagnostics using real-time plasmonic biosensor data and blockchain technology
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper proposes a secure and decentralized framework for biomedical diagnostics using plasmonic biosensor data by integrating federated learning, blockchain, post-quantum cryptography, meta-learning, and explainable AI (XAI). The proposed system addresses key limitations of centralized healthcare models, including data privacy risks, vulnerability to cyberattacks, and lack of transparency. A federated meta-learning approach is employed to improve model adaptability and accuracy across heterogeneous institutional datasets, while blockchain ensures secure data sharing, auditability, and resistance to model poisoning attacks. Additionally, a post-quantum cryptographic layer is incorporated to enhance long-term data security against emerging quantum threats. Experimental results demonstrate improved diagnostic accuracy, enhanced security, and scalable performance with acceptable latency overhead. The findings highlight the effectiveness of the proposed framework in enabling secure, collaborative, and trustworthy AI-driven healthcare systems.
papers.venue: Scientific Reports

papers.title: Collaborative localization of WGAN-GP and edge federated learning for single-phase grounding faults in distribution networks
papers.abstract: Abstract With the rapid development of new power systems, medium- and low-voltage distribution networks have become increasingly complex. This leads to low accuracy and poor generalization in traditional localization methods, which cannot meet the requirements for rapid self-healing and safe operation in intelligent distribution networks. To overcome the drawbacks of existing fault localization techniques—such as limited fault data, inadequate extraction of temporal information, multi-source data heterogeneity, and the need for lightweight models—a novel collaborative fault localization approach based on Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network with Gradient Penalty and edge federated learning is proposed. The improved Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network is used to generate high-quality fault samples and extract temporal features. Adaptive weighting and a region-weighted module are introduced into the Federated Averaging algorithm to improve global aggregation accuracy. This study utilizes the IEEE 123 simulation dataset and the on-site measured dataset as verification data, which consist of over 10,000 simulation electrical samples and 326 real single-phase grounding fault samples, respectively. According to the results, the Fréchet Inception Distance is 12.36 for fault sample generation, while the Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio reaches 27.94 dB. The proposed method achieves a localization accuracy of 94.85%. In cases of high resistance, arc faults, load variation, and noise, the localization accuracies reach 82.70%, 84.06%, 89.37%, and 82.25%, respectively. The proposed model also performs better than existing methods in terms of parameter size, inference time, and bandwidth consumption. The proposed model outperforms existing methods in terms of fault sample generation, localization accuracy, anti-interference capability, and lightweight performance. Moreover, it does not require the uploading of raw measurement data, thereby balancing data privacy protection with the deployment capability of edge terminals. It is highly suitable for complex on-site operating conditions and provides technical support for rapid and accurate fault localization, on-site troubleshooting, and self-healing in medium- and low-voltage distribution networks.
papers.venue: Discover Applied Sciences

papers.title: Federated Learning: Envisioning a Pathway to More Accessible and Equitable Cleft Care
papers.abstract: Cleft lip and palate represents the most common congenital craniofacial anomaly worldwide, with low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) bearing nearly 84% of the global disease burden. Despite the instrumental role of global nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) in expanding access to cleft care across LMICs, patient databases and healthcare infrastructure remain highly fragmented across centers and organizations. Recent advances in machine learning and deep learning hold considerable promise for improving cleft care through data-driven clinical decision-making. However, privacy regulations present significant barriers to the centralized aggregation of patient data required to train robust artificial intelligence models. Federated learning (FL) offers a potential solution by enabling multiple institutions to train a shared global model without transferring raw patient data to a central server. Through mechanisms such as federated averaging, differential privacy, and homomorphic encryption, FL substantially mitigates privacy risks while producing models that perform comparably to models trained on centralized pool data. Existing implementations, most notably the Federated Tumor Segmentation initiative spanning 71 institutions across 6 continents, demonstrate the feasibility of this approach in complex healthcare settings. This narrative review proposes a potential framework for applying FL to global cleft care, outlining how existing organizational infrastructure established by prominent cleft NGOs can provide a foundation for a federated network. Five key stakeholder categories: global cleft NGOs, academic medical centers, technology partners, funding entities, and local cleft centers have been identified as essential to realizing this vision. Numerous challenges and barriers have also been identified before realizing this endeavor.
papers.venue: The Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Journal

papers.title: Quantum AI for road safety and beyond: A scoping review of applications in intelligent transportation systems
papers.abstract: Background Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) increasingly draw on artificial intelligence for prediction, classification, and control tasks. Quantum computing and quantum machine learning (QML) have emerged as candidate tools, though current hardware remains in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. Objective This review maps the literature applying quantum or quantum-inspired AI to ITS, with attention to road-safety applications. Methods A PRISMA-ScR-adapted scoping review searched five databases (Web of Science, ScienceDirect, arXiv, Scopus, IEEE Xplore). Screening was conducted jointly by the review author and a co-author against structured eligibility criteria; an independent, criteria-blind AI-assisted second pass assessed reliability (substantial agreement, kappa = 0.77). From 271 records identified, 50 were synthesized: 41 primary studies and 9 background reviews. A five-item quality checklist was applied to the 15 primary studies with confirmed full-text access. Results The 41 primary studies span five application themes, led by collision/accident detection and avoidance (22 studies), ahead of traffic-state forecasting, ITS operations, electric-vehicle systems, and network security. Reported methods include quantum neural networks, support vector machines, variational circuits, game theory, annealing/QAOA, and federated learning. Quantum and hybrid approaches outperformed classical baselines on structured, interaction-heavy tasks using markedly fewer parameters, though fixed quantum-kernel methods showed recurring overfitting; most studies ran on simulators rather than physical hardware. Conclusion Quantum AI for ITS is a young, rapidly growing field (mostly 2024–2026) in which road safety is the largest application cluster. Reported advantage centers on parameter efficiency, not raw accuracy. Key gaps include near-absent physical-hardware validation, standardized benchmarks, and fully independent dual screening.
papers.venue: Transportation Research Interdisciplinary Perspectives

papers.title: A Comprehensive Framework for Targeted Transfer Learning: Privacy-Preserving, Secure, and Efficient Domain Adaptation
papers.abstract: Machine learning models deployed in tactical environments rely on high-quality labeled datasets, which are often challenging, expensive, and time-consuming to obtain. In addition, formal techniques for assuring model performance under dynamic conditions remain limited. Transfer learning has emerged as a promising solution, but its effectiveness is limited by domain coverage and similarity between source and target datasets. This dissertation presents a comprehensive, modelagnostic Targeted Transfer Learning (TTL) framework that addresses transferability challenges between domains with minimal data, demonstrating how targeted sample selection improves adaptation across image classification, network security, and privacy-preserving collaborative settings. First, we develop the TTL framework for scenarios where direct access to datasets is restricted. This metadata-driven approach applies to a combinatorial coverage method to estimate domain correlation and guide sample selection. Evaluation on a satellite imagery dataset showed that targeted selection outperformed zero-shot transfer and random selection while conserving computational resources. Second, we investigate the TTL framework in settings where both datasets are directly available. This data-driven approach uses optimal transport distance to quantify distributional differences and guide selection of informative target samples. Validation across a broad set of benchmark image classification datasets demonstrated consistent improvements over conventional transfer learning. Third, we address network malware classification through Selective Targeted Transfer Learning (STTL), projecting source and target traffic data into a shared latent feature space and selecting relevant samples using a Kullback–Leibler divergence-based similarity measure. Experimental results across multiple attack-family scenarios showed that STTL achieved higher performance than conventional transfer learning, confirming that targeted selection generalizes across data types and domains. Finally, we extend the TTL framework through two decentralized privacy-preserving mechanisms. In a federated learning setting, clients share only summary statistics, and a server computes aggregation weights that enable knowledge transfer without exposing local data. In a blockchain-based setting, cryptographic verification secures model weights throughout the transfer process, while a smart-contract mechanism rewards high-quality participation. Both mechanisms consistently outperformed non-targeted baselines while preserving data confidentiality and integrity. This research establishes targeted transfer learning as a practical framework that enables machine learning models to adapt reliably, securely, and efficiently across image classification, network security, and distributed collaborative environments.
papers.venue: Old Dominion University

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Edge AI with Graph Transformer for Secure Real-Time Smart Engineering Education in Dense Urban Areas
papers.abstract: Engineering education is becoming more advanced in rapidly expanding urban centers with smart connected classrooms, laboratories, wireless networks, indoor environment sensors, and digital learning platform technologies. This establishes three major challenges and requires real-time educational analytics, individual campus data protection, and a robust, deployable system capable of withstanding cyber risks, heavy congestion & heterogeneous edge hardware. However, the majority of existing literature on edge analytics and federated learning or graph-based models, or security monitoring , addresses them individually with limited attention to unifying real-time laurence of secure architectures supporting multi-buildings on engineering campuses. This paper proposes a privacy-preserving edge-graph transformer (PP-EGT) for secure real-time smart engineering education in dense urban environments. The model integrates local anonymization, temporal encoding, dynamic campus graph construction, graph-transformer reasoning, and federated secure aggregation. It jointly predicts a five-class zone state, a continuous Learning Readiness Index (LRI), and a cyber-physical incident probability using multimodal edge features from environmental, network, pedagogical, and security domains. A literature-grounded simulation benchmark representing 48 zones across six campus buildings was constructed over 12 weeks with 5 min sampling. Across five random seeds, PP-EGT achieved 91.89% macro-F1, 96.45% AUROC for incident detection, and 3.43 LRI MAE. Compared with the strongest baseline, ST-Transformer, PP-EGT improved macro-F1 by 1.45 points, reduced p95 latency from 49.59 ms to 44.02 ms, and decreased privacy-leakage AUC from 69.19% to 53.83%. Its novelty lies in jointly optimizing learning analytics, cyber-physical security, privacy, and edge deployment constraints.

papers.title: Securing the post-quantum era: a review of quantum computing, blockchain and artificial intelligence for cybersecurity
papers.abstract: Three technologies are changing what cybersecurity has to defend and what it can defend with. A large fault-tolerant quantum computer would break the public-key cryptography that protects most networks. Blockchains offer tamper-evident records without a central authority, yet they rest on the same threatened signatures. Artificial intelligence (AI) detects attacks at a speed analysts cannot match, and it also gives attackers new tools and new targets. This narrative review covers 150 sources on the three technologies and on their pairwise combinations. It summarizes the quantum threat and the resource estimates behind it, the post-quantum standards published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in 2024, quantum key distribution, the attack surface of blockchains, and the use and abuse of machine learning in security. It then examines where the technologies meet: post-quantum ledgers, blockchain-coordinated federated learning, and quantum machine learning. Four findings follow. Migration to post-quantum cryptography is the only one of these changes with a deadline set by an adversary, so it should come first. Blockchains need the same migration and are harder to migrate than client-server systems. AI-based detection has value only when its training data, models and outputs are themselves protected. Quantum machine learning has no demonstrated security advantage yet. The review proposes a five-layer reference architecture, a procedure for ranking systems for cryptographic migration, and a list of open problems, with attention to organizations that have small security teams and limited budgets.

papers.title: Toward Federated Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models: Progress, Challenges, and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been extensively used in downstream tasks, and the successful implementation of such tasks typically involves fine-tuning on domain-specific or user-specific data. As these data are generally not centralized but rather distributed among clients, federated learning (FL) of LLMs, also known as FedLLM, has emerged as a promising paradigm to decentralize LLM adaptation. Nevertheless, it is still challenging to directly apply traditional FL to LLM fine-tuning due to the amplification of model scale, client heterogeneity, communication cost, and privacy risks. This survey offers an overview of FedLLM fine-tuning from methodological and evaluation aspects. This paper first presents the fundamentals of FL, LLM fine-tuning, and their combination. Then this paper categorizes representative works into three groups: efficiency, heterogeneity and personalization, and privacy and security. In addition, this paper summarizes commonly used datasets and evaluation benchmarks to show how existing methods are evaluated under different client partitions and task settings. Finally, according to the given review, this paper identifies future directions such as resource-adaptive collaboration, split federated fine-tuning, continual personalization, and privacy-preserving safety alignment. All things considered, this survey takes FedLLM fine-tuning as its main point of attention, which gives a well-structured reference for researchers and practitioners to get to know about this field and find out potential research paths.
papers.venue: Applied and Computational Engineering

papers.title: Multi-Task Learning Framework for Reservoir Water Temperature Field Prediction Using Modal Decomposition and Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Reservoir thermal stratification affects withdrawal temperatures and downstream aquatic ecosystems, making water temperature prediction important for sustainable reservoir operation. However, predicting two-dimensional water temperature fields across different operating conditions remains challenging. This study proposes a framework integrating proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), mutual information, dual-channel BiLSTM, bidirectional residual cross-attention, multi-task learning, and personalized federated learning. POD reduces field dimensionality, while multi-task regression heads directly predict modal coefficients for different forecast days. To account for differences among operating conditions, feature-extraction networks remain local, and only regression-network parameters are aggregated. Experiments were conducted using EFDC-simulated temperature fields from 75 operating conditions of Wudongde Reservoir. The model achieved MAE and RMSE values of 0.120 °C and 0.183 °C for 2-day forecasts and 0.314 °C and 0.449 °C for 10-day forecasts, respectively. Compared with full-model aggregation, theoretical parameter communication was reduced by 96.29%, with slightly higher prediction errors. The predicted temperature fields may support the assessment of selective-withdrawal conditions and downstream ecological temperature requirements, contributing to sustainable reservoir management.

papers.title: Horizons in Computer Science Research. Volume 28
papers.abstract: This volume includes eight chapters that detail horizons in computer science research. Chapter 1 provides a comprehensive review of Federated Learning (FL), Continual Learning (CL), and Federated Continual Learning (FCL) methodologies within the robotics domain. Chapter 2 proposes the Dignity-Centered Digital Workplace Framework (DC-DWF), an integrated governance framework combining Ethical AI Governance, Responsible People Analytics, and Inclusive Innovation to protect human dignity in AI-enabled workplaces. Chapter 3 proposes a new Dynamic Optimized Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based load-balancing approach to provide accurate and reliable cloud platforms. Chapter 4 addresses the innovation in implementing mobile robotic systems (MRS) operating in ground-based and aerial environments for industrial applications and emergency response society. Chapter 5 first provides an in-depth analysis of how data complexity factors exacerbate the challenges of imbalanced learning, then critically examines the three main mitigation strategies, evaluates their practical trade-offs, and outlines key directions for future research. Chapter 6 describes the use of GenAI as an excellent catalyst that makes the application of UDL easy and efficient. Chapter 7 discusses the transformation of the drug discovery process in the pharmaceutical industry upon the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Finally, Chapter 8 provides a comprehensive guide to international cyber protection, highlighting the critical role of cybersecurity in our interconnected world.

papers.title: FedDeepRiskNet-Audit: Privacy and attack-aware federated learning for clinical time series analysis
papers.abstract: Background Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative clinical modeling without centralizing sensitive patient records. However, shared model information may expose private data, while malicious client contributions can compromise model integrity. Combining privacy protection, attack-aware screening, and encrypted aggregation also introduces important participation and communication trade-offs. Objective This study proposes FedDeepRiskNet-Audit, a privacy and attack-aware FL framework for clinical time-series analysis that integrates privacy accounting, protected client screening, and encrypted aggregation within an auditable architecture. Methods FedDeepRiskNet-Audit combines a convolutional neural network-long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) predictor with record-level differential privacy (DP) using Rényi differential privacy accounting, Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) homomorphic encryption, protected update sketches, common-mask sparsification, and an Adaptive Privacy and Byzantine-Resilience Scheduler (APBS). Evaluation using the PhysioNet/Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2012 dataset separately examined predictive discrimination, privacy-budget accumulation, attack behavior, scheduler performance, and analytical communication overhead. The centralized predictive benchmark and privacy-accounting experiments were evaluated over ten runs. Results The centralized CNN-LSTM benchmark achieved a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.781 (95% CI: 0.773–0.790) and an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.380 (95% CI: 0.363–0.396), compared with a mortality prevalence of 0.14. In the 100-round privacy-accounting simulation, the Audit policy remained within ε = 3 at δ = 10 −5 , while accepting approximately 30 of 400 planned client-rounds; unconstrained DP-FedAvg accepted all 400 and reached ε ≈ 90. Analytical communication was 7.01 MiB per round, representing a 74.8% reduction relative to CKKS-FedAvg (27.84 MiB). In a separate scheduler ablation, full APBS produced a worst-client ε of approximately 2.3 with an executed client-round fraction of 0.60. Conclusion FedDeepRiskNet-Audit provides an integrated framework for examining the interactions among privacy accounting, attack-aware client screening, encrypted aggregation, and communication efficiency in clinical FL. The results demonstrate explicit privacy-participation and encrypted-communication trade-offs, rather than establishing end-to-end clinical superiority or universal resistance to adaptive attacks. Further end-to-end and multi-institutional validation is required before clinical deployment.
papers.venue: Technology and Health Care

papers.title: TrustFL-Chain: lightweight reputation-aware defense with tamper-evident auditing for non-IID federated learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model without collecting clients’ raw data, but a server must still decide what to do with unreliable updates. Honest clients with different data can look unusual too. We study TrustFL-Chain, a lightweight prototype that scores updates, maintains recoverable client reputation, and writes aggregation decisions to a 256-bit Secure Hash Algorithm (SHA-256)-linked audit log. It does not require a trusted server dataset. Across 440 validated jobs, we test five Fashion-MNIST seeds, independent and identically distributed (IID) and non-IID partitions, six attacks, parameter sensitivity, unequal client sizes, and an exploratory Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR)-10 supplement. With Dirichlet α = 0.5 and 20% malicious clients, final-five-round accuracy exceeds Trimmed Mean by 6.18 percentage points under Gaussian noise. Under inner-product manipulation (IPM), TrustFL-Chain reaches 0.6457 accuracy against 0.3314 for the strongest observed baseline. Its 1.21-point mean lead over Cosine under sign flipping has a paired interval that crosses zero. Uniform averaging remains more accurate under the evaluated A Little Is Enough (ALIE)-style attack. In these experiments, reputation weighting helps most when manipulated updates leave a detectable signal.

papers.title: One-Shot Federated Graph Learning via High-Fidelity Proxies and Transferability-Guided Collaboration
papers.abstract: One-shot Federated Graph Learning (OFGL) has emerged as a communication-efficient paradigm for federated graph learning under strict bandwidth constraints, compressing collaboration into a single transmission round. Nevertheless, this extreme setting suffers from a fundamental Single-Transmission Bottleneck, which limits both the quality and utility of exchanged knowledge. First, while existing methods attempt to distill private graphs into shareable proxies, their aggressive one-shot compression inherently triggers a fidelity crisis. This compression distorts local graph topology and semantics across clients, leading to externalized knowledge underexpression. Second, although the server aggregates these proxies to update global models, current integration schemes suffer from transferability agnosticism. The server cannot reliably identify cross-client collaboration potential, thus resulting in integrated knowledge underutilization. To tackle these dual challenges, we propose FedHFT, an effective One-Shot Personalized Federated Graph Learning (OPFGL) framework that addresses this bottleneck from two perspectives, namely High-Fidelity Knowledge Externalization and Transferability-Ware Knowledge Integration. We use Fidelity-Driven Proxy Refinement to preserve client-side knowledge fidelity, and Transferability-Steered Personalized Collaboration to enable adaptive server-side collaboration. The superiority of FedHFT is validated through extensive experiments on both homophilic and heterophilic graphs. The code is available at https://github.com/Jumpy-Juice/FedHFT.

papers.title: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.

papers.title: Byzantine-Robust Muon: Resilient Momentum Orthogonalization for Distributed Learning
papers.abstract: Optimization methods, including the Muon optimizer based on the Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO) and momentum orthogonalization, have shown strong empirical performance in large-scale and distributed learning, yet their robustness to adversarial behavior and data heterogeneity is not well understood. We study these methods within a unified first-order trust-region framework and analyze Muon-based updates with robust aggregation for Byzantine-robust distributed and federated learning. Our analysis does not rely on the i.i.d. assumption and introduces a non-Euclidean notion of heterogeneity consistent with the trust-region geometry. Under this framework, we establish convergence guarantees for both general non-convex and star-convex objectives. Our results provide a theoretical characterization of Byzantine-robust Muon-based optimization, with an additive heterogeneity error floor consistent with known impossibility results, under explicit aggregation assumptions. Under an explicit additive oracle-error condition, the guarantees also cover inexact orthogonalization, with the non-convex Byzantine terms in the bound's numerator unchanged but a smaller progress denominator. In simulated federated training with ResNet-18 and ViT-Tiny on CIFAR-10, additional image benchmarks, and a 38M-parameter byte-level language model on TinyStories, the tested Muon configuration attains higher attacked accuracy (lower perplexity) than the tested SGD and normalized-SGD configurations, and than sign updates on CIFAR-10. Fixed-honest controls further show a substantial RFA advantage over averaging under a bounded RFA-query attack, higher attacked accuracy for Muon-NS than tensorwise Euclidean normalization from shared checkpoints, and lower held-out TinyStories perplexity than a tuned AdamW baseline.

papers.title: Harnessing Vision-Language Models for Federated Unsupervised Visual Recognition
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a promising research paradigm that enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without data sharing. To handle unlabeled data in local clients, existing unsupervised FL research has primarily focused on tasks like clustering and self-supervised representation learning, leaving the critical problem of unsupervised visual recognition largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce FedUR, the first framework designed for unsupervised recognition by leveraging the zero-shot capabilities of pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP. Specifically, FedUR addresses data heterogeneity through a pseudo-labeling mechanism with a class-aware data selection strategy. This strategy first estimates a global pseudo-label distribution, then allocates pseudo-labeled data to clients accordingly. To handle the uncertainty of conventional positive pseudo-labels, FedUR further incorporates class weights and a negative pseudo-labeling strategy. Furthermore, FedUR proposes a personalized prompt aggregation protocol where general visual prompts are aggregated on the server, and personalized text prompts encoding local knowledge are retained on clients. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedUR consistently outperforms baseline methods under both label-level and feature-level distribution shifts. We believe this work paves the way for further advances in federated unsupervised recognition. Code will be available at {github.com/tim-learn/FedUR/}}.

papers.title: Wireless AI Networks: Co-Adapting Communication Resources and Distributed Intelligence
papers.abstract: Distributed artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on wireless networks, where communication and computing resources shape how AI tasks are configured and executed. However, resource availability alone does not determine how effectively these tasks can be supported, since different information selections and transmission strategies may yield different AI performance under the same resource constraints. To address this challenge, this article presents Wireless AI Networks as a unified design perspective for bidirectional adaptation between wireless communication and distributed intelligence. Specifically, an AI-executable resource budget characterizes candidate AI configurations, while task-level information value guides their selection and wireless resource allocation. Building on these principles, a wireless-AI co-adaptation framework coordinates resource abstraction, joint configuration and allocation, and execution feedback. Two complementary experiments illustrate this perspective: update selection and statistical correction improve federated learning under identical model-update payload budgets, while sensitivity-aware power allocation reduces model accuracy degradation under the same average transmit-power constraint. Together, these results highlight the importance of coordinating resource feasibility and task-level information value in distributed AI execution.

papers.title: Breaking the $\sqrt{d}$ Communication Barrier in Federated Sampling with Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: This work proposes the Adaptive Federated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (AFHMC) for Bayesian federated learning (FL) tasks. The prior work on HMC applications for FL achieves $O(\sqrt{d}/ε)$ communication cost under log-convex distributions, already demonstrating its advantage over the Langevin dynamic-based counterpart. Based on a refined analysis, this paper further reveals the benefit of HMC for the FL regime by incorporating a control mechanism for local node shifts. We prove that AFHMC at most requires $O(\{d/ε^2\}^{1/3})$ communication cost up to a logarithmic term, which is significantly better than the existing results. Moreover, the proposed method adapts to client heterogeneity. Under low-heterogeneity settings (i.e., the target sampling precision $ε^2$ is higher than the heterogeneity level), the communication rate of AFHMC can be as good as $O(\log(d/ε^2))$, resembling the communication costs for FL optimization tools. To the best of our knowledge, this provides the first logarithmic communication complexity result for federated sampling, even though it requires low heterogeneity. Numerically, we also justify AFHMC's advantage under the low-heterogeneity regime. Our code is available at https://github.com/laaaarrywang/Adaptive-Federated-HMC

papers.title: Transfer-Aware Anomaly Detection for Sustainable AIoT-Enabled Water Infrastructures: A Systematic Review of Graph-Based Models, Tabular Foundation Models, and Privacy-Preserving Adaptation
papers.abstract: Early detection of leaks, bursts, process faults, and cyber-physical attacks is a direct lever for the sustainable management of water infrastructures: it reduces non-revenue water, the energy spent on treating and pumping lost water, and service interruptions (Sustainable Development Goal 6). Anomaly detectors for water distribution networks (WDNs) and wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are increasingly deployed through Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) architectures, yet a detector that performs well on one system cannot be assumed to transfer to another with a different topology, sensor layout, demand pattern, and label availability. This systematic review examines the literature through this transfer problem, with graph neural networks (GNNs) as topology-aware models, tabular foundation models (TFMs; in the retrieved evidence, the TabPFN family) as candidate local screeners, federated learning as privacy-preserving adaptation, and digital twins and explainable artificial intelligence as validation and trust layers. It follows PRISMA 2020 and is registered retrospectively in the Open Science Framework (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/D7RXU). Peer-reviewed articles, theses, and preprints in English or Spanish were identified through modular block searches (Google Scholar, publisher sites, three Spanish repositories), author-supplied sources, and citation chasing, verified against primary records on 6–7 September 2026, screened in two stages, coded with a predefined framework, appraised with a six-item checklist, and synthesized descriptively because tasks, datasets, and metrics are not commensurable. The corpus comprises 150 unique works: 76 water-specific experimental studies, 21 benchmark or testbed studies, and 53 method, review, or contextual works. Graph-based approaches have the stronger water-specific evidence for topology-dependent tasks in WDNs, whereas TabPFN-family TFMs rest on general tabular-learning evidence and one water-adjacent prediction study, with no validated water anomaly-detection use. Only 6 of the 76 experimental studies evaluate an explicit transfer mechanism, federated evidence is limited to one water study, and no study reports an operator evaluation of explanations. The review contributes a transfer taxonomy with study counts, an evidence-class scheme, a gap map of demonstrated and proposed components on a transfer-aware AIoT layout, and an evaluation agenda based on source–target protocols, and identifies the evidence utilities need before transferable detectors can support sustainable operation at scale.
papers.venue: Sustainability

papers.title: FedHyperM: modality-sensitive federated hypergraph learning for heterogeneous multimodal edge intelligence
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables edge devices to collaboratively train models in edge–cloud environments without sharing raw sensor data. In practical edge deployments, however, devices often have access to different subsets of modalities due to hardware heterogeneity, varying sensing conditions, or temporary sensor failures. Such modality heterogeneity makes conventional federated aggregation unreliable, as parameters learned from different modalities evidence may not be directly comparable. Meanwhile, this setting also raises privacy concerns, since image, depth, and signal data may reveal sensitive user or environmental information. To address these challenges, we propose FedHyperM, a privacy-preserving federated multimodal learning framework for edge devices. FedHyperM performs hypergraph-based multimodal prediction by treating modality-specific features as nodes and adaptively constructing hyperedges to capture high-order correlations among multimodal features. On the cloud server, FedHyperM further introduces modality-sensitive aggregation (MSA), which uses the minimum edit distance (MinED) between available modality names to weight uploaded hypergraph learning parameters during aggregation. Experiments on the UR-FALL dataset under different modality existence rate (MER) settings demonstrate that FedHyperM consistently outperforms representative federated multimodal baselines, including FedAvg, FedCor, FedProx, AutoFed, and FedInMM. Compared with the five baselines, FedHyperM improves average accuracy by 3.64% to 22.33% and average F1 score by 2.91% to 26.82%.

papers.title: AI-driven approaches for food risk assessment: current advances and future trends
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool to support food risk assessment and broader food safety activities in response to the growing complexity of global food supply chains, emerging foodborne hazards, and evolving food fraud practices. Unlike previous reviews that have largely focused on individual AI technologies or specific applications, this review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), transformer-based models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), multimodal learning, and emerging AI paradigms within a unified framework relevant to food risk assessment and food safety decision-making. The review examines their applications in hazard identification, contamination detection, predictive microbiology, risk classification, food fraud detection, surveillance, traceability, and decision-support systems. Particular attention is given to the strengths, limitations, interpretability, validation requirements, and implementation challenges associated with different AI approaches. The integration of AI with multimodal data sources, Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, spectroscopy, biosensors, and advanced analytical platforms is also discussed as a means to improve risk prediction, monitoring, and early-warning capabilities. Key challenges include data quality and availability, model generalizability, limited external validation, computational requirements, interpretability, and regulatory acceptance. Emerging developments, including foundation models, federated learning, blockchain, digital twins, edge AI, and multimodal frameworks, are highlighted as promising directions for future research. Overall, this review provides a critical comparative framework for understanding the evolving role of AI in food risk assessment and related food safety applications, while identifying key scientific, technical, and regulatory priorities for future development and implementation. papers.title: SEMCOMIIOT DELIVERABLE D4.2: STUDY AND EXPERIMENTATION ON SEMANTIC-AWARE TRANSMISSION ASPECTS
papers.abstract: This report describes how SemComIIoT can be be tested. It is written to be read on its own: the modelthat is tested is summarised in Chapter 3, and has been addressed in D4.1 [1]. D4.1 studied which decentralisedlearning approaches and which degrees of decentralisation can support Semantic communication (SemCom)in IIoT, and combined them in one model with two decisions: the degree of decentralisation of training perepoch, and, for each message, the serving Edge node and the place of encoding. D4.1 states three hypotheses(H1–H3) and ends with eight evaluation needs (N1-N8) that must be met before the model can be validated.D4.2 prepares that validation. It does not propose a new model. It analyses the simulators, emulators,frameworks, testbeds and applications that exist and are suitable to test SemComIIoT, explains what each isfor, and assesses how well each covers the eight needs: semantic quality, wireless and protocol behaviour,mobility, Edge-Cloud placement and offloading, decentralised learning, deterministic latency, energy, andknowledge-base consistency.The main finding is that no single tool, and no existing combination of tools, covers these needstogether. Link-level libraries (for example, Sionna) allow learning semantic codecs over realistic channels;network simulators (ns-3, OMNeT++) represent protocols, mobility and deterministic networking, but notsemantic models; Edge and fog simulators, emulators and testbeds represent placement, offloading and energy;and federated-learning frameworks represent training. The open work is at the interfaces between these tools.We identify five gaps: semantic quality and network behaviour are not integrated; learning, mobility andplacement are not treated together; knowledge-base consistency is not supported by any tool; the timingand energy of semantic inference on constrained devices are only approximated; and there is no commonbenchmark.The report therefore proposes a toolchain of four coupled layers (semantic codec, network, learning,Edge-Cloud testbed) with ns-3 as its basis. ns-3 is chosen because it combines wireless, mobility, deterministic-networking and radio-energy models with interfaces for AI/ML code and with an emulation mode in whichreal hosts and containers take part in the simulated network. An end-to-end design maps the federated-edgearchitecture onto ns-3, with the two decisions of the model realised per message and per epoch, and withthree stages of increasing realism: trace-driven, online-coupled and emulated. Seven experiments (E1-E7)are described, each with an ns-3 topology, the packages needed, baselines, metrics and output. They test thethree hypotheses and supply the parameters of the model. The experiments are planned and have not yetbeen executed, and the assessment of the tools is based on their documentation and on the literature, not onhands-on testing.

papers.title: SecAgg++: A Post-Quantum Privacy Perserving Federated Learning Protocol
papers.abstract: Secure aggregation is a fundamental building block for privacy-preserving federated learning, yet most existing masking-based secure aggregation protocols do not provide post-quantum security. In this work, we present SecAgg++, a masking-based post-quantum secure aggregation protocol for the single-server setting. SecAgg++ integrates post-quantum cryptographic primitives while preserving the communication and computational efficiency of classical frameworks such as SecAgg and SecAgg+, and supports client dropout handling through an efficient recovery procedure.

papers.title: Privacy-preserving Distributed Data Mining: Techniques, Challenges, Applications and Future Research Directions
papers.abstract: Distributed data mining has become central to extracting knowledge from data held by institutions, devices and organisations that cannot legitimately or safely pool their records. Yet keeping raw data at source does not, by itself, ensure privacy: intermediate statistics, gradients, identifiers, query patterns and final models can disclose information, while controls that prevent disclosure may weaken analytical validity or the detection of malicious participants. This critical narrative review evaluates the development of privacy-preserving distributed data mining from partition-aware secure computation to federated learning, differential privacy, protected record linkage and hybrid architectures. Scholarly literature was selected through topic-specific searches of accessible bibliographic resources, reference tracing and verification against publication and digital-object-identifier records, with an emphasis on peer-reviewed methodological, empirical and review evidence. The synthesis distinguishes cryptographic input confidentiality, statistical protection of released outputs and operational governance, showing why these objectives cannot be treated as interchangeable. Evidence supports the feasibility of selected secure aggregation, multiparty computation and cross-institutional modelling workflows, but performance and privacy claims depend materially on adversarial assumptions, participant numbers, data topology, privacy accounting, model access and deployment conditions. Demonstrations of gradient reconstruction and membership inference establish credible attack surfaces, whereas more recent experimental evidence shows that exploitability is conditional rather than uniform. Healthcare collaborations provide instructive feasibility evidence, but do not establish universal effectiveness, regulatory compliance or immunity from model leakage. Five evidence-mapping tables integrate architectural distinctions, protective mechanisms, adversarial findings, application maturity and research priorities. The review argues for evaluation based on the entire information-release lifecycle, joint testing of confidentiality, integrity and utility, and transparent reporting of threats, costs and residual risks. Future progress depends less on promoting a single technique than on auditable combinations whose guarantees remain meaningful under heterogeneous data, collusion, repeated analysis and institutional constraints.

papers.title: AOSI-RFC-0001: The AI Open Systems Interconnection (AOSI) Reference Model: A 7-Layer Stack for Generative AI Execution
papers.abstract: AOSI-RFC-0001 specifies the AI Open Systems Interconnection (AOSI) Reference Model, a seven-layer conceptual stack for generative AI execution: L1 Physical Infrastructure, L2 Framework & Runtime, L3 Model & Weight Architecture, L4 Inference & Serving, L5 Retrieval & Knowledge (RAG), L6 Orchestration & Gateway and L7 Application. For each layer it defines scope, components, the data-state transformation performed (JSON Payload → Enriched Prompt → Vector Chunks → Batched Tensors → Hidden States → Tensor IR → Silicon Voltages), interfaces, observability signals and failure modes, together with a layer-isolation Diagnostic & Troubleshooting Matrix, per-layer security considerations and a roadmap for Layer 8 (Agentic Workflows), Layer 9 (Distributed Inference / Federated Learning) and cross-layer Global Optimization. Version 1.2.1 is a Final Draft for RFC, released as a Proposed Standard for public comment. Author and Conceptual Architect: Divyendu Bhatt.
