papers.title: FusionNet Lite: Compact Federated Deep Learning for Predictive Maintenance under Label Heterogeneity and Temporal Generalization
papers.abstract: Abstract Federated learning (FL) supports collaborative predictive maintenance (PdM), but compactness alone does not establish reliable failure detection or consistent explanations. We evaluate FusionNet~Lite, a 1,420-parameter feature-axis classifier, against four lightweight baselines under centralized training and Federated Averaging (FedAvg). Ten matched core seeds and validation-selected checkpoints are used with stratified AI4I~2020 partitions and a fixed-row chronological MetroPT3 holdout. Separate studies extend the three-client core to ten clients and examine architectural, optimization and participation sensitivities. On MetroPT3, FedAvg FusionNet~Lite achieves area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) $0.9351\pm0.0462$ and area under the precision--recall curve (AUPRC) $0.2197\pm0.1971$, expressed as mean and sample standard deviation. Switching from original-grid validation-F$_1$ to expanded-grid validation-F$_2$ selection changes mean test F$_2$ from $0.0423\pm0.0995$ to $0.1566\pm0.2044$, retaining substantial variability. FusionNet~Lite has the smallest parameter count and lowest fixed-batch parameter--latency index among the five core architectures, while predictive rankings depend on dataset and configuration. Paired, class-specific Integrated Gradients (IG) comparisons across all five models show variable central--federated agreement. These findings support a conditional performance--complexity trade-off within a controlled benchmark. Forecasting lead time, physical energy savings and industrial deployment readiness remain unestablished; future work requires independent equipment, alternative aggregation and device-level validation.
papers.venue: Research Square

papers.title: IDENTIFICATION AND AUTHENTICATION SYSTEMS IN THE CONTEXT OF MODERN INFORMATION SECURITY THREATS
papers.abstract: The monograph aims to provide a detailed analysis of current biometric authentication technologies using electrocardiographic (ECG) signals and voice as two fundamentally different but complementary modalities. The relevance of the work is due to the ongoing and evolving crisis of password-based security mechanisms (annual leaks affecting billions of user accounts, and generative speech synthesis technologies moving towards levels where the human voice can be imitated in a matter of minutes). The combination of ECG (an innate marker of life that is almost impossible to fake) with voice (which provides simple contactless verification at a distance) forms a logical and specialized premise for a new generation of biometric structures. The first part is devoted to the basic theory of biometric technologies: nine principles (uniqueness, stability, measurability, universality, resistance to counterfeiting, security, accuracy, standardization and acceptability) for building systems; a comparative analysis of nine physiological and behavioral modalities; nine functional modules of a typical biometric system; architectural solutions from autonomous to cloud-based and adaptive with Zero Trust support; a system of quality assessment metrics – FAR/FRR/EER/DET/minDCF curves – and approaches to ensuring demographic equity. The second part is devoted exclusively to ECG-based biometrics. The unique characteristics of the electrocardiographic signal, arising from anatomical, electrophysiological and neurohumoral factors, are further explained in physiological terms. All processing stages are described – from signal acquisition (with contact and non-contact methods), noise filtering (adaptive LMS filter or 1D U-Net based on neural networks), cardiac cycle segmentation using the Pan–Tompkins algorithm, autoencoder architectures, formation of morphological, temporal and spectral features for average heart beat analysis and dimensionality reduction based on PCA/LDA – up to classification and decision making. Comparison of two-class SVM, k-NN, decision trees and neural networks in different configurations was performed using four datasets (MIT-BIH, PTB, Fantasia, Lviv Biometric Data Set). The highest identification accuracy (98.90%, FAR 0.18·10⁻³, FRR 7.32·10⁻³) was achieved by a neural network with a hidden layer architecture (256, 128). It was experimented with deep embedding architectures (1D-ResNet, Transformer) as well as metric loss functions (Triplet Loss, ArcFace) and tested whether it is possible to deploy it on edge devices. The third section contains the full voice biometric chain: classical MFCC, LPC and PNCC descriptors, speech preprocessing methods (spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering, VAD and neural network optimization using Wave-U-Net), and finally four modern neural network architectures for speaker embedding-ECAPA-TDNN/WavLM/TitaNet/PyAnnote. In the framework of the experimental study, it is shown that TitaNet achieves the highest verification accuracy (0.96), and ECAPA-TDNN – 0.95 and scales better with increasing number of users; while WavLM, under difficult conditions, demonstrates the highest sensitivity to channel variations. The fourth section covers several practical implementation topics: international legal regulation (GDPR, AI Act, BIPA, ISO/IEC 24745 and 30107 standards), ethical aspects of the use of biometric data, architectural solutions for industrial implementation (design of a template database with approximate search algorithms: HNSW and IVF-PQ; cancelable biometric methods; fault tolerance; integration of BioAPI and FIDO2), implementation scenarios in the e-ID industry: banking, telecommunications, medicine, public administration and corporate security; the topic of the user interface - from ease of use to accessibility and economic analysis of costs against return on investment. Strategic development opportunities are identified: multimodal integration of ECG and voice at the level of feature fusion, scoring and decision-making; adaptive systems based on federated learning with differentiated privacy against threats from generative AI; transfer to decentralized identification based on Zero-Knowledge Proof. The scientific novelty of the work is determined by a new integrated concept of biometric authentication with a combination of ECG and voice; a comparative study of modern embedding architectures not only with an assessment of accuracy, but also with a determination of the scalability of models and resistance to spoofing attacks, based on the most modern generative models; as well as a quantitative measurement of how serious a threat these models pose to voice biometrics systems. The practical significance depends on the ability to directly apply the results to build biometric systems in finance, telecommunications, medicine and other areas of social activity. The monograph is designed for researchers, graduate students and students of specialties in information security, digital signal processing and machine learning, as well as for practicing specialists in the field of design and implementation of biometric authentication systems.

papers.title: Finite-Shot Quantum Federated Learning: Trajectory-Dependent Update Discrepancies and Nonconvex Convergence under Proximal Dynamics
papers.abstract: We study quantum federated learning with variational quantum classifiers under finite-shot measurements, heterogeneous clients, multiple local updates, and partial participation. Finite-shot parameter-shift gradients are evaluated along recursively evolving proximal client trajectories, so their effect cannot be represented by simply adding an $O(1/S)$ variance term to a standard proximal federated bound. We therefore analyze the trajectory-dependent discrepancy between the actual federated update and an ideal global-gradient step. At the circuit level, we establish unbiasedness of the parameter-shift estimator, coordinatewise variance $O(1/S)$, and gradient mean-squared error $O(d_q/S)$. At the optimization level, we establish first-order stationarity guarantees for smooth nonconvex objectives with time-varying learning rates and proximal coefficients, without a Polyak--{\L}ojasiewicz condition. The analysis identifies two finite-shot effects: a direct stochastic-gradient residual and an indirect trajectory-mediated residual. It also shows that heterogeneity does not create an independent common-iterate $O(\zeta^2)$ error; instead, it acts through subsequent client drift. For uniform sampling without replacement, we derive an additional correction proportional to $(K-m)/(m(K-1))$ and terminal drift energy, which vanishes under full participation. Experiments confirm near-inverse-shot estimator scaling and illustrate the resulting drift and stationarity behavior.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: A Systematic Study of Computational Advancements in Chest X-ray Based Tuberculosis Detection
papers.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) is a topical issue in the world, as it is particularly high in countries which are developing or under developed. Although there has been an improvement in the diagnostic innovations, chest radiography remains at the forefront of the most available methods of TB screening besides being very cost-effective. The identification of TB in the context of chest X-ray (CXR) has been automated in recent years by applying computational techniques both for traditional machine learning (ML) algorithms and for sophisticated deep learning (DL) models. Our work discusses current computational methods, benchmark data, performance indicators and the limitations being faced in TB detection at chest x-rays. It has been shown that the deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are more accurate, sensitive and robust than the conventional ML methods. However, issues like imbalanced data, lack of understandability, and poor generalizability are still hindrances to the practical implementation. The paper also concludes with some recommendations of the trends in future research, such as the incorporation of federated learning strategies and explainable AI (XAI) to improve reliability and clinical utility.
papers.venue: CRC Press eBooks

papers.title: SeEFed: Self-Expressive Federated Learning for Networked Systems
papers.abstract: # SeEFed: Self-Expressive Federated Learning for Networked Systems This package contains the code, configurations, simulation utilities, reporting scripts, and documentation used to reproduce the computational experiments for: **Manuscript title:** *SeEFed: Self-Expressive Federated Learning for Networked Systems* The artifact supports three execution levels: 1. a small installation and functionality check;2. one representative manuscript scenario; and3. the complete simulation study. The code generates the synthetic data used in the experiments. No private input data are required for the simulation studies. The case-study datasets used in the manuscript are not publicly available for redistribution and are therefore not included in this artifact. The released package does not require those datasets to reproduce the simulation experiments. Reproducing the case studies requires authorized access to the original data and compliance with the applicable data-use, privacy, and institutional requirements. ## 1. Requirements We ran the reported experiments on a computer with an Intel Core i7 processor and 16 GB of RAM. The computations are CPU based and do not require a GPU. The code was tested with Python 3.12. The main dependencies are listed in `requirements-cli.txt` (or `requirements.txt`, if using the complete environment). The package uses NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn, NetworkX, and the plotting/reporting libraries listed in the requirements file. ## 2. Installation From the extracted artifact directory, run: ```bashpython3.12 -m venv .venvsource .venv/bin/activatepython -m pip install --upgrade pippython -m pip install -r requirements-cli.txt``` If `python3.12` is not available, use the installed Python 3.12 executable: ```bashpython3 -m venv .venvsource .venv/bin/activatepython -m pip install -r requirements-cli.txt``` All commands below should be executed from the package root, where `run_seefed.py` is located. ## 3. Quick installation check The smoke test uses a deliberately small configuration. It verifies that the code can generate data, fit the models, save checkpoints, and create result tables. It is not a manuscript result. ```bashpython run_seefed.py \ --profile smoke \ --epsilon-weighting 0.25 \ --smoothing-steps 1 \ --workers 1 \ --output quick_check_results``` The output is written to `quick_check_results/`. For an optional end-to-end dashboard check, run: ```bashpython tests/smoke_dashboard.py --output-dir dashboard_check``` ## 4. Representative manuscript scenario The representative configuration is stored in `configs/representative.json`. It uses: - 10 clients;- 50 features;- heterogeneity parameter `tau = 0.5`;- graph parameter `rho = 0.2`;- one generating graph; and- 10 repeated train/validation/test holdouts. To reproduce the representative main comparison, run: ```bashpython run_seefed.py \ --config configs/representative.json \ --analyses main \ --workers 1 \ --output results_representative``` For a faster run on a multi-core computer, `--workers 6` may be used: ```bashpython run_seefed.py \ --config configs/representative.json \ --analyses main \ --workers 6 \ --output results_representative``` The random seed is fixed through `base_seed` in the configuration. Use `--workers 1` when exact numerical reproducibility is the priority; parallel execution can cause negligible floating-point differences. The main fold-level results are written under: ```textresults_representative/<run-directory>/tables/main_fold_results.csv``` The exact path printed by the program should be retained for later collection or inspection. The public result tables report the selected methods using stable labels such as `KR`, `UR`, and `KR_equal`. Internal tuning configurations are not part of the reported results. ## 5. Optional Streamlit results viewer If the artifact includes the Streamlit viewer, launch it from the package root with: ```bashstreamlit run streamlit_app.py``` If the viewer has a different filename in the release, use the supplied launcher or replace `streamlit_app.py` with the name of the provided Streamlit entry point. Then open the local address printed by Streamlit, usually `http://localhost:8501`. Use the viewer to inspect the generated summary tables, MSE comparisons, graph diagnostics, cost proxies, traversal diagnostics, and solver information. Select the relevant run directory or result files when prompted. The viewer is optional; it does not change the underlying result files. ## 6. Selected manuscript rerun The selected rerun executes the configured main and traversal analyses used for the manuscript revision: ```bashpython run_selected_rerun.py \ --workers 6 \ --output selected_results``` Use a new output directory for a fresh run. Existing checkpoints may otherwise be reused. ## 7. Complete simulation study To run all configured studies and scenarios: ```bashbash run_full.sh``` Alternatively, run the main driver directly: ```bashpython run_seefed.py \ --config configs/full.json \ --analyses all \ --workers 6 \ --output results_full``` The complete workflow may require substantial CPU time. The five configured study families are the main comparison, sensitivity analysis, alignment analysis, factorial analysis, and traversal analysis. The configuration controls client counts, dimensions, heterogeneity, graph density, holdouts, graph replicates, tuning grids, and traversal policies. Before a long run, preview the plan without fitting: ```bashpython run_seefed.py \ --config configs/full.json \ --analyses all \ --dry-run``` ## 8. Resuming and collecting results The run directory contains the saved configuration, generated inputs, checkpoints, failures, and tables. A completed or partially completed run can be collected without refitting: ```bashpython run_seefed.py \ --run-dir results_full/<run-directory> \ --collect-only``` To resume a run, use the same run directory and omit `--collect-only`: ```bashpython run_seefed.py \ --run-dir results_full/<run-directory> \ --workers 6``` ## 9. CSV output files The driver writes the following CSV files to the `tables/` subdirectory of a run directory. This list matches the released result tables. Some traversal files are intentionally empty when the selected analysis does not generate traversal records. The public tables use stable method labels (`KR`, `UR`, and `KR_equal`, together with the benchmark methods); internal tuning configurations are not reported. ### Predictive-performance tables > [!IMPORTANT]> **`main_comparison.csv`:** Wide comparison table containing the average MSE and standard deviation for each reported method under each experimental setting.**This is the most convenient CSV for reproducing the main method-comparison tables.**- `main_fold_results.csv`: detailed fold-level results. Each row identifies a method, experimental setting, replicate, and holdout fold. The principal result columns are `mse`, `validation_mse`, and, when applicable, aggregate and personalized losses. The file also records execution status, runtime, seeds, and optimization diagnostics.- `main_summary.csv`: compact summary by experimental setting and method. `mean_mse` and `sd_mse` summarize the completed folds; `completed_folds`, `expected_folds`, `graphs_with_results`, and `complete` indicate whether the summary is complete.- `benchmarks.csv`: benchmark-comparison table in the same wide format, including centralized, local, federated, and SeEFed results together with their average and standard-deviation columns. ### Graph and parameter diagnostics - `graph_degree_statistics.csv`: graph-level degree summaries for the generating and learned graphs. It reports mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum in-degree and out-degree, including nonzero and thresholded learned degrees.- `graph_degrees_per_client.csv`: client-level degree information. It reports each client’s true in-degree and out-degree, learned nonzero and thresholded degrees, and realized graph densities.- `graph_recovery_per_graph.csv`: recovery metrics for each graph replicate and evaluation rule. It includes true/false positives and negatives, precision, recall, F1, Spearman correlation on true edges, relative Frobenius error, and coverage quantities.- `graph_recovery_summary.csv`: aggregated graph-recovery results. The `*_mean`, `*_std`, and `*_count` columns summarize recovery metrics across the available graph replicates.- `smoothing_weight_comparisons.csv`: comparison of fitted mixing weights with the simulation’s descriptive smoothing references. It reports RMSE, Frobenius and relative Frobenius errors, diagonal difference, and target mean self-weight. These are diagnostic agreement measures, not identifiable recovery of the SeEFed weights.- `covariance_alignment.csv`: checks the dependence induced by the data-generation smoothing step. It reports average correlations between adjacent and nonadjacent clients and whether those correlations were defined. ### Cost, solver, and traversal tables - `cost_proxies.csv`: communication and runtime proxies for each job. It includes wall-clock time, rounds, model payload size, messages, uploads, physical moves, client updates, optimization steps, and weight updates when those quantities apply. The `cost_interpretation` field explains how the proxy should be read; these are analytical proxies rather than direct network measurements.- `solver_and_visitation_diagnostics.csv`: optimization and visitation diagnostics. It reports simplex projected-gradient calls and iterations, SCAD majorization-minimization calls and iterations, residuals, convergence flags, and seed-client visitation counts.- `traversal_client_visits.csv`: client-visit records for restricted communication. It is populated when traversal records are produced and otherwise may be an empty CSV.- `traversal_validation_traces.csv`: validation-loss or reward traces associated with traversal decisions.

papers.title: BalanceFaaS: a decentralized load and energy-aware scheduling framework using federated resource modeling and distributed function orchestration in serverless edge computing
papers.abstract: Abstract The rapid proliferation of serverless computing in heterogeneous edge environments has introduced critical challenges in task scheduling, load balancing, energy efficiency, and orchestration, particularly due to the absence of centralized control and the resource-constrained nature of edge nodes. Existing approaches partially address these issues but often suffer from high latency, inefficient energy utilization, suboptimal load distribution, and limited scalability. To overcome these limitations, we propose BalanceFaaS, a decentralized, load- and energy-aware serverless scheduling framework that integrates key components, including Federated Multi-Objective Gaussian Process Regression (FMOGPR) jointly predicts latency and energy consumption, Ant Colony Optimization with Reinforcement Feedback (ACO-RF) for adaptive load-aware scheduling, Combinatorial Auction-Based Bidding (CAB-B) for dynamic cost-efficient task allocation, a Hierarchical Context-Aware Orchestration Engine (H-CAOE) for reinforcement learning-based orchestration, and a Multi-Agent Byzantine Fault-Tolerant protocol (MA-BFT) with Load-Aware Weighted Voting (LA-WV) for robust and reliable consensus in decentralized environments. BalanceFaaS enables edge nodes to collaboratively estimate execution latency and energy consumption, adaptively allocate tasks based on node status and resource availability, and ensure reliable, context-aware function orchestration without reliance on a central controller. The framework is evaluated using multiple real-world edge workloads, including Alibaba, GOOGLE CLUSTER, AZURE, and SmartCIoT, demonstrating consistent improvements across key performance metrics such as latency, energy consumption, Task Success Rate (TSR), Load Balancing Efficiency (LBE), resource utilization, and federated learning accuracy. Experimental results show that BalanceFaaS achieves up to 4% improvement across key performance metrics compared to baseline methods, highlighting its effectiveness in optimizing both operational efficiency and energy-aware performance in dynamic edge environments.
papers.venue: Computing

papers.title: Secure-Aggregation Federated Graph Attention Networks with SHAP-Based Edge Attribution for Advanced Persistent Threat Detection
papers.abstract: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) pose significant cybersecurity challenges due to their stealthy, prolonged activities and the limited visibility of malicious behaviour in host provenance data. Existing detection approaches often require centralized access to sensitive logs and provide limited interpretability, raising concerns about data confidentiality and analyst trust. To address these challenges, this study proposes a privacy-preserving and explainable federated learning framework for APT detection using provenance graphs. The proposed framework integrates edge-typed Graph Attention Networks (GATv2), self-supervised masked-feature learning, and federated prototype-based anomaly detection to identify suspicious activities without requiring labeled attack data during training. To preserve confidentiality, a dropout-resilient, Bonawitz-style secure aggregation protocol is employed to protect model updates and shared statistics, including normalization parameters, clustering information, and calibration distributions. Furthermore, edge-level Shapley value attribution is incorporated to provide interpretable explanations of detected anomalies and support security analysts during incident investigation. The framework is evaluated using the DARPA Transparent Computing Engagement 3 benchmark, specifically the THEIA and CADETS datasets, under a simulated four-client federated setting. Experimental results across three random seeds demonstrate strong detection performance, achieving Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC) values of 0.995 and 0.971 and Area Under the Precision–Recall Curve (AUPRC) values of 0.870 and 0.561 for THEIA and CADETS, respectively. The proposed secure aggregation mechanism maintains detection performance comparable to conventional federated averaging, introduces approximately 0.1% additional training time on THEIA, and reduces cross-round client-linkage attack accuracy from 85.6% to chance-level performance. Behaviour-level analysis demonstrates complete detection of scan-like attack activities at a calibrated 95% threshold, while other malicious activities exhibit threshold-dependent recall. The explainability analysis confirms the completeness of Shapley attributions and convergence of the highest-ranked contributing edges within 25 permutations, although their empirical fidelity is comparable to less computationally expensive explanation methods. Overall, the findings demonstrate the potential of combining secure federated learning, provenance-graph representation learning, and explainable AI for confidentiality-preserving APT detection, while highlighting important limitations related to threshold sensitivity, explanation fidelity, and semi-honest security assumptions.
papers.venue: Jordanian Journal of Informatics and Computing

papers.title: Federated learning framework with hybrid feature selection for heart disease prediction
papers.abstract: Abstract Since cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of death worldwide, accurate and privacy-preserving prediction methods are essential. Traditional machine learning models often rely on centralized data, which raises issues with data security, privacy, and heterogeneous data distribution among healthcare organizations. This study proposes a federated learning framework with hybrid feature selection (FL-HFS) for heart disease prediction to overcome these challenges. The framework assures data confidentiality by enabling collaborative model training without exchanging raw patient data. In order to determine important clinical features and improve model efficiency, a hybrid feature selection methodology that combines variance thresholding, mutual information, and L1 regularization is implemented. The model is evaluated on a diverse Dataset under a federated learning framework. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms baseline federated learning models with an accuracy of 88.3% and an F1-score of 91%. The results show that the proposed framework provides a robust, scalable, and privacy-aware solution for distributed healthcare applications. Clinical trial number : Not applicable.
papers.venue: Discover Computing

papers.title: Federated Learning in Low-Resource Environments: Optimizing Local Models for Privacy-Preserving IoT Deployments
papers.abstract: This paper presents a structured narrative review of optimization techniques for federated learning (FL) in low-resource Internet of Things (IoT) environments, with particular emphasis on privacy-preserving deployments. Although federated learning enables distributed model training without requiring raw data to leave individual devices, its practical implementation on resource-constrained IoT devices remains challenging due to limitations in computational capacity, memory, communication bandwidth, energy availability and heterogeneous data distributions. This review examines five interconnected dimensions of the problem: Computational and Memory Efficiency: Lightweight model architectures, weight quantization and TinyML-oriented training approaches. Communication Efficiency: Gradient sparsification, update compression, low-rank updates and communication-aware optimization. Statistical Heterogeneity: Approaches for addressing non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data across participating clients. Privacy Preservation: Differential privacy, secure aggregation and defenses against gradient inversion attacks. Energy Efficiency: Hardware-aware scheduling, adaptive federated learning rounds and energy-conscious client selection. The review synthesizes reported findings from existing research, highlighting the trade-offs between model accuracy, computational overhead, communication requirements, energy consumption and privacy guarantees. Particular attention is given to the limitations of existing evaluation practices, including the reliance on simulated environments, limited hardware-in-the-loop experimentation and the lack of integrated evaluations combining privacy, compression and statistical heterogeneity. The paper concludes by identifying research opportunities in joint optimization, hardware-grounded benchmarking, explicit threat modelling, resource-aware heterogeneity management and reproducible evaluation frameworks. Keywords: Federated Learning; Internet of Things (IoT); TinyML; Differential Privacy; Edge Computing; Model Optimization; Communication Efficiency; Resource-Constrained Devices; Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Understanding Early Diagnosis of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Using Next Gen-Techniques
papers.abstract: In the last couple of years, the field of medical science and research has evolved at a very high speed in terms of diagnosis and treatment. Nevertheless, there is still an issue with the early diagnosis of rare neurodegenerative diseases such as Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) also referred to as the Lou Gehrig Disease. ALS is an advanced neurodegenerative disorder that kills motor nerve cells, eventually paralyzes and causes muscle weakness and respiratory failure that results in death. This is because symptoms are non-specific, diagnosis is often delayed. It also makes it difficult as medical records are spread and cannot be merged due to the confidentiality regulations. The current study includes a systematic review of fluid biomarkers, neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and computational methodology. Researchers have established that the Neurofilaments and chitinases have emerged as good biomarker candidates and the EMG and imaging techniques continue to remain central in diagnosis. Transformer models, generative AI and federated learning, which are advanced techniques are hardly used in ALS compared to other related conditions. The review finds improvements as well as major gaps and focuses on the urgent need for integrated multimodal approach that could result in the earlier, precise, and specific diagnosis of ALS.
papers.venue: CRC Press eBooks

papers.title: Fed-VQCS: Vector-Quantized Content-Style State-Space Disentanglement for Federated EEG Generalization
papers.abstract: Federated learning provides a natural framework for decentralized EEG analysis, but learning shared and transferable representations remains challenging because task-relevant neural patterns are often entangled with subject-dependent characteristics in local EEG data. Existing federated EEG methods mainly focus on backbone design, aggregation strategies, or personalized optimization, while representation-level control of what information is globally shared remains insufficiently explored. In this work, we propose Fed-VQCS, a vector-quantized content-style state-space disentanglement framework for robust federated EEG learning. Fed-VQCS introduces a plug-and-play Vector-Quantized Content-Style State-Space (VQCS) module that can be inserted after different EEG feature extractors. Given a latent EEG representation, a bidirectional state-space semantic extractor first produces a continuous task-semantic representation, which is further mapped to globally shared discrete content prototypes through vector quantization. A complementary residual pathway captures variation outside the continuous semantic estimate and is adversarially constrained to suppress task-discriminative information. During federated training, the shared model parameters and content codebook are aggregated globally, while the residual pathway is evaluated within each client’s local training pass. Experiments on BCI Competition IV-2a and PhysioNet, repeated over five random seeds, show consistent improvements in accuracy and Cohen’s κ across four EEG backbones. Comparisons with representative federated learning methods, sensitivity analyses, ablation studies, low-data adaptation, and representation probing further support the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework under heterogeneous subject distributions.
papers.venue: International Journal of Network Dynamics and Intelligence

papers.title: Privacy-preserving blood cancer detection via vision transformers and federated learning
papers.abstract: Artificial Intelligence acts as a powerful tool to analyze medical images in smart healthcare. However, selecting a deep learning architecture is difficult in distributed computing environments due to privacy issues that prohibit centralized training. In this study, five architectures were considered for the evaluation of the performance of blood cancer image classification via federated learning (FL), where a baseline Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), ResNet50, DenseNet121, Xception, and a Vision Transformer (ViT) were selected. This setting allows the exploration of each architecture's performance in terms of image classification in a distributed, data-partitioned setting. These architectures were trained using the same federated learning framework. The experimental results show that such federated configurations offer competitive results compared with traditional methods used in centralized training of neural networks. According to our analysis, the best performance in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score was obtained with the ViT architecture, with a score of 0.98. Xception came second by obtaining accuracy and F1-score scores of 0.89, while ResNet50, CNN, and DenseNet121 achieved lower scores in the range of 0.82 - 0.86. The use of FL in conjunction with ViT yielded the highest score of accuracy and was more robust than the other FL methods.
papers.venue: CTU Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development

papers.title: Federated learning for remote IoT over LPWAN: Preliminary insights from structural health monitoring
papers.abstract: Realizing federated learning (FL) in remote regions lacking reliable cellular infrastructure is challenging, as it requires dependable communication among participating devices. Low-power wide-area networks (LPWANs) offer an attractive communication solution for such scenarios. However, their limited data rates necessitate careful investigation of the communication-learning trade-offs and mechanisms to reduce communication overhead. This paper presents an investigation of the Long Range (LoRa) LPWAN technology for FL-based structural health monitoring (SHM), a representative remote IoT application. We consider a SCAFFOLD-based FL framework for multi-class anomaly detection and analyze the latency-accuracy trade-off. We also examine strategies for allocating the LoRa spreading factor (SF) during model-update exchange. Numerical results show that, with appropriate SF allocation, LoRa-supported FL-SHM can achieve competitive learning accuracy. In particular, jointly accounting for link distances and clients' dataset sizes when selecting the SF provides a favorable balance between convergence performance and communication latency. These preliminary findings offer useful insights into the design of FL systems over LPWANs for remote IoT deployments.

papers.title: Preserving Malicious Client Detectability Under Differential Privacy Through Temporal Multi-Relation Graph Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning has emerged as a privacy-preserving paradigm that collaboratively trains a model without sharing raw data. However, federated learning remains highly vulnerable to abnormal or malicious participants. Differential privacy techniques are widely adopted to safeguard client data during federated optimization, but the added privacy noise makes it harder to detect such malicious behaviors. Existing malicious client detection techniques make the implicit assumption that behavioral signals are still identifiable. However, these signals are distorted by differential privacy, the very mechanism that protects client information, making it harder to identify between benign and malicious clients. Because of this, enhancing privacy often reduces attack detection effectiveness, a problem that is still mostly unsolved. We present a new privacy-preserving temporal multi-relational graph learning framework, which improves the ability to detect malicious clients in the differentially private setting. By taking into account the temporal and relational dependency structures of clients through the communication rounds, our framework minimizes the dependence on single behavioral information that is distorted due to privacy noise. In addition, exponential moving average smoothing and persistence-based temporal voting are introduced to ensure detector stability and minimize potential false positives due to privacy-induced perturbations. The proposed framework is comprehensively evaluated on three benchmark datasets, namely, FashionMNIST, CSE-CIC-IDS2018, and CIC-IoT2023, under both IID and non-IID data distributions across diverse adversarial scenarios, including label-flip, backdoor, gradient-lie, free-rider, and Sybil attacks. Experimental evaluation, supported by privacy-budget analysis, component-wise ablation studies, and comparisons with representative robust aggregation methods and recent malicious client detection baselines, demonstrates that the proposed approach consistently achieves a better balance among malicious client detection accuracy, attack mitigation, global model utility, and privacy preservation. On CIC-IoT2023, under the non-IID gradient-lie attack, the detector achieved a detection accuracy of 0.8467±0.0231 and a recall of 1.0000±0.0000 at a composed privacy budget of approximately ϵtotal=7.05, demonstrating that malicious client detection can be retained while providing stronger privacy protection. In addition to improving detection performance, the proposed work quantitatively assesses the degradation of malicious client separability caused by increased differential privacy and shows that temporal relational modeling significantly mitigates this effect.
papers.venue: Journal of Cybersecurity and Privacy

papers.title: H-VSAF: a verifiable and privacy-preserving federated learning framework for secure remote healthcare monitoring
papers.abstract: The sensitive patient data handled by remote healthcare monitoring systems requires reliable, secure learning methods. Federated learning enables collaborative healthcare analytics without storing raw medical data centrally. However, existing techniques still suffer from issues including privacy leakage, untrusted aggregation, and frequent device outages. In this work, we propose H-VSAF, a privacy-preserving, verifiable, and lightweight federated learning system for healthcare environments. H-VSAF uses linear homomorphic hashing, Bloom filter-based online authentication, Shamir secret sharing, Diffie-Hellman key generation, and single-mask Secure Aggregation to ensure secrecy, precision, and resilience. The security analysis provides informal guarantees against gradient inference, aggregation tampering and deletion, and forged dropout claims under the threat model and cryptographic assumptions above. We experimentally evaluate H-VSAF on healthcare datasets and demonstrate that it achieves model accuracy within 0.2-0.8% of standard federated learning while decreasing client compute cost by up to 32% and communication overhead by 28% compared to traditional secure aggregation methods. Moreover, the framework is resilient to 40% client dropouts and introduces verification latency < 35 ms each round. The results clearly show that H-VSAF provides a credible and practical platform for safe joint health care analytics.
papers.venue: Future Technology

papers.title: Leakage-aware federated-style simulation for fraud risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms
papers.abstract: AI-enabled FinTech platforms increasingly rely on automated fraud-risk prediction to secure high-volume digital payments, mobile-money transactions, and real-time financial services. However, fraud detection remains difficult because fraudulent transactions are rare, financial data are sensitive, and centralized machine-learning models may create privacy and data-governance risks. This study evaluates a leakage-aware and imbalance-aware federated-style simulation for fraud-risk prediction in AI-enabled FinTech platforms. The study does not implement FedAvg, cryptographic secure aggregation, differential privacy, or model-parameter exchange. Instead, the PaySim Synthetic Financial Dataset was partitioned into five simulated FinTech clients, local models were trained separately, and prediction-level aggregation was used to compare centralized and simulated decentralized learning settings. The experimental workflow included data-quality assessment, leakage-aware feature selection, feature engineering, class-imbalance analysis, centralized model development, threshold optimization, and federated-style model comparison. The results show that fraud cases represented only 0.0466% of all transactions and occurred only in CASH_OUT and TRANSFER operations. The best-balanced centralized model was the Improved Random Forest at a threshold of 0.33, achieving an F1-score of 0.3019. Federated Ensemble Aggregation achieved the highest PR-AUC of 0.2699 and a precision of 1.0000, but its recall remained low at 0.1429. The centralized Improved Random Forest retained the highest F1-score of 0.3019, indicating a stronger overall precision-recall balance. Global feature-importance analysis showed that transaction amount, log-transformed amount, temporal features, transaction type, and destination-account activity were the main fraud-risk indicators. These findings should be interpreted as evidence from simulated decentralized fraud-risk learning rather than a full secure federated learning implementation.

papers.title: A Federated Machine Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserving Distributed Data Analytics
papers.abstract: The increasing decentralization of data across organizations, edge devices, institutions and cyber-physical systems creates significant opportunities for collaborative machine learning while simultaneously limiting centralized data sharing because of privacy, ownership, security and governance constraints. Conventional federated learning preserves local data but primarily exchanges model parameters, while federated analytics focuses on distributed insights without providing sufficiently adaptive mechanisms for selecting what knowledge should be shared. This paper proposes FADA-X (Federated Adaptive Data Analytics Exchange), a privacy preserving framework that transforms local observations into multi-level analytical knowledge, estimates knowledge-exposure risk, adaptively selects privacy and abstraction levels and routes only task-relevant knowledge for federated fusion. A Federated Analytical Knowledge Graph (FAKG) maintains relationships among distributed patterns, features, predictions, confidence and provenance. The proposed experimental design considers 20 heterogeneous clients, 100 communication rounds, five local epochs and four distributed datasets. Targeted evaluation includes accuracy, F1-score, AUC, privacy exposure, communication overhead, analytical coverage and query-resolution rate. The framework targets ≥97.5% accuracy, ≥96.8% F1-score, 25–35% communication reduction and ≥30% reduction in analytical exposure com-pared with conventional federated baselines.

papers.title: From Robust Aggregation to Client Admission: Variational Quantum Trust Ranking under Partial Participation and Honest-Selection Bias
papers.abstract: Byzantine-robust federated learning (FL) typically suppresses suspicious contributions only after clients transmit high-dimensional updates. We instead ask which clients should be admitted to full-update aggregation in the first place. We propose variational quantum trust-aware selection (VQTAS), a two-stage framework in which clients first expose compact behavioral descriptors, a shallow variational quantum circuit ranks their trust, and only high-trust participants transmit complete updates. We show that random-hyperplane sketches separate honest and sign-flipped updates under directional heterogeneity, while entanglement enables multivariate feature interactions absent from the corresponding product-state model and finite-shot measurement preserves top-$s$ admission with margin-dependent shot complexity. Under partial participation, we derive an exact oracle floor on unavoidable Byzantine admission and bound the bias induced by nonuniform honest admission under non-IID data by $\|b_t^{\rm sel}\|_2^2\leq\zeta^2\chi^2(q_t\|u)$. These results yield a nonconvex convergence guarantee separating honest-selection distortion, unavoidable Byzantine contamination, and excess ranking error. Under severe non-IID heterogeneity with $30\%$ fixed sign-flip Byzantine clients, causal VQTAS reduces Byzantine aggregation mass from $30\%$ to $21.37\%$, preserves an effective honest population of $30.92$ out of $35$ clients, and reduces projected full-update uplink by approximately $30\%$.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Intent-Driven Computing: Minimizing Personal Data Exposure During Autonomous Internet Capability Invocation
papers.abstract: The increasing development of autonomous Internet interaction systems, generative artificial intelligence, and heterogeneous digital capability orchestration creates new opportunities for completing complex user tasks through coordinated interactions with multiple websites, APIs, AI models, and third-party services. However, these capabilities also introduce an important privacy challenge: autonomous systems may need to process personal information to accomplish a task, but individual services do not necessarily require access to the same information or to the user's complete personal context. When personal information is transferred indiscriminately across multiple services, unnecessary disclosure may occur even when each individual service receives information that appears relevant to the overall task. This paper proposes Privacy-Preserving Intent-Driven Computing (PPIDC), a conceptual framework designed to minimize unnecessary personal data exposure during autonomous Internet capability invocation. Rather than treating privacy protection exclusively as a static property of applications, websites, or databases, PPIDC treats privacy requirements as dynamic constraints associated with user intentions, task decomposition, individual execution stages, and the information requirements of specific Internet capabilities. The framework introduces Intent-Based Data Minimization (IDDM), Selective Context Disclosure (SCD), Capability-Specific Privacy Policies (CSPP), Sensitive Attribute Filtering (SAF), Privacy-Aware Execution Planning (PAEP), and Cross-Service Information Exposure Measurement (CSIEM). These mechanisms collectively determine which information is necessary for a particular execution step, which information can remain local, which attributes can be transformed into less revealing representations, and what information may be disclosed to an external capability under specified conditions. A central contribution of the proposed framework is the introduction of a privacy-aware capability invocation model in which task execution and information disclosure are jointly optimized. Instead of automatically transmitting the complete contextual information available to an intelligent system, the proposed approach seeks to identify the minimum sufficient information required by each capability while maintaining task feasibility, acceptable execution quality, and user authorization. The framework further introduces an information exposure model for examining cumulative disclosure across multiple services, recognizing that individually limited disclosures may collectively reveal substantial information about a user. Importantly, PPIDC is not intended to replace established privacy technologies such as encryption, anonymization, differential privacy, federated learning, or access control. Instead, it proposes an intent-centered orchestration layer through which these technologies and privacy policies can be incorporated into autonomous Internet execution. This paper develops the framework's conceptual architecture, information disclosure model, privacy-aware decision mechanisms, potential advantages, research propositions, evaluation methodology, and implementation considerations. It presents a conceptual research framework and does not claim completed experimental validation or demonstrated performance superiority.

papers.title: Elements of Bayes and Information Theory: A Predictive Theory of Inference: Information, Algorithms, and Large Deviations
papers.abstract: Bayesian inference is a predictive act. This book builds it from three ideas: de Finetti supplies the structure, writing exchangeable beliefs as mixtures of independent laws; Sanov supplies the asymptotics, the exponential concentration of empirical measures at a rate given by the Kullback Leibler divergence; and Bayes supplies the updating, an exponential tilt of the predictive law. Together they give a tilted de Finetti theorem: conditioning an exchangeable sequence on empirical moment constraints yields predictive laws that are I projections of a baseline measure, so parameters emerge as limits of empirical functionals and maximum entropy appears as a predictive limit rather than a postulate. Testing, shrinkage, asymptotics and decision are then read on one moderate deviation scale. Results the book proves, most first stated in the authors' papers with Daniel Zantedeschi and Jyotishka Datta: a finite sample total variation bound between a block drawn under a moment window and independent draws from the I projection, and the projected de Finetti limit behind it; a split of the predictive Kullback Leibler Bayes risk into a Sanov term and a posterior contraction term,; a condition for a scalar learning rate to calibrate credible sets at moderate scale, namely that model curvature and score covariance be proportional; one control variate form for Bayes linear and prediction powered inference estimators, with the optimal gain in closed form; the global posterior of federated learning as a product of local experts under exchangeability; and a convergence rate for the policy that maximizes posterior expected utility in generative Bayesian computation. Several results are stated conditionally or as open problems, and the book says which. Later chapters treat computation, universal portfolios, causal machine learning and medicine. Scripts reproducing every computed figure and number are in the repository.

papers.title: Fed-PriLoRA: A Synergistic Framework for Private and Robust Federated Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.abstract: Utilizing federated learning to fine-tune large language models on sensitive private data while achieving strong privacy protection without sacrificing model utility remains a fundamental challenge. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA significantly reduce communication overhead, integrating them with differential privacy introduces issues including multiplicative noise amplification, cross-round noise accumulation, and consequent training instability, leading to severe performance degradation under strict privacy constraints. To address the above challenges, this paper proposes the Fed-PriLoRA (Private and Robust Federated Low-Rank Adaptation) framework. The framework decomposes each client’s low-rank update into separable vector pairs. It then employs structured freezing to suppress multiplicative amplification of differential privacy noise, and leverages Fisher information for noise-aware parameter importance evaluation to distinguish generalizable features from noise interference. By using Fisher information to assess parameter importance, the client locally discards low-contribution components to mitigate noise interference prior to uploading, thereby reducing communication overhead. Fed-PriLoRA achieves higher accuracy than the non-private StackLoRA baseline on both the Dolly-15K and WizardLM datasets. In terms of communication efficiency, the per-round communication overhead is reduced to just 0.051% of that incurred in full fine-tuning. Ablation experiments demonstrate that Fisher-guided pruning yields a relative accuracy increase of 39% over random pruning.
papers.venue: Electronics

papers.title: Optimal Byzantine-resilient Federated Learning with User-level Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: Real-world deployment of federated learning (FL) requires resilience against adversarial clients and data privacy. Byzantine fault captures the worst-case behavior of adversarial clients, while differential privacy (DP) provides statistical guarantees against privacy loss. In particular, user-level DP guards a client's entire contribution and provides more realistic protection against information leakage. Despite intensive efforts, the minimax-optimal convergence bound of Byzantine-resilient FL with user-level DP remains open. We establish an information-theoretic lower bound for any Byzantine-resilient empirical risk minimization problem under user-level DP and heterogeneous clients. We propose ByzULDP, a central DP algorithm featuring a two-level momentum across the client and server. Client-side momentum mitigates stochastic gradient variance during robust aggregation. Unlike the fault-free case, naively combining non-linear Byzantine-resilient aggregation with central DP noise can be insufficient to guarantee convergence to a bounded neighborhood of a stationary point. Our key contribution is a server-side momentum that leverages a property specific to user-level DP, where privacy sensitivity depends on how client updates are constructed, to empower convergence. ByzULDP achieves the order-optimal convergence bound for strongly-convex objectives, with vanishing error terms decaying at the optimal $O(1/T)$ and $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ rates for strongly-convex and non-convex objectives, respectively. We corroborate our analysis with numerical experiments on real-world datasets across diverse privacy budgets.

papers.title: Performance Benchmarking of Federated Learning Frameworks for Medical Image Classification
papers.abstract: Selecting a Federated Learning (FL) framework requires understanding the resource demands of its training and evaluation workflow. This work compares Flower, NVIDIA FLARE, and FedBioMed using two-dimensional MedNIST classification with ResNet-10 in a containerized, single-host environment. Following a dated review of repository activity and documented medical applications, we evaluated nine configurations per framework, with three random seeds, for a total of 81 executions. The configurations varied federation size, communication rounds, and batch size. We monitored execution time, CPU and RAM consumption, host-level GPU utilization, server network traffic rates, and model accuracy at the end of each execution. The implementations shared nominal learning settings while retaining differences in data splitting and federated evaluation. Configuration-blocked non-parametric analysis identified differences in execution time, client and server memory, GPU utilization, and network traffic rates. NVIDIA FLARE exhibited the lowest server-memory consumption and the highest host-level GPU utilization, Flower exhibited the highest average server network traffic rate, and FedBioMed required more client memory and longer execution time. No statistically significant difference in final accuracy was detected within the evaluated short training schedules; this does not establish convergence or equivalent predictive performance. The results characterize the configured workflows under shared hardware resources. They provide a concrete case study of system behavior, with conclusions bounded by workflow asymmetries, local networking, and the lightweight MedNIST workload.

papers.title: Quantum-resistant blockchain-assisted federated secure cancer diagnosis framework using hierarchical window pattern cognition network
papers.abstract: Abstract Breast cancer is still a major cause of cancer mortality in women, and the development of efficient, reliable and explainable diagnostic systems capable of inter-hospital data sharing while maintaining privacy of data is essential. This study proposes a Hierarchical Window Pattern Cognition Network for breast cancer diagnosis using the Breast Histopathology Images (IDC Regular Patches) dataset. The workflow starts with data collection, then the Patient-Level Data Partitioning process by applying patient identifiers to avoid training-testing overlap. The framework uses CLAHE and data augmentation, image normalization and image resizing to enhance the image consistency. The network learns hierarchical histological and cellular morphological patterns by the modules: Global Histological Representation, Cellular Morphology Learning, Adaptive Tissue Fusion and Diagnostic Probability Estimation. A federated learning framework with five clients uses Federated Averaging (FedAvg) to aggregate models and share model updates securely. The security layer uses an AES-256-GCM encryption algorithm, a SHA3-512 hashing algorithm, and a mechanism simulating those of CRYSTALS-Kyber and CRYSTALS-Dilithium for cryptographic security. Record-integrity verification is supported by a local hash-chain audit log, and predictions of the model are explained with visual and feature-level explanations by using GradCAM + + and SHAP. The proposed centralized model achieved an accuracy of 94.23%, precision of 94.00%, recall of 94.47%, F1-score of 94.24%, and ROC-AUC of 0.9651. These findings highlight the promise of combining the histopathology classification, privacy-preserving federated learning, cryptographic protection, tamper-evident audit logging and explainable artificial intelligence within a unified diagnostic framework.
papers.venue: Scientific Reports

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning Platform using Differential Privacy And Secure Aggregation
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables decentralized machine learning model training on distributed client devices whilepreserving raw data privacy. However, vulnerability to model inversion and gradient leakage attacks remains acritical security threat during parameter communication. This paper proposes a comprehensive Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning (PPFL) framework integrating Differential Privacy (DP) via per-sample gradient clipping and Gaussian noise addition with cryptographic Secure Aggregation(SecAgg). In the proposed platform, participating edge clients retain their datasets locally and execute private model training. Local updates are privatized using Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) accounting before undergoing double-masked secret sharing for secure server-side aggregation. Experimental validation using Python PyTorch,Flower FLwr, and Opacus frameworks demonstrates robust privacy protection with minimal utility degradation across multi-round distributed training.

papers.title: FedKD-MR: Enabling Heterogeneous Federated Learning through Multi-Round Knowledge Distillation
papers.abstract: In heterogeneous IoT deployments, federated learning is challenged not only by distributed, non-IID data but also by the possibility that participating devices may rely on incompatible model architectures. Under these conditions, classical parameter aggregation becomes difficult to apply because client weights cannot be meaningfully combined. FedKD-MR addresses this problem by shifting coordination from the parameter space to the output space: clients exchange logits computed on a shared, public reference dataset, enabling collaboration across heterogeneous models under a common input-label interface. Its main contribution is to organize this output-space exchange into a multi-round process in which consensus logits are repeatedly aggregated, redistributed, and reused during local distillation and supervised fine-tuning. We evaluate FedKD-MR on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 under heterogeneous, non-IID client configurations, including cases in which parameter aggregation cannot be applied to the full client population. The results show gains over isolated local training. We further evaluate the method on UCI-HAR to examine a sensor-oriented setting and the role of the public anchor dataset. This analysis shows that public-set size, class coverage, and distributional quality directly affect the usefulness of consensus logits. Overall, the results support the use of multi-round logit reuse as a practical alternative for coordinating heterogeneous IoT clients when shared model weights are not feasible.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Technologies for Secure Data Management in Digital Systems: A Review of Encryption, Anonymization, Differential Privacy, Federated Learning and Secure Computation
papers.abstract: Digital platforms, cloud services, online transactions and data-driven applications collect and process large volumes of personal and confidential information every day, increasing the risk of data breaches, unauthorized access, identity theft and misuse. Protecting privacy while still allowing data to be used for legitimate purposes has therefore become a core requirement of modern systems. This paper reviews the principal privacy-preserving technologies and how they can be combined for secure data management. It covers data encryption at rest and in transit, anonymization models such as k-anonymity and l-diversity together with the risk of re-identification, differential privacy, which adds calibrated noise to protect individuals, federated learning, which trains models without centralizing raw data, homomorphic encryption, which allows computation on encrypted data, secure multi-party computation and trusted execution environments. Attacks such as membership inference that motivate these defences are discussed. A layered architecture for privacy-aware data management is proposed, with a research gap analysis, objectives and a comparison of techniques by protection level, performance cost and maturity. Regulatory drivers, including India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 and the GDPR, are considered. The review concludes that no single technique is sufficient and that layered combinations matched to the threat model provide the best balance of privacy, utility and performance.

papers.title: Collaborative Intelligence over Resource-Constrained Networks
papers.abstract: Intelligence is increasingly distributed across networks, where edge devices collect multimodal data and run models ranging from task-specific networks to lightweight large language models (LLMs), while cloud servers host LLMs at a substantially larger scale. No single endpoint can serve this spectrum alone, since on-device computation is limited in capability and memory, whereas cloud computation incurs communication latency, usage cost, and privacy exposure. This dissertation studies collaborative intelligence over resource-constrained networks, in which heterogeneous parties cooperate to achieve performance beyond the reach of any one of them, subject to constraints on communication, latency, cost, and privacy as well as user preferences.The first part of this dissertation focuses on collaboration across the device-cloud boundary. For multimodal federated learning, we decompose the model into globally aggregated modality encoders and locally retained fusion modules, and propose a joint modality and client selection mechanism that weighs Shapley-based modality impact against communication overhead. For LLM inference offloading, we develop a resource-constrained reinforcement learning policy that selects the inference location and the modalities to transmit in multi-modal, multi-task, and multi-turn conversations. We propose a privacy-aware agentic framework in which the cloud agent plans over typed placeholders, while the lightweight on-device agent identifies sensitive spans, executes actions, and judges their outcomes.The second part of this dissertation examines collaboration among interacting agents, where each party holds only part of the information that a joint decision requires. For personalized multi-objective planning, an LLM interprets each user's preferences and constraints, such as the available time and the opening hours of the places to visit, from a natural-language request, and a graph search algorithm computes a plan guaranteed to satisfy these constraints. For multi-agent coordination when communication is costly or unavailable, we identify the symmetry trap, in which homogeneous LLM agents acting concurrently collide on targets they need to divide and scatter on targets they need to share. We propose a reasoning schema in which each agent infers from the shared scene whether each target is to be divided, shared, or taken in turn, and identifies its own part from its public role.

papers.title: FMGCF-EWC: an operational, vulnerability-aware early warning chain for climate-related health risk
papers.abstract: Runnable, tested early warning chain developed from the FMGCF-EWC, MVI-HGP and FairGLA frameworks of Blueprints for Future Living: AI-Driven Urban Innovation and Resilient Cities (Springer Nature, 2027), Chapter 6. It combines a cross-border regional graph, federated learning across countries with optional client-level differential privacy, a Gaussian-process vulnerability index, warnings whose threshold depends on regional vulnerability, fairness focused on missed warnings, and verification scores with bootstrap confidence intervals. It is evaluated on synthetic data and on weekly mortality (Eurostat) and temperature (Open-Meteo) data for the NUTS 2 regions of Greece, Italy, Spain and Portugal.

papers.title: Resilient and Sustainable Federated-Edge AI for Autism Care: Integrating Multi-Modal Data, Privacy, and Global Ethical Standards
papers.abstract: This article presents a comprehensive review of resilient and sustainable federated-edge artificial intelligence (AI) for autism care, integrating multimodal data processing, privacy-preserving technologies, and global ethical standards. It explores how federated learning, edge computing, explainable AI, and differential privacy can support secure and efficient healthcare systems for individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).The article examines the integration of multiple data sources, including speech, behavioral, motion, and physiological information, to support personalized monitoring and clinical decision-making. It also discusses data security, patient privacy, transparency, interoperability, and ethical challenges associated with implementing AI-driven healthcare solutions.The research highlights the potential of federated-edge AI to improve healthcare accessibility, computational efficiency, data protection, and responsible AI adoption in autism care. It contributes to ongoing research at the intersection of artificial intelligence, healthcare informatics, privacy engineering, and sustainable digital health systems.Original publication: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews (WJARR), 2025, 28(1), 208–214.DOI: https://doi.org/10.30574/wjarr.2025.28.1.3363
papers.venue: Figshare

papers.title: Securing supply chain transactions with deep learning based autoencoders for fraud detection and zero knowledge proof blockchain for data security
papers.abstract: Purpose This research presents a privacy-preserving fraud detection framework that involves integrating an Autoencoder using a Deep Learning algorithm with Zero Knowledge Proof (ZKP) blockchain technology for secure transactions in the supply chain.Methodology The framework employs analysis of transaction, inventory, and shipment data that are extracted from the Kaggle supply chain management dataset in order to detect unusual transaction patterns as well as verify fraud detection results without any compromise on the privacy of the transaction.Key Findings The proposed DL-Autoencoder model yields an accuracy of 99.99%, precision of 99.87%, recall of 99.98%, and F1-score of 99.54%. These results are better than those obtained through Federated Learning, Anti-Adversarial Hierarchical Ensemble Learning with Multi-Layer Multi-Anomaly Detection (AHEAD), and Blockchain-based African Buffalo (BbAB). The use of ZKP-based verification facilitates privacy-preserving validation, while blockchain technology ensures immutability and traceability of verified fraud results.Policy Implication The framework provides a way for secure and scalable transaction of fraud detection in a supply chain environment.Original Contribution Therefore, the major contribution of the framework is the integration of autoencoder-based anomaly detection, ZKP-based verification, and blockchain-based record-keeping into supply chain fraud detection.
papers.venue: African Journal of Science Technology Innovation and Development

papers.title: Predictive Modeling of Healthcare Arbitration: Evidence, Methodological Challenges, and Machine-Learning Research Directions for Federal IDR
papers.abstract: The federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process established under the No Surprises Act creates an important setting for machine-learning research on administrative decision-making. However, descriptive evidence about arbitration outcomes should not be confused with evidence that a predictive system is accurate, generalizable, or beneficial. This targeted narrative review synthesizes federal reporting, peer-reviewed outcome studies, and relevant machine-learning methodology to develop a research agenda for IDR prediction. The available evidence identifies substantial outcome imbalance, repeated interactions among disputing organizations, heterogeneity in payment benchmarks, and important restrictions in public-use data. We distinguish prediction of escalation, procedural disposition, contested offer selection, payment, and resolution time, each requiring a different population and information set. A proposed evaluation framework emphasizes release-aware temporal validation, dispute-level dependence, probability calibration, uncertainty quantification, and prospective assessment of decision utility. The discussion addresses selective labels, regulatory change, strategic feedback, legally permissible evidence, and unequal access to analytic resources. Eight testable hypotheses concern stage-specific models, relational learning, document-grounded systems, temporal adaptation, uncertainty-aware review, tabular foundation models, federated learning, and decision-focused deployment. No new predictive experiments are reported. The central contribution is a falsifiable and reproducible agenda for establishing when machine learning adds value beyond simple baselines without mistaking predictive associations for legal justification or causal policy effects.
