papers.title: Confidential Computing for Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning Across Distributed Enterprise Cloud Environments
papers.abstract: The increasing adoption of machine learning (ML) across distributed enterprise cloud environments has created significant challenges concerning data privacy, information security, regulatory compliance, and secure computational processes. Traditional security mechanisms primarily protect data during storage and transmission, leaving sensitive information vulnerable while being processed. Confidential computing addresses this limitation by utilizing hardware-based trusted execution environments (TEEs) to protect data and computational workloads during execution. This research examines the role of confidential computing in enabling privacy-preserving machine learning across distributed enterprise cloud infrastructures. It explores how secure enclaves, remote attestation, encrypted computation, federated learning, and trusted hardware technologies can strengthen data confidentiality while supporting collaborative model development. The study adopts a qualitative research methodology based on secondary literature, technical documentation, academic publications, and comparative analysis of existing confidential computing frameworks. Particular attention is given to architectural integration, computational overhead, scalability, interoperability, and governance challenges associated with implementing confidential machine learning across multi-cloud and hybrid environments. The research aims to develop an integrated conceptual framework for secure distributed ML operations that balances privacy protection, computational efficiency, and enterprise requirements. The findings are intended to contribute to the understanding of confidential computing as an emerging foundation for trustworthy, scalable, and privacy-preserving enterprise artificial intelligence.
papers.venue: Journal of Integrated Science Technology and Management

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pulmonary Hypertension: Advancements, Opportunities, and Challenges
papers.abstract: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a progressive cardiopulmonary disorder associated with high morbidity and mortality. Delayed diagnosis, heterogeneous disease phenotypes, and variable treatment responses remain major clinical challenges. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a promising tool for improving PH management. AI-based models have demonstrated promising performance in screening, diagnosis, classification, risk stratification, and prognosis prediction using multimodal data such as electrocardiography, chest radiography, computed tomography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, echocardiography, and electronic health records. Furthermore, AI may support individualized risk assessment, treatment-response prediction, early identification of right ventricular deterioration, and longitudinal remote monitoring. Emerging technologies, including explainable AI, federated learning, large language models, and digital twins, may further advance precision medicine in PH. Despite these advances, data quality, interpretability, privacy, and clinical implementation of AI remain challenges. This review summarizes current applications, opportunities, and challenges of AI in PH and discusses future directions for AI-assisted precision healthcare.
papers.venue: Journal of Clinical Medicine

papers.title: A Multimodal Fatigue-Driving-Detection Algorithm Using Federated Learning and DS-Evidence Theory
papers.abstract: Fatigue-driving detection is of great significance for reducing traffic accidents and enhancing the active safety level of vehicles. To solve the problems of insufficient single-modal information and data-privacy protection, in this paper, a multimodal fatigue-driving-detection algorithm using federated learning (FL) and Dempster–Shafer (DS)-evidence theory is proposed. Three types of information (facial image, electroencephalogram (EEG) signal, and vehicle behavior) are proposed to compensate for the instability of single-modal detection. Meanwhile, DS-evidence theory is used for fusion, which can improve the detection performance. Additionally, the FL mechanism is introduced to achieve collaborative training among multiple clients without directly sharing raw data. It solves the problem of data-privacy protection. The experiment results show that, compared with the single-modality-based FL method, the accuracy, recall and F1 score increase by 4.5%, 1.50% and 3.7%, respectively. The AUC-ROC has increased from 0.870 to 0.937 and the EER has decreased from 0.200 to 0.135. Compared with the multimodal fusion of the single client method, the accuracy, recall and F1 score have increased by 2.2%, 2.5% and 1.4%. The AUC-ROC has increased from 0.915 to 0.937 and the EER has decreased from 0.155 to 0.135.
papers.venue: Vehicles

papers.title: PSL-RGHA: Parallel Split Learning with Reference Gradient Half-Space Alignment for Mitigating Gradient Divergence
papers.abstract: The escalating complexity of deep neural networks hinders the deployment of federated learning (FL) on resource-constrained devices, especially for multimedia applications such as on-device image classification and speech recognition. Parallel split learning (PSL) has emerged as a promising solution by offloading a substantial portion of the computational workload to the server through layer-wise model partitioning, making it particularly suitable for resource-limited visual and speech intelligence scenarios. However, the absence of client-side aggregation renders PSL sus ceptible to severe training divergence and potential convergence failure under heterogeneous data distributions. To address this challenge, we propose PSL-RGHA, a gradient-aligned PSL framework that employs reference gradient half-space alignment mechanism to mitigate training divergence among client devices. PSL-RGHA comprises two novel components: reference gradient progressive construction (RGPC) and gradient half-space alignment (GHA). Specifically, RGPC evaluates the directional consistency of client gradients and progressively synthesizes a robust reference gradient via Weiszfeld updates, effectively approximating the global descent direction. Then, GHA constrains client gradients within the reference half-space defined by RGPC to mitigate gradient conflicts and rectify local updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our PSL-RGHA framework outperforms existing baselines in various settings.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

papers.title: FedLoVA: Value-Only Aggregation for Federated LoRA Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a popular parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method for fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), especially in federated learning, due to its strong performance and communication efficiency. In practice, LoRA is applied to the query and value projections of transformer layers without considering the distinct roles of these components. In this work, we analyze the impact of these projections in federated fine-tuning of LLMs using LoRA and observe that the value projection converges significantly faster than the query projection. Motivated by this finding, we propose FedLoVA, a federated fine-tuning framework that trains LoRA adapters on both query and value projections locally while sharing only the value projection with the server. This approach reduces communication overhead while improving convergence efficiency. Experiments on natural language understanding, multilingual sentiment analysis, and generation tasks show that FedLoVA reduces the communication cost by up to $7.8\times$ compared to existing federated LLM fine-tuning baselines while achieving comparable or better performance. The code is available at: https://github.com/EnsiehKhazaei/FedLoVA.

papers.title: Breaking the Privacy Promise: Gradient Inversion Attacks on Federated Low-Rank Adapted Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been increasingly adopted to fine-tune pretrained models with low computational cost and is therefore also preferred in the federated learning paradigm to reduce computational and communication overhead. In this work, we investigate the sparsely explored problem of the risk of private data leakage in LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers (ViTs), where low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server with access to individual client updates. We show that quality of reconstruction is limited by two coupled ambiguities: reduced information in LoRA gradients and missing spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. To address this, we propose a spatially anchored generative inversion framework that incorporates server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings into ViT blocks during fine-tuning at clients. The resulting positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, providing additional positional cues, while the generative prior keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold, reducing duplicate-data and patch-permutation artifacts, {which produce similar gradients as those produced when the target client images are used}. Adding our proposed spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45, and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, as well as PSNR gains of 7.83 and 11.74 dB on high-resolution CelebA and CARS datasets, respectively, in the FedSGD setting. Such gains in reconstructed image quality metrics are also maintained at higher batch sizes and in FedAvg settings. These results indicate that LoRA-based PEFT does not, by itself, prevent data leakage in FL, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can help in exposing private information.

papers.title: Towards Sustainable Federated Learning via Carbon-Aware Client Selection
papers.abstract: The Information/Communication Technology (ICT) industry is severely challenging the global environment due to the sharply rising carbon emissions generated by machine learning (ML) workloads. Federated Learning (FL) is one of the prominent distributed ML systems used in applications with billions of client devices, such as Google Gboard and Apple Siri. Nearly half of the total carbon footprint in FL originates from client-side computation during local training. However, existing client selection strategies in FL primarily focus on minimizing energy consumption rather than carbon emissions, despite the fact that carbon impact depends not only on computational load but also on the underlying carbon intensity of the energy source. In this paper, we address this gap by proposing a carbon-aware fair client selection strategy (CA-FCS) designed to minimize the carbon emissions associated with model training on client devices. In contrast to existing approaches for reducing carbon emissions in FL, we incorporate hourly carbon intensity and a realistic energy consumption model developed using empirical measurements from Google Pixel smartphones to estimate client-side carbon emissions in FL. Since repeatedly selecting low-carbon clients may reduce data diversity and degrade global model performance, particularly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data settings, CA-FCS incorporates fairness into client selection to mitigate this issue. We conduct extensive experiments under realistic FL settings for mobile devices, where client participation is constrained by device availability conditions, such as charging status and Wi-Fi connectivity. The results demonstrate that our method reduces client-side carbon emissions by up to 46% while maintaining competitive model accuracy.

papers.title: Consensus-Constrained Dual-Federated Optimization with Client-Side Dynamic Weighting for Distributed Android Device Threat Defense
papers.abstract: Smartphones, smart-home hubs, and wearables are increasingly exposed to sophisticated Android malware, while centralized threat-detection pipelines raise privacy and scalability concerns. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without collecting raw client data, but partial participation and variation in local model quality can destabilize global optimization. In this article, we propose DW-FedADMM, a federated optimization framework that combines primal-dual coordination with performance-dependent client-side weighting. The dynamic coefficient modulates each participating client's local state before the augmented-Lagrangian update, while the dual variables regulate disagreement between local and global model states. We evaluate DW-FedADMM on three Android malware benchmarks, namely Drebin, Malgenome, and TUANDROMD, with 5, 10, and 15 clients holding IID data shards, partial client participation, and communication budgets of 5 and 10 rounds. Each configuration is repeated with ten random seeds. DW-FedADMM obtains the highest seed-averaged accuracy on Drebin (97.64% +/- 0.20%) and the best mean accuracy in 9 of the 18 dataset-client-round configurations, including 7 of the 9 configurations with a 10-round budget. Pooled over all configurations, it reaches 95.42% accuracy, 94.62% F1-score, 96.06% precision, and 99.45% AUC, compared with 95.32%, 94.51%, 95.56%, and 99.41% for FedADMM, while also giving the lowest mean false-positive rate and the smallest client update norm among the six compared methods. Both primal-dual methods are well ahead of the averaging- and proximal-based baselines on Malgenome and TUANDROMD, where the latter often remain at the majority-class solution when clients are fragmented. The gain of dynamic weighting over FedADMM is most pronounced on Drebin and with the longer communication budget, where it also reduces the variation across seeds.

papers.title: Diversity-Aware Client Selection for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw data, making it attractive for privacy-sensitive and bandwidth-constrained applications. A practical challenge in deploying FL is reducing communication overhead while maintaining model performance under heterogeneous, non-IID data distributions. Selecting which subset of clients participates in each training round offers a principled way to address both challenges simultaneously, yet its impact on data diversity and representativeness remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate three client selection strategies, Power-of-Choice, Fisher information, and Centered Kernel Alignment, evaluating them not only by accuracy and convergence, but through the lens of participation diversity using the Gini coefficient and KL divergence. Under non-IID conditions, restricting participation to 15% of clients per round achieves significant communication savings, and when selection promotes diverse and balanced contributions, it also improves generalization over biased alternatives. This work provides a systematic and reproducible analysis demonstrating that diversity-focused client selection renders communication efficiency and model quality complementary rather than competing objectives.

papers.title: Federated Forensics: Jurisdictional constraints as a design driver for multi-agency federated learning
papers.abstract: Digital forensic investigations increasingly cross borders, and law enforcement agencies need to build analytical models together without centralizing their data. Federated Learning (FL) keeps data local, yet neither FL nor its frameworks enforce the jurisdictional, governance, and accountability rules that multi-agency forensic work requires. This paper takes a design-first approach to that gap. First, we derive seven requirements that a federated learning system must meet in a forensic setting. Second, we propose Federated Forensics, a three-layer reference architecture whose middle layer, unlike in existing hierarchical FL designs, sits at a jurisdictional border and can use a model update locally while blocking it from crossing that border. Third, we build a prototype of the architecture and test it on a malware-family classification task. In a prototype evaluation, the policy gate blocked every restricted update at the border with zero violations, and restricted-class accuracy rose from 0% under today's compliant alternative to 93.0%, only 4.4 points below ignoring the restriction.

papers.title: Tensor Coupled Federated Multi-view Clustering with Multi-order Anchor Graph
papers.abstract: Graph-based federated multi-view clustering (FMVC) enables privacy-preserving collaborative analysis, yet traditional methods rely on full-sample graphs and suffer from prohibitive O(N2) complexities, especially on large-scale data. Recent advances have introduced anchor graphs into FMVC, effectively reducing overhead to linear complexity. Despite efficiency, existing anchor-based FMVC methods exhibit two critical limitations: 1) They strictly rely on first-order similarities, failing to mine the latent high-order nonlinear semantics of complex data. 2) Due to the independent construction of local anchor spaces, there is a severe lack of correlation and geometric alignment among them. To tackle these issues, we propose a novel framework termed Tensor Coupled Federated Multi-View Clustering with Multi-order Anchor Graph (TFedMAG). Specifically, on the client, TFedMAG employs a multi-order anchor graph learning strategy to capture high-order correlations, while utilizing virtual anchors for privacy protection, and further produces a unified anchor graph. On the server, TFedMAG receives and splices fused graphs uploaded by each client into a third-order tensor to capture global multi-client features. Then, a tensor low-rank constraint is applied to enhance consistency and complementarity among clients. Additionally, extensive experiments are conducted on several real-world datasets, and the corresponding results demonstrate that the TFedMAG method achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance compared to existing FMVC methods.

papers.title: EFGTC: An explainable federated graph learning framework for encrypted traffic classification
papers.abstract: With the development of Decentralized Applications (DApps) and Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), encrypted traffic classification has become a core task of network security supervision. However, the implementation of data privacy regulations restricts the application of traditional centralized classification methods, making the problem of data silos increasingly prominent. Although Federated Learning (FL) provides a privacy-preserving paradigm for solving this problem, existing FL-based schemes mostly ignore the intrinsic topological structure of traffic data, leading to difficulties in extracting comprehensive features and a lack of interpretability in model decisions. To address these issues, this paper proposes EFGTC , an Explainable Federated Graph Learning Framework for Encrypted Traffic Classification. First, we propose a time-aware weighted graph construction method. Unlike traditional methods that purely use connection relationships, we construct a weighted topology graph rich in temporal rhythm by jointly encoding packet direction, length, and inter-arrival time, thereby enabling the graph data to more accurately express the interaction patterns of encrypted traffic. Second, we design a multi-scale feature extraction module based on an attention mechanism. This module not only captures comprehensive features from local handshake details to global flow patterns through multi-level aggregation but also achieves automatic screening and focusing of key data packets through an attention pooling mechanism, effectively suppressing data noise. Finally, experiments on three public datasets within the FL framework show that EFGTC consistently outperforms baselines across all metrics and exhibits strong robustness. Attention-weight visualizations further confirm that the model identifies key traffic-category fingerprints, enhancing interpretability.

papers.title: TOFD: Target-Oriented Feature Decoupling against Poisoning Attacks in Split Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) facilitates privacy-preserving collaborative training with reduced client-side overhead. However, its split architecture introduces unique attack surfaces, rendering it vulnerable to diverse poisoning attacks. Most existing defenses fail to exploit the split paradigm, limiting their ability to detect and contain malicious behaviors at an early stage. To bridge this gap, we propose Target-Oriented Feature Decoupling (TOFD), a unified framework that jointly enables proactive detection and robust optimization against a wide range of poisoning attacks. TOFD operates in three stages: (1) Target Inference, which identifies potential attack targets by refining class-wise safe zones via class-specific Margin Perturbation (MP); (2) Sample Purification, which adaptively filters poisoned smashed data using thresholds calibrated through cross-class min–max normalization of MP; and (3) Decoupling Optimization, which leverages an adversarial guidance model to capture attack-induced patterns and decouple their influence during optimization, thereby suppressing residual adversarial effects. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of TOFD. Extensive experiments on five datasets demonstrate that TOFD consistently outperforms state-of-the-art defenses under diverse attack scenarios, achieving superior robustness with low computational overhead suitable for practical deployment.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

papers.title: FedADB: Class Anchor-Driven Dual-Branch Federated Learning for Mitigating Forgetting
papers.abstract: Multimodal data collected by heterogeneous devices are used for collaborative training, where federated learning (FL) serves as a key paradigm for effective distributed modeling with data privacy preservation. However, local training suffers from the forgetting of previously learned global knowledge under cross-client data heterogeneity, which leads to significant declines in both performance and convergence speed. Most previous studies rely on global alignment strategies to retain global knowledge, which hinder local optimization and lead to inadequate supervision of missing classes. Some studies introduce proxy datasets to supplement supervision for missing classes. However, it remains a challenge to balance class-wise global consistency and local optimization objectives without proxy datasets. In this work, we propose FedADB, a Class Anchor–Driven Dual-Branch FL framework. Specifically, the server generates class anchors optimized in a differentiable input space, which are shared across clients. These class anchors serve as global references that provide supervision for missing classes during local training. A dual-branch collaborative training mechanism is designed for clients. In this mechanism, the anchor-based global branch focuses on learning with global consistency, achieving global knowledge alignment by class-anchor balanced sampling. The local calibration branch focuses on learning discriminative local features, mitigating the degradation of local representations caused by excessive global alignment. Extensive experiments across multiple medical and natural datasets demonstrate that FedADB achieves significant improvements in both accuracy and convergence speed.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

papers.title: Fed-HDDH: A Hyperbolic Directional Diffusion Hypernetwork for Federated Learning
papers.abstract: The Diffusion Hypernetwork (DH) integrates diffusion-based optimization with hypernetwork-driven parameter generation, offering a powerful paradigm for modeling complex and structured data. However, in heterogeneous distributed settings such as federated learning, existing DH frameworks face fundamental limitations. First, they rely on a single perturbation mechanism, which fails to jointly accommodate heterogeneous modalities — continuous data typically require Gaussian noise, while discrete data depend on auxiliary latent transformations — hindering unified diffusion modeling. Second, we show that hypernetwork-generated weights exhibit severe geometric anisotropy in hyperbolic space under heterogeneous federation; ignoring this anisotropy leads to distorted gradients and unstable optimization, a challenge largely overlooked by prior DH methods. To address these issues, we propose Fed-HDDH, a Federated Hyperbolic Directional Diffusion Hypernetwork. Fed-HDDH treats model weights as diffusion objects in hyperbolic space and introduces a radial–angular constrained forward diffusion that preserves intrinsic anisotropy while enabling cross-client conditional reverse denoising. Extensive experiments across diverse modalities demonstrate that Fed-HDDH consistently outperforms both Euclidean and hyperbolic baselines by an average of 5.7% and improves hypernetwork adaptability by 5.2%.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

papers.title: Multi-Dimensional Clustering with Multi-Weight Aggregation for Asynchronous Federated Learning in Low-Altitude Networks
papers.abstract: Asynchronous federated learning (AFL) is essential for low-altitude networks due to its benefits in reducing communication bandwidth, lowering transmission delays, and preserving data privacy. However, the highly dynamic mobility of drones, combined with inherent heterogeneities in AFL, including variations in data volume, data distribution, and device capability, introduces severe challenges, such as inconsistent model update frequencies, biased local training, and inefficient global aggregation. Consequently, these issues lead to significant accuracy degradation and hinder practical deployment. In this paper, we propose a novel AFL framework tailored for low-altitude networks to address these challenges, which combines a multi-dimensional clustering mechanism with a multi-weight aggregation mechanism (MDC-MWA). To mitigate local model bias induced by data heterogeneity, the multi-dimensional clustering allows the cloud server to compute a comprehensive score for each drone based on multiple dimensions, including the label distribution, the gradient direction, and the local data proportion. It then employs K-Means clustering to partition drones into highly homogeneous subgroups, each managed by a dedicated roadside unit (RSU). Within each subgroup, after performing local updates, each drone synchronously uploads parameters to its RSU. Between these subgroups, to address inconsistent update frequencies caused by imbalanced computing capabilities, RSUs perform asynchronous training via the multi-weight aggregation mechanism, which updates the global model considering staleness weight and direction consistency weight. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms baseline approaches in highly heterogeneous scenarios, achieving a 4.74% absolute improvement in training accuracy on the CIFAR-10 dataset. This work provides a practical framework for distributed intelligent applications in dynamic and resource-constrained low-altitude networks.

papers.title: Federated learning for IoMT-enabled predictive healthcare and remote patient monitoring: a systematic review
papers.abstract: Background The rapid growth of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has enabled continuous monitoring of physiological signals and data-driven healthcare services, supporting predictive analytics, personalized treatment, and remote patient monitoring. However, conventional centralized machine learning approaches require sensitive patient data to be aggregated on centralized servers, raising concerns regarding privacy, security, regulatory compliance, scalability, and communication overhead. This systematic review critically evaluates federated learning (FL) approaches for IoMT-enabled predictive healthcare and remote patient monitoring, focusing on FL architectures, aggregation strategies, privacy-preserving mechanisms, communication efficiency, scalability, and practical deployment challenges. Methods This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines. Relevant literature was collected from IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, ACM Digital Library, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Following screening and eligibility assessment, 69 studies published between 2020 and 2026 were included. The selected studies were evaluated using a structured quality assessment framework covering dataset validity, experimental rigor, reproducibility, scalability evaluation, privacy protection, and reporting quality. The evidence was synthesized to compare FL architectures, aggregation techniques, security mechanisms, communication performance, and healthcare applications. Results The findings indicate that FL enables collaborative model training without directly sharing raw patient data. Hierarchical and edge-assisted FL architectures can reduce communication overhead and improve scalability in distributed healthcare environments. Differential privacy, secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, and blockchain integration were identified as privacy-preserving mechanisms used in the reviewed studies. Many studies reported predictive accuracies exceeding 90%, while communication cost reductions of up to 45% were reported for certain hierarchical FL deployments. However, challenges involving non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data, device heterogeneity, limited computational resources, real-time adaptability, and adversarial robustness remain unresolved. Conclusion Federated learning represents a promising approach to secure, scalable, and privacy-preserving healthcare analytics in IoMT ecosystems. Future research should prioritize adaptive federated architectures, lightweight privacy mechanisms, personalized federated learning, robust defenses against adversarial attacks, and large-scale real-world validation to support clinical adoption and improve healthcare outcomes.
papers.venue: BMC Digital Health

papers.title: Federated variational inference for incomplete multimodal learning
authors: for the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative
papers.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) often preceding its onset. Early prediction of MCI progression to AD is crucial for effective intervention. Although multimodal neuroimaging can improve prediction accuracy, incomplete datasets and strict privacy regulations hinder broad implementation in machine learning (ML) models. Current federated learning (FL) solutions in neuroimaging typically focus on unimodal data, thereby missing the synergistic advantages of multimodal approaches. We propose Federated Variational Inference for Cross-Model Learning (FedVICML), a novel FL framework that allows institutions with varying neuroimaging modalities to collaboratively train predictive models without centralized data sharing, thus keeping raw patient data local to each site. FedVICML uniquely combines FL with a new cross-model variational inference (VI) method, using two distinct Bayesian neural networks for multimodal and unimodal data respectively, and an extended VI-based mechanism for knowledge transfer. This decentralized, data-local approach enables robust learning with incomplete multimodal data by integrating FL and cross-model VI, without pooling raw data across sites. We apply FedVICML to simulated and real-world datasets from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), demonstrating improved performance and uncertainty quantification over conventional FL baselines for predicting MCI to AD progression. Our results highlight FedVICML’s promise for collaborative medical research in heterogeneous data environments.

papers.title: AdvSE: Effective and Persistent Backdoor Attacks in Federated Continual Learning via Adversarial Feature Separation and Selective Embedding
papers.abstract: Federated Continual Learning (FCL), extending Federated Learning (FL) across dynamically evolving tasks, is becoming increasingly important in multimodal applications. Given the established vulnerability of FL to backdoor attacks, FCL constitutes a natural target for similar threats. However, our experiments show that various backdoor attacks formulated for FL are ineffective when applied to FCL, resulting in an average decline of 89.42% in ASR. This counterintuitive phenomenon raises a critical question: does FCL truly provide inherent resistance to backdoor attacks? To answer this question, we conduct an investigation, which reveals that partial parameter sharing restricts the propagation of backdoors. More importantly, catastrophic forgetting caused by subsequent task updates erases injected malicious features in a manner similar to the degradation of clean task performance. Leveraging these insights, we propose AdvSE, the first backdoor attack specifically designed for FCL. Specifically, we employ a dynamic adversarial mechanism to navigate multiple potential backdoor activation pathways and isolate the optimal one, forging a robust malicious shortcut that is distinctly separated from benign feature mappings to maximize attack efficacy. To shield this optimized pathway from catastrophic forgetting during task transitions, we further introduce a selective backdoor embedding strategy that anchors malicious updates within shared stable parameters, preventing them from being overwritten by subsequent benign updates. Experiments on multimodal datasets demonstrate that AdvSE improves the ASR by approximately 90% compared to baseline methods. Notably, it consistently achieves an attack success rate above 92%, with a peak of 99.57%, even under robust defense mechanisms such as MultiKrum and Flame, without sacrificing the accuracy of the main task.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Predictive Computing for Generative AI: A Federated and Privacy-Aware Framework for Forecasting Future Computational Demand Without Exposing User Information
papers.abstract: The increasing deployment of generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems has created substantial opportunities for predictive computational optimization. By analyzing historical request patterns, emerging information trends, and user interaction signals, generative AI infrastructures may anticipate future computational demand and prepare appropriate resources before actual requests arrive. However, the predictive analysis of user behavior introduces an important privacy challenge. Historical queries, interaction frequencies, contextual preferences, temporal usage patterns, and inferred information interests may contain sensitive personal information. Centralizing these signals to improve demand prediction can expose users to profiling, membership inference, behavioral reconstruction, and unauthorized information disclosure. Consequently, predictive computing must address not only whether future computational demand can be accurately anticipated, but also whether such anticipation can be achieved without unnecessarily exposing the private information underlying user behavior. This paper introduces Privacy-Preserving Predictive Computing for Generative AI (PPPC-GAI), a conceptual framework that integrates privacy-preserving demand forecasting with predictive inference preparation and computational resource orchestration. The framework investigates how generative AI systems can estimate future computational requirements using distributed, aggregated, anonymized, and privacy-protected information signals while minimizing the exposure of individual user interactions. Its architecture integrates seven interconnected functions: (1) privacy-aware information signal acquisition, (2) local and federated demand forecasting, (3) privacy-preserving future workload estimation, (4) differential privacy and secure aggregation, (5) privacy-constrained predictive computational preparation, (6) adaptive privacy-budget and resource management, and (7) privacy-aware computational evaluation. Unlike conventional predictive computing architectures that may depend on centralized historical request information, PPPC-GAI investigates whether future demand can be estimated through collaborative forecasting without requiring raw user queries to be transferred to a central prediction service. The framework considers federated learning, differential privacy, secure aggregation, local statistical processing, privacy-preserving feature extraction, and aggregate demand modeling as complementary mechanisms. It further distinguishes between user-level privacy, request-level privacy, and aggregate workload information, recognizing that the protection of individual records does not automatically prevent the disclosure of sensitive population-level patterns. A unified optimization formulation is developed to jointly characterize prediction accuracy, computational preparation benefits, privacy loss, communication overhead, resource expenditure, and service-level requirements. The framework introduces privacy-adjusted predictive computational utility to determine whether a predicted workload should be prepared when both expected computational savings and potential privacy costs are considered. It also establishes a privacy-aware experimental methodology involving forecasting accuracy, differential privacy guarantees, membership inference resistance, information leakage, computational overhead, and realized inference savings. The proposed framework does not assume that federated learning, anonymization, or differential privacy independently guarantees complete privacy protection. Rather, it investigates how multiple privacy-enhancing mechanisms can be coordinated within a predictive computing architecture, with explicit consideration of adversarial threats, privacy-budget composition, model-update leakage, aggregate disclosure, and the trade-off between forecasting accuracy and privacy protection. Its practical effectiveness remains subject to empirical validation.

papers.title: High-Performance Big Data Architectures for Advanced Microbiological Research
papers.abstract: The convergence of high-throughput sequencing, systems biology and distributed computing has made microbiology a data-intensive field, generating vast genomic, proteomic and metabolomic datasets. Traditional infrastructures—single servers, relational databases and sequential pipelines—are no longer sufficient to manage the scale and complexity of modern data. This chapter analyzes high-performance big data architectures designed for advanced microbiological research. It begins with the data challenges in contemporary microbiology and explores distributed frameworks such as Apache Hadoop, Spark, Kafka and Flink, alongside cloud-native platforms, containerized pipelines, real-time surveillance systems and machine learning integration. It also addresses governance and security for ethical and reliable data sharing. Supported by architectural figures and comparative tables, the chapter bridges theory and practice. It concludes by highlighting emerging technologies like quantum-classical computing, neuromorphic biosensing and federated learning shaping future microbiological data systems.
papers.venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series

papers.title: A Comprehensive Review on Contemporary Challenges and Emerging Solutions in Deep Learning and Machine Learning: Limitations, Trends, and Future Directions
papers.abstract: Deep Learning and Machine Learning have emerged as transformative technologies driving innovation across healthcare, finance, autonomous systems, and generative intelligence. Despite their remarkable success, the rapid scaling and deployment of these models have exposed a series of critical challenges that limit their reliability, efficiency, and real-world applicability. This comprehensive review paper presents a systematic analysis of contemporary problems and prospective solutions in the field, based on literature published between 2022 and 2026. Major challenges identified include data-related issues such as bias, scarcity, poor quality, and privacy concerns; model-centric limitations including the black-box nature leading to lack of interpretability and explainability, poor generalization to out-of-distribution data, and vulnerability to adversarial attacks and hallucinations in generative models. Furthermore, we highlight the escalating computational costs, high energy consumption, and environmental impact associated with training large-scale models, alongside growing ethical and regulatory concerns. In response, this review examines emerging solutions shaping the next generation of AI. These include efficient architectures such as Vision Transformers, Mamba models, model quantization, pruning, and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (LoRA), data-centric approaches like synthetic data generation and federated learning, and trust-centric methods including Explainable AI (XAI) using SHAP and LIME, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for hallucination mitigation, and robust and trustworthy AI frameworks. The paper concludes by outlining key research gaps and future directions towards developing more trustworthy, efficient, scalable, and sustainable AI systems.
papers.venue: International Journal of Science and Research (IJSR)

papers.title: Fairness Is Not Universal: Towards Contextualized and Autonomous Fairness in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Much of the existing work in fairness-aware federated learning (FL) treats fairness as a global property, i.e. a constraint or objective that can be defined and applied uniformly across all clients. In this paper, we argue that this paradigm is fundamentally insufficient. Fairness is contextual, population-dependent, and often governed by domain- or jurisdiction-specific values. We evaluate fair FL methods against two client-side post-training interventions: model output post-processing and final-layer fine-tuning. Across four datasets of different modalities (tabular, signal, and image) and multiple data heterogeneity settings, we show that even when all clients nominally commit to the same fairness metric, fairness-aware FL algorithms do not provide consistent context-sensitive fairness improvements. We find that the post-training interventions are more promising, but at the same time note that, as they currently stand, they remain only partial remedies. Our empirical diagnosis helps identify the future research directions for novel FL frameworks that explicitly support contextual and autonomous fairness.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

papers.title: HiveWatch: Framework-agnostic observability for federated learning
papers.abstract: We present HiveWatch , an open-source, framework-agnostic observability toolkit for federated learning (FL). HiveWatch provides a minimal five-call training-lifecycle API and an FL-native schema for round summaries, client updates, communication volume, resource utilization, staleness measurements, failure events, and geographic metadata. A pluggable emitter interface routes a single normalized event stream simultaneously to replayable local JSONL artifacts and a geographic dashboard through GeoEmitter , to Weights & Biases through WandbEmitter , and to MLflow through MLflowEmitter . We demonstrate HiveWatch ’s portability across three architecturally distinct FL frameworks, APPFL, Flower, and NVIDIA FLARE, using the same API in each case. In a synthetic server-side microbenchmark of 50 rounds and 20 clients per round on an AWS EC2 t3.medium instance with 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB of RAM, internal bookkeeping required an average of 7.3 𝜇 s per client-update call and 102.3 𝜇 s per round-summary call, whereas the synchronous GeoEmitter required 3.02 ms and 3.52 ms, respectively. The software, framework integrations, examples, tests, and benchmark artifacts are available under the MIT License in the versioned v0.3.1 release.
papers.venue: SoftwareX

papers.title: ATLAS: Adaptive Task-Aware Federated Learning with Heterogeneous LoRA and Split Learning for Edge LLMs
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) can adapt large language models (LLMs) without centralizing private data, but deployment on heterogeneous edge clients is constrained by task diversity, device variability, and communication cost. Standard task-agnostic aggregation and uniform-rank low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often cause negative transfer and poor resource matching. This paper presents ATLAS, a task-aware framework for parameter-efficient federated fine-tuning of transformer LLMs on heterogeneous clients. ATLAS combines representation-based task discovery, budget-aware heterogeneous LoRA allocation, state-consistent split federated learning, and LoRA-only graph regularization, together with INT8 LoRA communication and FP32 server-side computation. On a heterogeneous GLUE federation with three tasks, nine clients, and three backbones, ATLAS improves the macroaverage task score over standard FedAvg by 16.18 points on DistilBERT, 24.83 points on GPT-2, and 6.86 points on Qwen-2.5-0.5B, while reducing LoRA synchronization traffic and eliminating low-resource-client failures.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

papers.title: Federated Learning on Resource-Constrained IoT and TinyML Devices: review protocol and extraction data
papers.abstract: Protocol (version 1.5, 6 November 2026) and supporting materials for a systematic literature review of federated learning (FL) on resource-constrained IoT and TinyML devices. The review identifies, classifies and synthesizes primary research on this topic, with emphasis on deployment evidence, resource optimization and feasibility, security and privacy overhead, benchmarking, and reproducibility. The protocol defines the research questions, the PICOC scope, the search strategy, the eligibility criteria, study selection, the device-tier classification, data extraction, quality assessment and the synthesis plan. Its amendment and deviation log records every change made after version 1.0 (19 August 2026), with its date and rationale. A copy with tracked changes shows what version 1.5 changed from version 1.4. The record also contains the search strings as run in each of the seven sources (searched 26–27 August 2026), the PICOC elements of each research question, and the completed data-extraction workbook for the 93 included studies (96 reports). In the workbook, each extracted value is linked to a verbatim quote and page in its source report. A README describes every file and workbook sheet.

papers.title: A Review on Changing Trends in Mobile Security Utilizing FPGA-Based Lightweight Cryptography, AI-Based Threat Analytics, and Decentralized Identity Protocols
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of mobile and Internet of Things (IoT) systems has created crucial security challenges as many devices have limited computing power, are expanded across different networks, and are facing continuously changing cyber threats. Traditional methods like fixed intrusion detection, Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)-based encryption, and centralized login systems are becoming less effective in protecting today’s mobile infrastructure as they are not adaptable to these changes. In order to protect mobile devices from these security threats, three modern technologies were invented. The first is blockchain-based decentralized identity (DID), which will manage user authentication and access without relying on a central authority, and make the system more secure. The second is AI-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs), which apply machine learning to detect unusual behavior or threats in real time. The third is lightweight cryptography (LWC), which will secure data protection while using less power and processing, and this feature is making it ideal for small devices. This review will inspect these three approaches along with its working mechanism with their advantages and challenges, with a primary focus on field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-based implementations of LWC to deal with the needs of VLSI integration. It will also provide a comparison framework, and it will investigate how the application of these technologies can be combined in the future to build more secure mobile systems. Lastly, it will also focus on major issues like compatibility, system delay, and scalability, and it will suggest future research directions, which include federated learning (FL), quantum-resistant encryption, and lightweight blockchain protocols that are designed for mobile environments.
papers.venue: CRC Press eBooks

papers.title: FedGAT: Federated Geometry-Aware and Topological Condensation
papers.abstract: Federated learning has emerged as a promising paradigm for privacy-preserving collaborative learning across distributed clients. However, the data owned by different clients are usually highly heterogeneous and severely Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (Non-IID), which leads to client drift and unsatisfactory global model performance. Although existing federated learning methods have attempted to alleviate the Non-IID problem, most of them mainly operate at the model level and still rely on frequent communication. In this paper, we propose a novel data-centric federated learning framework called FedGAT, to address severe data heterogeneity under limited communication budgets. On the client side, we improve the quality and diversity of condensed knowledge by preserving local geometric structure and prioritizing insufficiently learned yet non-redundant samples. On the server side, we further enhance global discrimination under heterogeneous data distributions by adaptively aligning class prototypes. Extensive experiments on eight medical and natural image datasets against ten state-of-the-art methods demonstrate that FedGAT achieves superior accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 16.48 percentage points.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

papers.title: Mechanism Matters: Modality Informativeness and Fusion Routing Determine Missing-Modality Robustness in Multi-Modal Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) is increasingly used in tactical multi-sensor systems where camera feeds, inertial telemetry, acoustic streams, and radio-frequency (RF) spectra are held by physically separate clients. In real deployments, any modality can fail for physical reasons, including glare or overexposure in vision, IMU saturation, ambient masking in audio, and RF jamming or interference. These failures are often self-masking, meaning that the chance of losing an observation depends on the value the sensor would have reported. However, federated robustness is still usually tested with missing completely at random (MCAR) corruption, which cannot represent this behavior. It is therefore natural to assume that the more realistic missing not at random MNAR) mechanism is always harder. We show that this is not generally true. Using frozen ImageBind encoders and a controlled per-modality MCAR and MNAR sparsity injector, we evaluate four experimental setups: a Vision+IMU bi-modal model on the U-AIR UAV dataset, two tri-modal AU-AIR variants, and a tri-modal Vision+Audio+RF model on a three-class drone-identification task with an independent held-out RF validation split. The relative damage caused by MCAR and MNAR depends on which modality carries the predictive signal and whether the server-side gated fusion can route around a degraded client. When one informative modality is self-masked and the only alternative is uninformative, MNAR is harder. When a healthy alternative exists, CAR can be harder because independent dropouts create joint-missing events where every modality is absent on the same sample and the gate has nowhere to route, while MNAR's self-selection tends to leave at least one modality available. On the external drone-identification task, the ordering changes with the sparsity rate, and the held-out RF split shows that the learned gate collapses onto a single modality. As a result, a strong aggregate score can hide an RF client that contributes almost nothing. We argue that trustworthy VFL benchmarks should report results by missingness mechanism and by modality, and should treat MNAR as a standard corruption mechanism alongside MCAR.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

papers.title: FedMMDP: A Federated Multimodal Domain Personalization Framework with Modality Alignment and Privacy Preservation
papers.abstract: While multimodal federated learning offers a decentralized alternative for image-text retrieval, existing methods face two intertwined issues: 1) a persistent modality gap in pretrained encoders that compromises cross-modal alignment under scarce, non-IID data, 2) the challenge of enabling domain-aware personalization without exposing private client representations. These two issues are closely coupled: unreliable cross-modal geometry hinders domain-aware transfer, while privacy constraints make such transfer harder to achieve. To address them, we propose FedMMDP, a federated multimodal domain-personalization framework that unifies modality-gap reduction, secure domain recognition, and centroid-guided personalized optimization. Unlike prior work, FedMMDP first pretrains a lightweight projector on public multimodal data to improve cross-modal alignment. It then performs secure domain recognition via securely aggregated Lloyd-style K-means, enabling the server-side centroid updates without accessing client representations. These centroids guide personalized local adaptation on heterogeneous clients. Evaluated on ImageNet-derived and IAPR TC-12 benchmarks using CLIP and SigLIP backbones, FedMMDP achieves the state-of-the-art results under the primary preproj setting, outperforming the second-best baseline by 20.0 Rsum points on ImageNet+CLIP. The results support FedMMDP as an effective solution for privacy-preserving, domain-aware multimodal federated retrieval. The supporting code for this paper is available at https://github.com/Toony254/FedMMDP.
papers.venue: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)

papers.title: Quantum-Assisted Client Selection for Federated Learning-based Intrusion Detection Systems via QAOA
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is emerging as a distributed privacy-preserving paradigm, aiming to build a strong machine learning (ML) model in a distributed manner. Client selection in FL is a critical challenge for building intrusion detection systems, especially in heterogeneous Internet of Things (IoT) networks, where Non-Independent and Identically Distributed (Non-IID) data partitioning causes classical selection strategies to suffer from catastrophic forgetting of minority attack classes. This paper presents a Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) based framework that formulates client selection as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem encoding client utility, communication latency, a cardinality constraint, and an optional group diversity term, solved at each communication round using the QAOA. To reduce quantum circuit width for near-term hardware compatibility, we investigate two qubit reduction strategies in this paper: hierarchical client clustering and classical pre-filtering. Extensive experiments on three IoT intrusion detection benchmarks under heterogeneous Non-IID distributions show that our proposed approach improves macro F1-score by up to 30% over Greedy-TopK selection and by up to 29% over random client selection. Our ablation studies confirm that the quantum-assisted selection advantage emerges specifically under Non-IID distributions. On the most challenging dataset, where two attack categories represent less than 0.5% of the data, the proposed method achieves superior results than other client selection methods on aggregate metrics while offering superior precision and convergence stability.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

papers.title: AI-Enabled Digital Forensics and Data Integrity in Smart Microbiology Laboratories
papers.abstract: The clinical microbiology laboratory is shifting from traditional culture-based, manual systems to automated, AI-driven smart laboratories. These platforms use real-time sensors, computer vision, and advanced algorithms to reduce human error, speed up workflows, and cut turnaround times significantly. Machine and deep learning models achieve over 95% accuracy in pathogen detection and can predict antimicrobial resistance using genomic, proteomic, or phenotypic data, supporting targeted therapy and stewardship. Data integrity is maintained through regulatory compliance, audit trails, and AI-based quality control, while privacy is protected using federated learning and encryption. Ethical oversight, regulation, and interdisciplinary collaboration remain essential.
papers.venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series

papers.title: Anticipated Future Developments and Integration of Emerging Tech in AutoML Networks
papers.abstract: Emerging technologies are going to include the significantly developing automated machine learning. It has promised to fundamentally redefine the landscape of AI applications. It examines the developments that are most crucial for AutoML networks. Such explorations always lead the way from innovations such as quantum computing, federated learning, and enhanced AI governance frameworks. Quantum computing is going to revolutionize AutoML and sustain the real-time computation of complex computations that result in faster optimization of a model. Meaning, federated learning will support decentralized collaboration of the parties involved, which then can easily utilize the diversified datasets for efficient consumption without compromising the privacy of the users. On the other hand, robust AI governance frameworks will be adopted to consider ethics in the development process. Ethics typically entail accountability and transparency. Based on this analysis, efficiencies as such are shown to be highly promising when AutoML systems are in question, and consequently, guaranteed innovation is brought to different sectors. A focus on always finding that balance between technological advancement and embracing responsibility may well ensure that the future of AutoML can positively contribute to society and address the needs in order to meet the requirements of a data-driven world.
papers.venue: River Publishers eBooks

papers.title: Trust- and Energy-Aware Federated Learning for Robust and Sustainable IoT Edge Intelligence: Full-System Evaluation on PAMAP2 and Cross-Domain Robustness Assessment on CICIoT2023
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) supports collaborative edge intelligence without centralizing raw data, but non-IID data, Byzantine attacks, and limited client energy complicate IoT deployment. We study two complementary server-side mechanisms: TEA-FL, which couples consistency-based trust with residual energy in client selection and aggregation, and ARL-FL, which separates risk/lifetime-aware scheduling from pressure-adaptive robust aggregation. A matched two-domain protocol distinguishes full-system PAMAP2 evidence from aggregation-focused CICIoT2023 evidence and combines fold/seed-level inference with ablations, targeted sensitivities, and complete-round overhead measurements. Under the primary simulated resource model, TEA-FL achieved the highest overall PAMAP2 Macro-F1 and lowest normalized energy, but reduced participation fairness and did not complete every nominal-horizon run. ARL-FL preserved the largest active-client population and completed all PAMAP2 runs, but failed under the strongest sign-flip attack. Focused controls showed that trust drives TEA-FL’s sign-flip robustness, energy-aware selection drives ARL-FL’s sustainability benefit, and simpler fixed clipping-plus-trimming can be competitive under strong attack. The results support context-dependent robustness–sustainability trade-offs rather than universal superiority.
papers.venue: Applied Sciences

papers.title: Federated Tick Tack
papers.venue: Lecture notes in computer science

papers.title: Federated Learning for Collaborative AutoML in Zero-touch Network and Service Management: Applications and Challenges
papers.abstract: Federated learning has brought a revolution that has enabled the training of data-driven models in collaboration without necessarily aggregating data. This fits well with the distributed approach brought forth by ZTNSM, driven by requirements around privacy and efficiency. Network operators can dynamically optimize network performance with the help of AutoML integrated into an FL paradigm, reduce human intervention, and ensure robust management in complex systems. This chapter discusses the confluence of FL and collaborative AutoML for transforming ZTNSM. This means that FL keeps data secure by handling it close to where the process takes place, and AutoML takes on tasks like finding and putting into practice machine learning solutions. All of these aspects will join together to support dealing with major issues such as detecting out-of-the-ordinary events as they occur, predicting when network resources must be managed, and adjusting network slicing in multi-service environments. We will highlight a number of significant applications of FL-powered AutoML solutions in ZTNSM and outline their role in proactive and scalable network tools. Conversations in this area also tackle issues with dealing with limited resources, more communication 216 activity, and difficulties in keeping federated models in sync. For this reason, the field needs greater progress in optimization, safe communication, and smart model structures. The integration of edge computing and 6G networks with FL-enabled AutoML is examined to increase the scalability and intelligence of future networks. As a result, FL and AutoML working together provide a new method for running networks automatically, which can offer ZTNSM secure and effective management solutions.
papers.venue: River Publishers eBooks

papers.title: Quantum Federated Learning for Multimodal Perception: A Proof-of-Concept Vision Study
papers.abstract: We present a preliminary proof-of-concept study for using quantum federated learning (QFL) with multi-modal sensor data across distributed platforms. Our approach uses a hybrid quantum-classical model in which each sensing modality is first processed by its own classical encoder. The resulting features are then combined using a learned, entropy-regularized gating mechanism, passed through a variational quantum circuit, and trained using federated averaging. Both the classical model parameters and the quantum circuit parameters are shared and aggregated across clients during training. We evaluate the approach in two separate studies using the AU-AIR aerial UAV dataset and the nuScenes autonomous-driving mini split. Each dataset is federated independently across four clients and represented using four sensing modalities. All results are evaluated on held-out test data across five random seeds and compared with an equivalent classical pipeline in which the quantum circuit is replaced by a classical layer of similar size. The results show that the overall QFL pipeline can be trained successfully. Entropy regularization keeps the modality contributions nearly balanced, and the quantum parameters converge under federated aggregation. On the nuScenes categories represented in the mini split, the quantum model achieves a performance of macro averaged F1-score of of 0.869 and an accuracy of 0.913 . However, the classical baseline performs similarly, with the F1 of 0.853, and the difference is not statistically significant. On AU-AIR, the results are weaker as severe class imbalance and limited circuit capacity reduce held-out accuracy to 0.452. Because the overall results are mixed, the study shows that QFL can be applied to real multi-modal sensing data while also highlighting important limitations. The findings emphasize the need for skew-aware metrics, strong classical baselines, and further work on scalable and reliable quantum federated perception.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Symposium Series

papers.title: Adaptive Federated Learning for Brain Tumor Segmentation: A Clustered Approach with Bias-Variance Balancing
papers.venue: Lecture notes in computer science

papers.title: Blockchain-Integrated Machine Learning Framework for Mitigating Cybersecurity Risks in IoT Ecosystems
papers.abstract: The unparalleled growth of Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems has brought up complicated cybersecurity issues since devices are heterogeneous, interconnected on a vast scale, and attack patterns are undergoing change. This chapter focuses on the aspects of the threat surfaces designed to be utilized by the IoT and the drawbacks of the traditional centralized security controls. It discusses the use of blockchain technology to offer decentralized trust, immutable data and safe logging, and machine learning methods to detect anomalies in real-time and prevent intrusions. A blockchain-machine learning model is suggested to improve the resilience, transparency, and automated access control in IoT settings. Supervised learning, deep learning, federated learning and protocol-specific intrusion detection model have proven to be effective as shown in experimental use cases. The chapter also addresses the main constraints, such as the scalability, adversarial vulnerability, interpretation issues, and the research perspectives in the future in terms of secure and sustainable IoT ecosystems.
papers.venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series

papers.title: Adversarial Machine Learning in Cybersecurity
papers.abstract: Adversarial machine learning (AML) is a major threat to machine learning-based Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS). This chapter examines AML techniques in cybersecurity, including evasion attacks, training-time poisoning, backdoor injection, and GAN-driven evasion exploiting classifier vulnerabilities. It addresses the challenge of crafting adversarial examples that meet network constraints while evading detection, alongside defenses such as adversarial training, certified robustness, detection screening, and explainability-guided hardening. The chapter analyses white-, gray-, and black-box threat models, and compares benchmarks including NSL-KDD, CICIDS2017/2018, and UNSW-NB15. Defense strategies are evaluated for accuracy recovery, overhead, and robustness. It also considers links to federated learning, explainable AI, IoT monitoring, and malware detection, and outlines research directions for resilient NIDS.
papers.venue: Advances in computational intelligence and robotics book series
