papers.title: zk-DEAP: A Zero-Knowledge Decentralized Encrypted Aggregation Protocol
papers.abstract: Secure aggregation in domains such as federated learning, Internet of Things, and voting requires operating on private inputs while preserving confidentiality, verifying that each input satisfies constraints, and avoiding trusted parties. Existing protocols achieve at most two of these requirements. We present zk-DEAP, a protocol combining lifted ElGamal homomorphic encryption, FROST threshold cryptography, and zero-knowledge proofs (Bulletproofs, zk-SNARKs, or zk-STARKs) for fully decentralized, verifiable, privacy-preserving aggregation. Our core technical contribution is a cryptographic binding mechanism preventing substitution attacks, where a valid proof for one input is paired with a ciphertext encrypting a different, malicious value. For Bulletproofs, we bind via ciphertext-derived randomness modification. For zk-SNARKs/zk-STARKs, to bind across algebraic structures (a well-known challenge in practical cryptography), we introduce a novel blinded arithmetic hash commitment with an embedded Schnorr constraint. These binding techniques force the ZKP's private witness to equal the encrypted value, ensuring any circuit-verified constraint applies to the ciphertext. We implement three production-ready, defense-in-depth variants in Rust and evaluate across 5-500 participants. Compared to unverified aggregation, zk-DEAP adds modest overhead while providing cryptographic guarantees against input manipulation that statistical defenses cannot match.

papers.title: Server-Side Sparse Assignment for Federated Mixture-of-Experts
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly recognized for their remarkable capabilities; federated learning (FL) offers a promising framework for collaboratively fine-tuning LLMs on edge devices while achieving data privacy. However, edge devices are inherently heterogeneous: clients may exhibit diverse data distributions and resource constraints, including limited memory and computation budgets. Recent federated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address these challenges by using sparse expert activation or partial expert loading. However, existing partial-expert methods rely on heuristic full-pool observations or prioritize system-wide load balance, without guarantees for recovering client-specific relevant experts from partial observations. We propose $S^3$-MoE, a server-side sparse expert assignment framework that estimates client-specific expert relevance from partial observations and refines assignments through an exploit--explore mechanism. We also establish relevance-estimation error and exact Top-$K$ recovery guarantees. Experiments using a CNN-based MoE on CIFAR-100 show that $S^3$-MoE recovers task-dependent client--expert preferences and reduces conflicts caused by correlated expert selection across clients. Compared with Full-20 FedAvg, which gives each client access to all 20 experts for local Top-5 routing, $S^3$-MoE achieves 1.31 percentage points higher mean final accuracy while loading only $5$ experts per client.

papers.title: FedFiOT: Fisher-Weighted Optimal Transport for Model Merging in One-Shot and Few-Round Federated Learning
papers.abstract: One-shot and few-round federated learning (FL) reduce communication burden by constructing a global model within one or a few communication rounds, but often achieve lower performance than conventional multi-round FL. Without frequent synchronization, client models may drift apart, causing neurons that learn similar features to occupy different positions across clients. At the same time, local data heterogeneity can cause corresponding parameters to differ in their importance to each client's predictions. Together, these challenges cause direct averaging to combine mismatched neurons and assign equal weight to parameters despite differences in their importance. We propose FedFiOT, a Fisher-weighted optimal transport framework for one-shot and few-round FL that leverages Fisher information to quantify parameter importance and guide neuron alignment and model aggregation. FedFiOT jointly optimizes neuron correspondences and global model parameters through alternating minimization of a shared Fisher-weighted objective. Theoretically, we show that FedFiOT's optimization procedure monotonically decreases the layer-wise merging objective and establish a stationarity bound that quantifies the effects of client heterogeneity and nonuniform Fisher weighting.Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over competing baselines in both one-shot and few-round federated learning settings.

papers.title: Transversal Passivity: Dissipation Relative to Input and Output Manifolds
papers.abstract: This paper introduces transversal passivity, a local dissipation property for regulating input and output signals to prescribed manifolds. Its supply rate is built from the transverse port errors induced by nearest-point projections, so that motion along the manifolds is not penalized. We give a necessary condition and a constructive sufficient condition for the property and relate it to existing passivity notions. For feedback interconnections through negative-adjoint linear channels, power conservation no longer cancels the transverse supply. The residual is governed by compatibility defects that depend only on the channels and the prescribed manifolds, so it can be assessed before any closed-loop analysis, and it falls into a hierarchy of exact compatibility, quadratic cancellation, and nonzero quadratic residuals. Since transversal storages are only positive semidefinite, port convergence is obtained by combining compact confinement, for instance by conserved quantities, with a dissipation margin, and we identify a geometric obstruction under which no quadratic margin is available near the feasible states. A federated learning case study with heterogeneous data shows that port convergence can be certified even though no server target is compatible with the interconnection, and that the obstruction arises for a natural choice of target.

papers.title: Learning From Static Context in Federated Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Time series forecasting is shifting from locally trained, per-series models to global models trained across many heterogeneous series, which requires learning what sets the series apart. When the raw data cannot be centralized, such a global model is trained with federated learning (FL), one client per data owner. State-of-the-art forecasters such as the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) tell series apart through a static input that describes each series and does not change over time. In the special case of a federated setting where each client holds a single series, this static input is constant within each client and varies only across clients. We ask whether a federated TFT can learn from it. Per-batch FedAdam, which aggregates gradients after every batch, uses the static input almost as well as central training, whereas communication-efficient schemes with local epochs (FedAvg, FedAdam+Prox) extract far less from it and gain nothing significant on either application dataset. At the same local computation, an Adam-compatible SCAFFOLD keeps the static pathway responsive on wind power and gains significantly there. On building energy its error still drops, but the static pathway falls silent, so drift and communication frequency cannot be fully separated as the cause. Only per-batch FedAdam matches or beats the per-client local models across all datasets. We confirm the effect on building-energy meter data, a wind-power dataset, and a controlled synthetic dataset. The loss is not specific to the TFT: on the synthetic and the wind data two further architectures with different static-conditioning mechanisms show it as well.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence for water quality monitoring: a PRISMA-based systematic literature review, taxonomy, comparative analysis, and future research directions
papers.abstract: Abstract Accurate and reliable water quality monitoring (WQM) has become increasingly important due to rapid urbanization, industrialization, climate change, and anthropogenic activities that threaten global freshwater resources. Conventional water quality assessment methods primarily rely on manual sampling and laboratory analysis, which are labour-intensive, time-consuming, costly, and unsuitable for continuous real-time monitoring of large-scale aquatic environments. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), and sensing technologies have enabled intelligent, data-driven approaches capable of modelling complex nonlinear relationships, detecting contamination events, and improving predictive decision-making. This study presents a systematic literature review (SLR) of AI-based water quality monitoring using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework. A systematic search of IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink identified studies published between 2020 and 2026, of which 91 met the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Review and survey articles were excluded from the analytical corpus so that secondary literature was not pooled with primary studies. A structured taxonomy is developed to characterise the strengths, limitations, interpretability and reported applicability of these model families. Because the included studies differ in target variable, dataset, preprocessing and validation protocol, no pooled performance comparison across model categories is reported and no meta-analysis was undertaken. The review identifies key challenges, including heterogeneous datasets, limited model generalization, overfitting, computational complexity, sensor calibration issues, data inconsistency, and the lack of standardized benchmark datasets. Furthermore, emerging research directions comprising Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Federated Learning, Edge AI, Graph Neural Networks, Digital Twins, Foundation Models, and multimodal environmental intelligence are discussed. The findings provide researchers, practitioners and policymakers with a structured reference to the current evidence base on AI-based water quality monitoring, together with the methodological limitations of that evidence, to inform the development of future monitoring systems for sustainable water resource management.
papers.venue: Artificial Intelligence Review

papers.title: FL-SDMN: Federated Learning-Based Software-Defined Mobile Networking for Intelligent Handover Optimization
papers.abstract: The rapid growth in mobile users and the increasing adoption of data-intensive applications have created high network demands for low-latency and reliable mobility management in mobile communication networks. However, the traditional handover approaches are rule-based and rely solely on signal strength thresholds with hysteresis margins, which are prone to ping-pong effects and limiting their ability to adapt to dynamic network conditions. Machine Learning (ML) models have been integrated for handover prediction, but their centralized architecture compromises user data privacy, potentially conflicting with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The centralized ML approaches also introduce scalability constraints that limit their effectiveness in dense network deployments. To address these challenges, this work proposes a Federated Learning framework for Software-Defined Mobile Networking (FL-SDMN) that combines privacy-preserving federated learning with centralized network coordination to enable intelligent handover optimization in 5G and beyond networks. The framework leverages a lightweight federated ExtraTrees ensemble model with weighted tree-based aggregation and SDMN controller to provide global network coordination. The federated learning framework has a three-layer decision pipeline that transforms handover control from a reactive threshold-based mechanism into a predictive, A3-derived optimization process without TTT persistence. The model was trained using real-world 5G mobility data, while handover performance, controller decision latency and scalability were evaluated separately using a discrete-time system level simulator. The findings demonstrate that integrating FL, Extra Trees, and SDMN provides a scalable and deployment-oriented approach to intelligent mobility management for 5G and beyond networks.
papers.venue: Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction

papers.title: Physics-Attested Federated Learning: Securing Collaborative Anomaly Detection in Critical Water Infrastructure
papers.abstract: Federated learning enables industrial operators to train shared intrusion detection models without disclosing proprietary operational telemetry. However, existing defences operate strictly in update space, leaving aggregators blind to data poisoning; model updates derived from fabricated telemetry remain indistinguishable from honest contributions. We repurpose process invariants, physical relations that always hold in normal operation, such as the conservation of mass, from runtime detection heuristics into a verifiable admission requirement for federated updates, mined automatically from clean operational data. We evaluate this admission gate across two physical water testbeds (SWaT and WADI) and a distribution benchmark (BATADAL), testing seven aggregation rules against telemetry fabrication, exposure-only replay poisoning, and an invariant-aware adaptive adversary. Across three testbeds, the mined invariants reject none of 25 honest shards except every cross-channel fabrication on SWaT and BATADAL, including optimised perturbations that the similarity-based FoolsGold admits in full. On real telemetry, five mined invariants detect 12 of SWaT’s 35 attacks, while nine invariants detect 20. With nine invariants, the admission gate removes 78% of the targeted-attack recall lost to replay poisoning (95% CI 57–97%, p<0.001 over 20 seeds) across five standard aggregators and 82% under FedAvg. To reconcile physical admission control with federated data privacy, we show invariant compliance using zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) to allow clients to prove batch adherence without revealing operational telemetry.
papers.venue: Information

papers.title: MF-EFLJD: Multi-faceted ensemble federated learning for jamming detection in private 5G-enabled IIoT networks
papers.abstract: Wireless network security is a growing concern in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) as jamming attacks disrupt communication of IIoT entities in Private 5G networks. While machine learning (ML) algorithms detect jamming attacks effectively, centralized data collection from entities compromises sensitive information and privacy in distributed IIoT environment. This article presents a multi-faceted ensemble federated learning-based jamming detection framework, MF-EFLJD, to detect and further improve detection performance. To address the issue of non-independent and identical distribution (non-IID) and high-dimensional wireless channel data persisting across femtocells, this framework proposes sequential integration of Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Genetic Algorithm (GA), and Shapley Additive Explanation (SHAP) values to obtain optimized and structured data. Moreover, the framework trains 1D-CNN-based Federated Learning (FL) component on optimized data of entities to detect jamming attacks under non-IID conditions at each femtocell. Furthermore, to boost the performance detection of FL under non-IID, we propose Random Forest (RF)-based stacking ensemble component with an unweighted majority soft voting approach. Under non-IID setting α = 0.7 , the proposed system demonstrates that FL achieves accuracies of 0.9376 ( ± 0.0134 ) , 0.8806 ( ± 0.0178 ) , and 0.9576 ( ± 0.0169 ) for femtocells F 1 , F 2 , and F 3 , respectively, in detecting jammed and non-jammed signals. Additionally, the ensemble component achieves 0.9963 ( ± 0.0031 ) accuracy, depicting improvement in performance across femtocells.
papers.venue: Ad Hoc Networks

papers.title: AI-Driven Membrane-Integrated Wastewater Biorefineries for Resource Recovery and Hydrogen Production: A Critical Review
papers.abstract: Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are being reconceived as biorefineries that recover water, nutrients and energy, and membrane processes are central to this transition. This critical review examines how artificial intelligence (AI), and in particular, its data-driven subset machine learning (ML), is applied across membrane-integrated wastewater biorefineries: aeration control, membrane bioreactor fouling prediction, membrane-based nutrient recovery (membrane contactors, forward osmosis, electrodialysis, membrane distillation), struvite crystallisation, biohydrogen production by dark fermentation and microbial electrolysis, thermochemical sludge conversion, and hydrogen purification by gas-separation membranes. Reported model accuracies are high (coefficients of determination, R2, above 0.9 for several resource-recovery tasks), but they measure model fit rather than reactor performance and were obtained mostly on small laboratory or literature-compiled datasets (municipal, industrial, mixed or synthetic wastewaters and other organic feedstocks) with heterogeneous validation schemes and are, therefore, not directly comparable. Documented full-scale evidence is concentrated in aeration control (19.8% lower total operating cost than fuzzy-logic (knowledge-based AI) control at one plant; 26–30% lower aeration energy in a vendor-reported case) and membrane fouling forecasting. Validation practice, cross-plant transferability, the gap between explainable-AI attribution and mechanistic understanding, and the scarcity of techno-economic evidence are identified as the main barriers. A research agenda based on hybrid mechanistic–ML models, federated learning and a proposed plant-wide “resource ledger” is outlined for pilot-scale validation.
papers.venue: Membranes

papers.title: Lightweight adaptive split federated learning for patient-independent ECG arrhythmia classification
papers.abstract: Wearable electrocardiogram monitoring in the Internet of Medical Things requires arrhythmia classifiers that run on resource-constrained devices and learn across hospitals without pooling patient data. We propose FedIoMT-RPM, a split federated learning framework in which each device trains only a 28.4 KiB client-side network, 6.8 times smaller than in full-model federated learning, while a bounded adaptive weighted aggregation adjusts each client''s contribution to its smoothed validation performance. Under the patient-independent inter-patient protocol of the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, with five clients holding complete patient records and six seeds per method, its detection performance was statistically comparable to that of the best federated baselines, with an accuracy of 93.97 ± 1.72%, a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.731 ± 0.039 and a macro-F1 score of 60.07 ± 2.41%. This macro-F1 reflects limited detection of supraventricular beats, with a sensitivity of 64.8%, and near-zero detection of fusion beats, and 1,381 of the 1,781 supraventricular test beats come from a single record. Among the split methods, FedIoMT-RPM averaged 18.9% less communication than SplitFed. Zero-shot INCART and PTB-XL benchmarks gave results comparable to the federated baselines. Reconstruction attacks recovered the ECG from the transmitted activations, which need protection before clinical use; membership inference stayed near chance.
papers.venue: Scientific Reports

papers.title: Mathematical modelling of ensemble-based federated learning framework for false data injection attacks detection in artificial intelligence of things
papers.abstract: Abstract Rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) has allowed intelligent data-driven decision-making under several cyber-physical systems (CPS) like smart cities, smart grids, industrial automation, and healthcare monitoring. AIoT incorporates artificial intelligence (AI) methods with IoT devices to develop large volumes of sensor data and improve system efficacy, automation, and predictive proficiencies. Among different forms of attacks, the false data injection attack (FDIA) has proven that high-priority cyber-related problem and has received more attention recently. The FDIA detection is an important security process in the smart grid controller system and is resolved by data-driven machine learning (ML) algorithms. Now, Federated Learning (FL) is a well-known ML method that assists in addressing data privacy problems by permitting users to collect its raw data locally and transferring it local model parameters only to the aggregator server to collectively train a shared global model. This paper develops a Federated Learning-Based Framework for Detecting Attacks Using an Ensemble Classification Model (FLFDA-ECM) in distributed cybersecurity systems within the Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) environment. The major intention of the FLFDA-ECM paper is to propose an FL-based cybersecurity framework for detecting and classifying FDIA in AIoT- enabled distributed systems while preserving data privacy. At first, the data pre-processing contains dual levels, such as handling missing data and feature scaling to regularize the input data. In the feature selection stage, the hybrid approach integrates minimum redundancy maximum relevance and ReliefF techniques to recognize the most appropriate attributes. Furthermore, an ensemble-based weighted majority voting approach incorporating bi-directional gated recurrent unit, variational autoencoder, and temporal convolutional network models is employed for attack detection. Finally, the parameter fine-tuned model has been executed by the Adan optimizer to enhance the classifier solution. The performance evaluation of the FLFDA-ECM technique occurs using a benchmark dataset. The empirical outcomes specified the boosted performance of the FLFDA-ECM model in comparison with recent techniques.
papers.venue: Scientific Reports

papers.title: AI-Powered Hybrid Healthcare Surveillance and Emergency Response System for Next-Generation Smart Cities
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of smart cities has increased the demand for intelligent healthcare systems that can provide continuous patient monitoring, early disease detection, and efficient emergency response. Conventional healthcare surveillance systems often face challenges such as delayed emergency services, fragmented medical data, limited interoperability, and inadequate real-time decision-making. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an AI-Powered Hybrid Healthcare Surveillance and Emergency Response System (AI-HHSERS) for next-generation smart cities. The proposed framework integrates the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), Edge Computing, Cloud Computing, Federated Learning, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Digital Twin technology, and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to provide intelligent healthcare monitoring and emergency management. Physiological data collected from wearable sensors, medical devices, Electronic Health Records (EHRs), smart cameras, and environmental sensors are analyzed using hybrid AI models to predict disease risks, detect health anomalies, and generate early warning alerts. Edge computing enables low-latency processing for real-time decision-making, while cloud computing supports large-scale data storage and long-term analytics. Federated Learning ensures privacy-preserving collaborative model training without sharing sensitive patient data, and Explainable AI enhances the transparency and reliability of clinical decisions. In emergency situations, the GIS-enabled response module identifies the nearest ambulance, optimizes routing based on real-time traffic conditions, and automatically notifies hospitals to improve patient care. The proposed framework is expected to improve disease prediction accuracy, reduce emergency response time, enhance healthcare interoperability, and strengthen data security. Furthermore, it supports smart hospitals, remote patient monitoring, elderly care, epidemic surveillance, and disaster management, making it a scalable and reliable healthcare solution for future smart city ecosystems.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Federated and GAN-Augmented Deep Learning Frameworks for Brain Tumor Diagnosis: A Comprehensive Survey
papers.abstract: Deep learning has transformed brain tumor detection and segmentation, yet clinical translation is impeded by data scarcity, class imbalance, heterogeneous imaging protocols, interpretability gaps and heavy computational demands This review brings together recent developments and highlights Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Federated Learning as central elements in practical applications. GANs expand limited datasets with high‑fidelity synthetic images that improve diversity, robustness and resolution for training, while federated learning enables privacy‑preserving, multi‑institutional model development that enhances generalization without exchanging raw patient data. We contrast GANs with VAEs and diffusion models, highlighting trade-offs among fidelity, interpretability, stability and efficiency, and examine hybrid CNN-transformer architectures, multimodal fusion, radiomics and optimization strategies that bolster performance. Key future directions include hybrid generative frameworks, explainable AI for transparent grading, fine‑grained tumor staging, multimodal integration, scalable architectures for resource‑limited settings and standardized benchmarks for reproducibility. By situating GANs and federated learning within an ethical and reproducible framework, AI systems may be developed to support clinical reliability, safeguard privacy and prioritize patient needs by helping to connect research with practical application.
papers.venue: ADCAIJ ADVANCES IN DISTRIBUTED COMPUTING AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE JOURNAL

papers.title: Threat adaptive trust weighted federated learning for Byzantine resilient cybersecurity across healthcare edge networks
papers.abstract: The rising adoption of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices, edge computing, and distributed healthcare platforms brings with it a host of cybersecurity threats, whereas the centralized learning approach also brings with it privacy, communication, and single point of failure concerns. This study introduces the threat-adaptive Trust-weighted Federated Optimization (TrustFedHealth) framework for Byzantine-resilient healthcare cybersecurity, which combines the multi-signal client reliability estimation, temporal trust updating, norm clipping, error-feedback Top-k compression, and threat-guided Multi-Krum aggregation, with trust-weighted FedYogi optimization. The experiments were run on 15 k healthcare records with 52 attributes, with 12 k of them used for training and 3 k of them being future-held-out for testing, in 60 edge-node clients. Three tasks were assessed: security-risk classification, health-risk classification and health-risk regression. FedAdam showed the best security classification, with 93.67% accuracy, 0.9028 Macro-F1, 0.8867 MCC and 0.9898 ROC–AUC, while FedYogi attained the best ROC–AUC of 0.9904 and regression performance with 0.0516 MAE, 0.0651 RMSE and an R 2 of 0.6562. Multi-Krum has 0.8892 ROC–AUC and 75.77% security-classification accuracy when the attack rate is less than 20% malicious-client participation. A gender Macro-F1 gap of 0.0089 was achieved in the subgroup analysis and the expected calibration error was reduced from 0.0274 to 0.0185 by temperature scaling. The highest compressed checkpoint's accuracy is 90.46% and the highest Macro-F1 score is 0.8480, with a 22.25% cumulative communication reduction. The results show the promise of TrustFedHealth for secure, calibrated, equitable and communication efficient collaborative intelligence in the healthcare domain.
papers.venue: Scientific Reports

papers.title: PBS-FL: Anonymous Federated Learning with Verifiable Update Inclusion

papers.title: FLHyHE: Federated Learning with Hybrid Homomorphic Encryption
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables distributed and collaborative training while keeping sensitive data on clients' devices. This approach is considered more privacy-preserving since only model updates are shared with an aggregator. However, several studies have shown that these updates can still leak private information, making them vulnerable to various attacks. Privacy-preserving techniques, such as Differential Privacy and Homomorphic Encryption, can be combined with FL to enhance security. However, these methods often introduce a loss in accuracy and increase computational and communication overhead on the network. Hybrid Homomorphic Encryption (HHE) is a relatively recent type of cryptographic primitive that has been experimentally applied to FL to mitigate client-side overhead while preserving privacy. In this work, we propose a general construction for FL systems employing HHE, denoted FLHyHE, and analyse its security. We instantiate this construction on top of the Flower framework using the PASTA/FV HHE scheme and evaluate it experimentally. Experiments conducted on two well-known datasets, MNIST and CIFAR-10, using two convolutional neural network models show that model accuracy is mainly preserved for MNIST (≈2% drop), while performance on CIFAR-10 is noticeably affected by the use of HHE (≈20% drop). On the other hand, it is clear that a solution of this kind is significantly more efficient for clients in terms of computational and communication costs compared to solutions relying solely on Homomorphic Encryption, since it uses Symmetric Encryption as the main encryption tool. Especially as models get more complex and consist of more parameters.
papers.venue: Workshop on Encrypted Computing & Applied Homomorphic Cryptography (WAHC)

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Medical Image Diagnosis using Federated Learning and Vision Transformers
papers.abstract: Deep learning model training is a central approach, which poses risks to patient data privacy and hampers data sharing for medical image classification, essential for computer-assisted diagnosis. In this study, a privacy-preserving medical image classification system is presented that combines Vision Transformers (ViTs) with Federated Learning (FL) for the classification of four categories of white blood cells: eosinophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, and neutrophils. The framework uses model training on local data in three simulated clients and uses Federated Averaging (FedAvg) to merge model updates without sharing raw images. A conventional Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and a centralized ViT are used as baseline models. The preliminary results indicate that the centralized ViT can attain an accuracy of 58.50% and a macro-F1 score of 51.82%, which is better than the CNN baseline (53.50% accuracy). The overall performance of the federated ViT can be seen as good with an accuracy score of 49.50% and a recall score of 96.00% for the class of monocytes, which suggests good class-specific recognition and, simultaneously, room for improvement at the overall level. An additional enhancement that can help prevent information leakage from model updates is proposed as differential privacy. Additional rounds of communication, larger sets of training data, hyperparameter optimization and formal guarantees of privacy will be explored in further work. This is a framework to give a basis for co-operative privacy-aware medical image classification.

papers.abstract: First archived release of the code and committed results accompanying Federated Learning for Wind Turbine Fault Detection on CARE to Compare (P. Mundhra, D. Poojary, A. Sharma, P. K. Loharkar; in preparation).
