papers.title: AI-Driven Federated Learning Frameworks for Privacy-Preserving Smart Urban Energy Management
papers.abstract: The growing complexity of urban energy systems with smartness requires intelligent solutions that are privacy friendly to manage the distributed energy resources efficiently. This chapter introduces a federated learning model that is AI-powered and in this system, model training is performed in an intelligent grid, micro grid, and IoT-based devices, without the exchange of raw data. The strategy improves accuracy in load forecasting, efficiency of energy use, and lessens the amount of overhead in communication besides maintaining data privacy and security. The framework combines edge computing and state-of-the-art AI to promote scalable and adaptive energy management to add to sustainable, resilient, and human-centric smart city ecosystems.
papers.venue: IGI Global eBooks

papers.title: Di-fedDIL: Distributed fault diagnosis of idler bearings of long-distance belt conveyor under cloud-edge resource constraints
papers.abstract: In long-distance belt conveyor systems, idler bearings are widely distributed along the transportation route, making distributed fault diagnosis necessary. A cloud-edge architecture provides a feasible solution by enabling local inference at edge devices and collaborative model training through the cloud. However, distributed idler-bearing diagnosis still faces two major challenges: (1) heterogeneous sensor data across different idlers and time-varying fault features under evolving operating conditions and (2) limited edge computing and communication resources. To address these challenges, this study proposes Di-FedDIL, a distributed fault diagnosis framework for idler bearings under cloud-edge collaboration. The framework consists of the dilated separable attention convolution network (DiSAC-Net), federated learning via contrastive alignment and progressive Euclidean regularization (FedCAP), and dual-anchor incremental learning (DIL). For edge diagnosis, DiSAC-Net performs lightweight feature extraction and online fault inference at edge devices. For federated collaborative learning, FedCAP enables distributed clients to collaboratively learn shared diagnostic knowledge while adapting to heterogeneous local data. For incremental updating, DIL continuously adapts personalized models to evolving operating conditions while balancing new knowledge acquisition and historical knowledge retention. In addition, a hierarchical greedy optimization strategy jointly performs task offloading and bandwidth allocation to reduce diagnostic response time under cloud-edge resource constraints. Experimental results show that Di-FedDIL outperforms the compared federated learning methods. The proposed resource-allocation strategy reduces task completion time by approximately 25% compared with fully local computing. These results demonstrate that Di-FedDIL provides a practical solution for distributed idler-bearing fault diagnosis while improving execution efficiency under limited cloud-edge computing and communication resources.
papers.venue: Journal of Vibration and Control

papers.title: Smart Technologies in Construction and Transportation Infrastructure: A Review of AI, IoT, and Data-Driven Innovations
papers.abstract: While the field of civil engineering has traditionally been dominated by hands-on and experience-based techniques, the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), and data analytics are transforming it. This paper provides a structured outcome-oriented narrative review of the applications of smart technology in two dominant areas: construction management and transportation infrastructure. It is based on 37 peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, and technical reports from 2015 to 2026 that were selected purposively, without using a registered systematic search. The evidence has been grouped into eight application themes: AI/ML in construction project management; IoT-enabled site and structural monitoring; AI-driven intelligent transportation systems; IoT-based smart pavement and road monitoring; machine-learning-based structural health monitoring; digital twins and blockchain; UAV and computer-vision monitoring; and cybersecurity in smart infrastructure. The reported outcomes represent distinct performance dimensions and are not directly compared: examples include a 0.12% cost variance for AI/ML project models, a concrete strength prediction error within 1–2 MPa alongside a maximum UWB worker positioning error of 1.44 m for an IoT-based system, a 98.6% traffic-monitoring performance for a machine-learning classification model, and a hardhat-detection precision of 93.1% for Faster R-CNN. Themes of AI and IoT integration are most frequently associated with improved prediction, monitoring, and decision support, while digital twins and blockchain are primarily associated with data trust, traceability, and operational latency reduction. Recurring barriers include data interoperability, data security, implementation costs, and metric heterogeneity across literature. This review concludes with a research agenda prioritizing interoperable data standards, edge-AI and federated learning, cybersecurity-by-design, and standardized outcome reporting.
papers.venue: International Journal of Applied Smart Interdisciplinary Technologies

papers.title: Securing the Swarm:
papers.abstract: Since Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) swarms are more widely employed in mission-critical missions, they serve as potential targets of dual-vector attacks, e.g. Denial of Service (DoS) or GPS spoofing attacks that exploit cyber vulnerabilities and physical sensor dependencies, respectively. Most traditional Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) treat these domains independently or use centralized data processing which leads to single points of failure as well as privacy concerns. To overcome these limitations, this paper presents a Multi-Boundary Federated Intrusion Detection System (MB-FIDS) which builds upon disparate cyber-physical defense layers without sacrificing swarm privacy. Initially, we propose a Cyber Boundary defense based on the ensemble Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) with Borderline-SMOTE. This novel balancing method refines the decision boundary in problematic “Grayhole” attacks and enhances recall of minority classes compared with conventional resampling methods. Second, we introduce a Physical Boundary defense based on an unsupervised OCSVM combined with Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Thresholding. The rolling statistical properties of flight telemetry are learned, and an adaptive threshold is calculated that minimizes false positives caused by environmental noise (e.g wind gusts). Finally, we implement a Federated Learning framework using the FedYogi strategy, allowing the swarm to collaboratively update detection models while retaining sensitive flight logs locally. Experimental results on the WSN-DS and T-ITS datasets demonstrate that MB-FIDS achieves a detection accuracy of 99.2% for cyber threats and reduces physical false alarm rates by significant margins compared to static thresholding. Furthermore, the federated swarm is shown to converge within 15 communication rounds, proving the system's viability for resource-constrained, privacy-sensitive UAV operations.
papers.venue: CRC Press eBooks

papers.title: BCFL-DAI-PUB: Blockchain-integrated federated learning with dynamic adaptive incentives for privacy-utility balanced credit risk modelling
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of loan defaulters through collaborative analysis of financial data across multiple institutions is critical for maintaining financial stability and strengthening credit risk management. Although Federated Learning (FL) enables organizations to train models without exchanging raw data, its reliance on a centralized server introduces serious trust concerns, including vulnerability to gradient inversion and membership inference attacks. Blockchain-based Federated Learning (BCFL) addresses these challenges by cryptographically protecting and aggregating model updates through a smart contract, thereby providing a tamper-resistant learning process. In spite of these security enhancements, current BCFL frameworks do not ensure sustained client participation in real-world settings. Moreover, while traditional incentive mechanisms promote truthful participation and discourage free-riding and malicious behavior, they mainly reward model utility and neglect privacy contribution. To mitigate this limitation, we propose BCFL-DAI-PUB, a blockchain-federated learning framework integrating an innovative Dynamic Adaptive Incentive (DAI) mechanism to achieve a Privacy-Utility Balance (PUB). The proposed DAI dynamically applies three complementary incentive components, such as SCAFFOLD-based correction, adaptive differential privacy (DP-Boost), and monetary rewards, to jointly optimize learning utility and privacy protection. This work promotes honest participation, discourages dishonest behavior, and enables rapid recovery from malicious attacks, thereby improving global convergence and overall model effectiveness. The proposed BCFL-DAI-PUB achieves a final AUC of 0.91, improving upon the HE-based BCFL-PS-HER baseline (0.86) by 1.06×. By replacing homomorphic encryption with adaptive differential privacy and combining it with a dynamic incentive mechanism, the proposed framework improves both efficiency and resilience over the baseline, which relies on static reputation-based coordination. Compared with the baseline BCFL-PS-HER model, BCFL-DAI-PUB recovers from malicious disruption 1.82× faster and achieves approximately 1.22× higher MIA resistance, while the baseline incurs approximately 1.09× higher communication overhead and 1.14× higher storage overhead. These results show that BCFL-DAI-PUB improves predictive performance, strengthens privacy protection, reduces system cost, and provides more robust operation in blockchain-enabled federated credit-risk modelling.
papers.venue: PLoS ONE

papers.title: The limits of privacy enhancement in healthcare federated learning: a ELSA perspective in the EU context
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) usage is steadily increasing in healthcare. Offering an attractive alternative to centralized data processing, FL is often promoted as a privacy-enhancing technology (PET) because it keeps patient-level data local, exchanging only aggregated data or model updates. As such, it is frequently presented as a means of addressing the ethical, legal and societal challenges associated with the use of sensitive health data. This framing has contributed to growing policy interest in FL within initiatives such as the European Health Data Space (EHDS). This paper examines FL from an ethical, legal and societal (ELSA) perspective in the EU context, focusing on its interaction with the European data protection framework and contemporary debates on health data governance. First, it analyzes the interaction between FL architectures and the General Data Protection regulation (GDPR), showing that questions of controllership, joint responsibility, and identifiability persist despite decentralization, particularly in complex multi-institutional settings. Second, it argues that privacy-centric approaches to health data governance remain ethically insufficient because harmful inferences, discrimination, and collective harms may arise even when data remains formally anonymous. The dominant focus on reidentification risk thus reflects a narrow and individualistic conception of privacy that is poorly adapted to the contemporary data landscape of the EU. It fails to capture broader forms of harm, including group-level discrimination, inferential profiling, and structural power asymmetries. The paper concludes that, despite its framing as a PET, the use of FL alone is not sufficient to guarantee appropriate health data protection. Indeed, FL should also be approached as a distributed data-processing paradigm in which risks and benefits depend on implementation choices, institutional arrangements, and regulatory interpretation. Accordingly, FL should be situated within broader questions of data governance, including how access, accountability, and collaboration are structured and distributed across institutions.
papers.venue: Frontiers in Big Data

papers.title: A secure social credit evaluation system based on blockchain and federated learning: architecture design, encrypted aggregation algorithm, and experimental evaluation
papers.abstract: Aiming at the common engineering challenges of data silos, privacy leakage, untraceable authorization and insufficient model interpretability existing in social credit assessment scenarios, this paper constructs a distributed secure credit evaluation system integrating block chain and federated learning. A federated aggregation algorithm based on homomorphic encryption is proposed to support privacy-preserving collaborative modeling across multi-institution platforms. Meanwhile, a smart contract-enabled authorization mechanism is established to realize full lifecycle data traceability and standardized service compliance. Verified on the UCI German Credit Dataset, the proposed system achieves an AUC value of 0.83, which is 9.2% higher than that of traditional centralized architectures. In the scenario of 5000 concurrent credit assessment requests, the system throughput reaches 2800 TPS with an end-to-end delay of 350 ms. Superior to conventional schemes in assessment accuracy, operational performance and data security, the system can provide a reliable technical reference for practical social credit assessment applications.

papers.title: TOPOLOGICAL FLUID DYNAMICS OF COLLECTIVE CONSCIOUSNESS: A MATHEMATICAL FRAMEWORK FOR KNOWLEDGE FLOW AND IDEA PROPAGATION THROUGH NON-EUCLIDEAN SOCIAL MANIFOLDS
papers.abstract: TOPOLOGICAL FLUID DYNAMICS OF COLLECTIVE CONSCIOUSNESS Summary Author: Dr. Mohamed Kamal Arafa El-Rakhawi, Independent Researcher, 2026 This groundbreaking work proposes a revolutionary paradigm shift in computational sociology: treating collective human consciousness not as a discrete network, but as a continuous topological fluid flowing through non-Euclidean social manifolds. The El-Rakhawi Collective Fluidity Framework adapts the Navier-Stokes equations to model knowledge momentum, ideological pressure, and cognitive velocity, while employing algebraic topology—specifically persistent homology and Betti numbers—to quantify the topological stability of ideological vortices in high-dimensional semantic spaces generated by Large Language Models. The framework introduces four rigorously defined, dimensionless indices: the Cognitive Viscosity Index (CVI) measuring resistance to cognitive change, the Ideological Vortex Index (IVI) quantifying echo chamber entrapment, the Social Turbulence Index (STI) predicting systemic phase transitions, and the innovative Phase Transition Direction Coefficient (PTDC) distinguishing between destructive chaos and constructive social transformation. The Unified Collective Fluidity Index (UCFI) provides a single metric for societal health through a geometric mean that prevents stability-washing. Methodologically, the work bridges theory and empirics through an operationalization pipeline using LLM embeddings, persistent homology computation via Gudhi/Ripser libraries, and the Mapper algorithm for topological landscape visualization. Critically, it implements privacy-preserving computation through federated learning and differential privacy, ensuring compliance with GDPR, CCPA, and Arab data protection laws. Empirical validation includes both in-silico simulations and retrospective analysis of the 2018-2019 French Yellow Vests movement using 12 million tweets, demonstrating that the STI threshold of 0.75 reliably preceded major protests by 7 days, while persistent homology identified three distinct ideological vortices. Comparative analysis of destructive versus constructive phase transitions (2005 French riots vs. 1989 Berlin Wall fall) confirmed the PTDC's discriminative power. The framework makes four falsifiable predictions, proposes a 12-year experimental roadmap requiring 545 million USD, and establishes ethical safeguards including algorithmic transparency and independent oversight. Licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 for academic use with commercial licensing reserved, this work establishes the foundation for a new field: the physics of collective consciousness, offering unprecedented tools for predicting social unrest, combating misinformation through topological inoculation, and supporting constructive democratic transformation while preserving cognitive liberty and individual privacy.

papers.venue: Lecture notes in computer science

papers.title: Explainable Federated Learning Framework for IoT Malware and Network-Based Attack Detection
papers.abstract: The size and complexity of Internet of Things (IoT) botnets have brought the traditional intrusion-detection model to its breaking point, where sensitive networktraffic from various systems and devices must be aggregated to a centralized pointfor analysis. Federated Learning (FL) solves this by allowing each site to learn locally and only sharing the model updates, however, FL detectors come with threepractical problems that the deployable system must face, namely that the data oneach of the sites is not in the same statistical distribution (known as non-IID data),that the FL detector cannot fully explain the reasons behind the decision made bythe shared model, and that it is susceptible to malicious participants. This Phase2 (P2) report takes the phase 1 proposal a step further and presents the completeframework as it has been implemented and evaluated in practice. A hash-level,leak-free train/validation/test split of multi-architecture IoT traffic from the CICYNU-IoTMal 2026 dataset (ARM, MIPS, MIPSEL and x86 flow records) is createdfollowed by a correlation-based feature pruning, architecture-aware outlier removaland a per-client resampling pipeline. This pipeline is contrasted with pooled Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Random Forest and XGBoost baseline, a personalisedvariant which fine-tunes the shared FedProx model on each client’s own data, anda Hierarchical Cascade which first gates Benign traffic out with a near-perfect binary Random Forest before a dedicated XGBoost sub-classifier separates the threemalware families; this cascade achieves the highest row-level macro-F1 of the entirestudy (0.589), outperforming all flat and federated alternatives. Explainability isassessed using SHAP DeepExplainer independently for each architecture client, andthe cross-client explainability consistency score is calculated using pairwise Pearson and Spearman correlation between feature attributions, which yields a meanpairwise Spearman correlation of 0.9745, and a top-5 feature Jaccard similarity of1.0, suggesting that regardless of the client’s traffic, the shared global model relieson essentially the same evidence. Robustness is tested with two of the four federated clients subjected to a label-flipping poisoning attack with poisoning rates of25%, 50%, and 100%: FedProx gracefully degrades under moderate poisoning butexperiences collapse once poisoning dominates the affected clients’ local data. Combined, these results show that the main remaining limitation of the framework isDarkNexus/Gafgyt confusion, the accuracy penalty of federation and personalisation compared to pooled training, and that explanations generated by the frameworkare consistent enough across the various types of IoT hardware to be relied upon bya human analyst.
papers.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

papers.title: Utkarsh-SafeMind: Unified Reproducibility Package for Privacy-Preserving Student Mental Well-Being Assessment
papers.abstract: This repository provides a unified reproducibility package for Utkarsh–SafeMind: A Unified On-Device and Federated Learning Framework for Privacy-Preserving Student Mental Well-Being Assessment.The package integrates the Utkarsh on-device behavioral assessment pipeline, the SafeMind federated learning framework, and the Federated Behavioral Model Refinement (FBMR) bridge. The framework is designed to support privacy-aware refinement of a seven-dimensional Composite Well-being Score (CWS) without requiring the centralized collection of sensitive student-level information.The associated study evaluates the integration using synthetic, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data representing four simulated colleges, across four experimental configurations and three random seeds. The reported evaluation includes CWS calibration, probability-simplex constraint preservation, communication overhead, cryptographic mask-cancellation error, and differential privacy accounting.The package is intended to support inspection, reproducibility, and further development of the reported experimental workflow. The results are based on synthetic evaluation data and do not establish clinical effectiveness or generalizability to real student populations.The deposited archive contains the integrated source code, experiment and test materials, setup instructions, documentation, and applicable license and citation information, to the extent included in the final package. Please consult the README and validation report for the exact contents, execution instructions, dependencies, and validation status.
papers.venue: Figshare

papers.title: TrustLite-FL: multi-statistic trust aggregation for robust federated learning in consumer IoT
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) trains shared models on consumer IoT devices without moving raw data off the device, but poisoning can compromise it. We propose TrustLite-FL , a trust-weighted aggregation framework that mitigates several poisoning behaviors. It scores client updates by entropy, magnitude and direction relative to the round, smooths those scores over time, clips update norms, and logs suspicious behavior for audit. Its aggregation and scoring scale linearly with clients and model parameters. We prove that update entropy is invariant to positive scaling and sign flips, so entropy alone cannot detect them. We evaluate it in simulation on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10, benchmark proxies for consumer device data, with non-IID clients, five attacks plus a clean setting, 30% adversaries, seven baselines and three seeds. It has the highest mean accuracy, or matches it, in 9 of 15 attacked settings, and is within one percentage point of the best in 13. Ablation shows that the norm clip provides most of this robustness. The trust layer excludes every Gaussian noise adversary, excluding at most 2.9% of benign clients, but no sign flipping or ALIE adversary. Aggregation is 11 times slower than FedAvg at 1,000 clients but faster than Krum from 500 clients.
papers.venue: Scientific Reports

papers.title: Solar Thermal District Heating and Cooling for Smart, Sustainable, AI-Optimized Cities
papers.abstract: Rapid urbanization and climate imperatives place cities at the center of energy transformation, yet thermal demand roughly half of urban energy end-use remains under addressed by electricity focused renewable strategies. This chapter, per the authors, examines solar thermal district heating and cooling (STDHC) systems as foundational infrastructure for sustainable smart cities. It reviews collector technologies and seasonal thermal storage configurations, then analyzes integration across the physical, cyber, and application layers of smart city architecture, emphasizing digital twins, IoT sensing, and machine-learning optimization including model predictive control and reinforcement learning. International case studies from Canada, Denmark, Croatia, and China demonstrate solar fractions above 50% and substantial carbon reductions. Lifecycle, cost, and energy-justice analyses benchmark performance and equity, while the closing sections identify deployment barriers and propose a research agenda spanning compact storage, federated learning, and policy alignment with SDG 7 and SDG 11.
papers.venue: IGI Global eBooks

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-driven precision management of Helicobacter pylori: an integrated framework from endoscopy and multi-omics to vaccine design and digital care
papers.abstract: Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection, affecting half of the world’s population, is the principal cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer, yet its clinical management is increasingly undermined by the rapidly escalating global burden of antibiotic resistance, the suboptimal accuracy of conventional diagnostic methods, and the declining efficacy of empirical therapeutic regimens. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping this landscape, but existing research remains fragmented across single modalities. We propose a conceptual five-module framework that integrates AI approaches across the H. pylori care continuum: (1) global disease burden and the evolutionary dynamics of H. pylori drug resistance; (2) the application of multimodal AI, from convolutional neural networks to vision-language foundation models, for endoscopic early screening, pathological identification, and functional assessment; (3) the harnessing of machine learning (ML) on genomic and electronic health record data to decipher resistance mechanisms and generate personalized eradication regimens; (4) AI-driven vaccine target discovery and generative design, spanning reverse vaccinology to de novo immunogen creation; and (5) a digital closed-loop patient management platform that leverages new media and reinforcement learning to enhance adherence and eradication rates. We further delineate the core challenges of data bias, cross-scenario generalization, and the critical absence of prospective randomized evidence, and propose a future direction anchored in multimodal foundation models, federated learning, and continuous AI quality improvement. Rather than an established clinical pathway, this framework is proposed as a conceptual blueprint that, once prospectively validated, could upgrade AI-enabled H. pylori care from isolated image recognition toward an end-to-end “perception–reasoning–intervention” system, offering a blueprint for precision prevention and control.
papers.venue: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

papers.title: Privacy protection and data security mechanisms for artificial intelligence-based psychological counseling systems
papers.abstract: This paper investigates advanced privacy protection and data security mechanisms for artificial intelligence-based psychological counseling systems. The study designed a hierarchical security framework that integrates technologies such as hybrid encryption, dynamic multi-dimensional anonymization, adaptive access control, differential privacy federated learning, and automated compliance auditing to address the technical challenges of the entire data lifecycle. The proposed techniques are experimentally validated on large-scale anonymized datasets in a secure cloud infrastructure to simulate distributed and centralized application scenarios. The experimental results show that the method has little impact on the model accuracy and computational performance, and at the same time, it has a significant reduction in the risk of adversarial inference rate and data leakage. The combination of federated optimization and strong cryptographic protocols effectively reduces centralized data vulnerabilities and enhances distributed privacy protection. The automated audit mechanism ensures traceability and compliance of the system in all running stages. These findings suggest that it is essential to protect sensitive mental health data driven by artificial intelligence. These findings set a benchmark for the secure engineering of digital mental health services.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence and Data-Driven Innovation: A Comprehensive Multidisciplinary Review of Machine Learning, Big Data Analytics, Healthcare, Industry, Business, and Intelligent Decision-Making
papers.abstract: Advanced analytics, predictive modelling and intelligent decision making are reshaping a wide range of industries with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) and data innovation. This review compares the applications of machine learning, deep learning and big data analytics in healthcare, business, manufacturing, agriculture, smart-cities and public governance. It delves into their role in enhancing operational efficiency, predictive intelligence, resource optimization, and quality management. Key challenges that are included in the discussion are data privacy, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity, scalability, and model interpretability. In addition, new developments like federated learning, edge computing, and generative AI are taken into account. The proper application and good governance of technologies is still necessary for sustainable technological development.
papers.venue: Global Trends in Science and Technology

papers.title: Integrating Blockchain and Artificial Intelligence for Resilient and Intelligent Supply Chain Management
papers.abstract: Resilient and intelligent supply chains are the need of the hour as disruptions are growing, information is becoming more fragmented and markets are changing rapidly. This review explores how blockchain and AI can be used together to enhance supply-chain visibility, security, prediction, coordination and adaptability. While blockchain offers decentralized, immutability, and traceability, AI is about turning operational data into forecasts, optimized decision making and automated responses. They are integrated and support the supplier management, demand forecast, inventory management, predictive maintenance, logistics, product authentication, disruption management and sustainable circular operations. The review also identifies the potential for smart contracts, federated learning, IoT, edge computing and digital twins to amplify the blockchain–AI's scope to span interwoven supply chains. However, these advantages are mitigated by scalability, interoperability, data privacy and security, cost, limited knowledge, opacity of algorithms, regulatory uncertainty and governance issues. What's needed for future progress are real-world validation, explainable and privacy-preserving AI, energy-efficient blockchain architectures, common technical standards, and meaningful human oversight. In general, the combination of blockchain and AI presents a viable potential for transparent, predictive, responsive, secure, sustainable, and learning supply chains.
papers.venue: Computer and decision making.

papers.title: BAFL-IIoT: blockchain-authenticated adaptive federated learning for anomaly detection in Industrial Internet of Things networks
papers.abstract: Securing Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments against anomalies requires frameworks that can concurrently ensure data privacy, withstand adversarial manipulation, and operate efficiently under resource-constrained conditions. Prevailing federated learning (FL) methods are hampered by susceptibility to adversarial attacks, data heterogeneity across non-IID devices, and prohibitive communication demands. To address these shortcomings, this paper introduces the BAFL-IIoT, a Secure Adaptive Federated Network comprising three novel components: (1) a Blockchain-Based Authentication (BBA) mechanism that leverages smart contracts to validate model updates prior to global aggregation, thereby neutralising poisoning attacks; (2) an Adaptive Autoencoder-LSTM (AAEL) module that autonomously tunes learning rate and dropout hyperparameters in response to real-time IIoT feedback, supporting reliable detection across heterogeneous non-IID environments; and (3) quantised and sparse model update strategies that curtail communication overhead by 30% (measured as data transmission cost reduction relative to full-precision FedAVG), with a bandwidth reduction ratio (BRR) of 0.67 representing the fractional reduction in per-update transmission size due to 8-bit quantisation alone. Experiments on the TON_IoT and Edge-IIoTset benchmark datasets yield an anomaly detection accuracy of 94.7%, an authentication success rate (ASR) of 98.5%, and a malicious update detection (MUD) rate of 91.2%, with convergence achieved within 40 global training rounds. These outcomes affirm BAFL-IIoT as a scalable, secure, and computationally practical solution for IIoT anomaly detection.
papers.venue: Journal of Cloud Computing Advances Systems and Applications

papers.title: Fed-IGTD: A federated learning-based framework for tabular-to-image encoding
papers.abstract: Tabular-to-image encoding methods, which transform tabular data into image-like representations, have shown promising results in predictive tasks. Despite their benefits, these methods follow a centralized paradigm, in which the data are collected and models are trained on a central device. This raises privacy and security concerns, particularly the risk of data leakage, unauthorized data collection and access to users' private information. Federated Learning (FL) provides a decentralized framework in which multiple clients jointly optimize a shared model without directly sharing training data. We introduce Fed-IGTD, a horizontal FL-based approach in which clients share a common feature space and upload only local statistics, from which the server reconstructs the global correlation matrix and obtains a feature-to-pixel mapping to train a convolutional neural network via Federated Averaging (FedAvg). We studied two differential privacy (DP) mechanisms: (i) a one-shot Gaussian mechanism protecting the correlation-aggregation step; and (ii) a client-level DP-FedAvg variant protecting the training with privacy loss composed via a Renyi-DP accountant. We evaluated Fed-IGTD on five datasets under a systematic sweep of non-IID severity and privacy budgets. Privacy protection applied to the mapping-construction step has little impact on predictive performance. By contrast, DP-FedAvg substantially degrades utility at moderate privacy budgets with a small client cohort (K=5). Ablation study indicates that this degradation is driven mainly by the injected noise rather than by uniform averaging or update clipping. Macro-F1 exhibits sensitivity to performance degradation than accuracy under non-IID heterogeneity and class imbalance.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Clustered Federated Learning in Non-IID Wireless Networks
papers.abstract: Current and emerging mobile networks face increasing privacy, scalability, and performance challenges as distributed learning becomes essential for advanced 6G services. These challenges are amplified by the presence of non-IID data, naturally arising in heterogeneous wireless environments, that degrade the performance of standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches. To address non-IID data across clients, we propose a Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) framework that assigns clients to specialized models during training. Data-domain clustering initializes model-based clustering, enabling identification and exploitation of client similarities without sharing raw data while reducing communication cost. Motivated by mmWave beam selection, we evaluate our methods on a wireless simulation dataset (DeepMIMO) and complement it with two non-IID benchmarks (FEMNIST, Rotated CIFAR-10) to isolate different non-IID characteristics. Our best configurations improve accuracy over IFCA by 4.8 pp on DeepMIMO and 10.6 pp on FEMNIST while reducing downlink data volume by 83.1 % on FEMNIST compared to IFCA. We demonstrate that different clustering strategies suit different non-IID characteristics. These results show that our CFL methods enable resource-efficient, and high-performance distributed learning in future 6G networks.

papers.title: Trustworthy Distributed Machine Learning in Cloud-Edge-IoT Systems: A Heterogeneity-Aware Survey of Security, Privacy, and Robustness
papers.abstract: Distributed machine learning (DML), including conventional distributed training and federated learning (FL), enables collaborative model development across cloud-edge-IoT systems without fully centralizing raw data. However, distributing data, computation, updates, and orchestration increases the attack surface and introduces coupled challenges across privacy, robustness, reliability, fairness, and governance. This survey presents a security-centered, heterogeneity-aware roadmap for trustworthy DML, with FL treated as a prominent high-risk case. We first characterize the assets, adversaries, trust assumptions, and coordination patterns that define DML/FL security boundaries. We then analyze how statistical, system, and trust heterogeneity, including non-IID data, resource asymmetry, intermittent participation, and cross-silo/cross-device trust differences, affect convergence, fairness, attack detectability, and defense reliability. Next, we synthesize attack-defense interactions across poisoning, backdoors, Byzantine manipulation, privacy leakage, model extraction, network/orchestration attacks, Sybil behavior, and strategic participation. We further compare layered defenses, including robust aggregation, drift-aware optimization, differential privacy, secure aggregation, homomorphic encryption, secure multiparty computation, trusted execution environments, watermarking, provenance, authenticated communication, and monitoring. Finally, we discuss deployment, evaluation, governance, and open research guidelines, emphasizing reproducible, non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) partitions, attack-aware benchmarks, privacy budgets, attack success rate, client-level disparity, latency, communication, memory, energy/carbon overhead, and auditable lifecycle artifacts.

papers.title: On the Generalization Gap of Streaming Federated Learning with Markovian Data
papers.abstract: Streaming federated learning (SFL) allows clients to train a shared model from continuously arriving data without retaining large local datasets. Such streams often exhibit temporal dependence, yet its effect on generalization remains poorly understood. In this paper we study the expected generalization gap of the aggregated model when client data follow Markov processes, using information-theoretic and rate-distortion techniques. Our framework accommodates heterogeneous Markovian dynamics across clients and distinguishes temporal dependence from information acquired during local learning. We establish bounds under cross-entropy loss, specializing them to Linear Next-Token Prediction (LNTP) and Self-Attention Next-Token Prediction (SANTP). These results quantify the effects of client count, communication rounds, sample size, data dimension, mixing time, and context length. In particular, they reveal a communication--generalization tradeoff: although frequent aggregation may help optimization, it can weaken generalization guarantees. They also suggest a potential advantage of distributed over centralized streaming learning under a fixed total data budget. Temporal dependence enters through the square root of the mixing time. By analyzing the history-state process, we obtain refined bounds with improved context-length dependence under suitable mixing conditions. Experiments on GPT-style language-model pretraining with TinyStories and real-world time-series forecasting illustrate how collaboration and communication frequency influence generalization under temporal dependence

papers.title: Governance-Aware Federated Learning for Multi-Agent AI Systems: A Policy-Driven Framework for Trustworthy Collaborative AI
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without exchanging raw data, but conventional FL provides limited runtime governance, evidence verification, fairness assessment, explainability monitoring, and auditability. This paper proposes Governance-Aware Federated Learning (GAFL), which combines independent governance-evidence verification, temporal trust, fairness and explanation assessment, anomaly detection, policy enforcement, normalized aggregation, and tamper-evident audit logging. Client-reported governance values are authenticated, bound to their submitted model updates, and independently recomputed before aggregation. A cross-silo prototype with 10 participants was evaluated on the Adult Income dataset under honest, benign non-IID, biased-data, malicious-update, non-compliant, falsified-evidence, and mixed-threat scenarios. Four methods were compared across five random seeds: FedAvg, FedAvg with anomaly filtering, GAFL without independent verification, and complete GAFL. Complete GAFL intervened on all affected participants at the final round across the evaluated risk scenarios, including identifying 100% of falsified-evidence participants, whereas GAFL without verification identified none of the falsified-evidence participants. Final macro-F1 ranged from 0.7520 to 0.7733 across GAFL scenarios. Complete GAFL required 173.67 plus or minus 26.94 ms of governance processing per round, compared with 3.82 plus or minus 0.79 ms for FedAvg. A strict demographic-parity threshold also caused frequent interventions for honest participants, demonstrating a significant fairness-policy and utility trade-off.

papers.title: Data Amount Heterogeneity Improves Performance in Federated Learning for Neuroimaging
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) allows for secure analysis of distributed data without data sharing. We and others have successfully applied FL to neuroimaging tasks, such as Alzheimer's disease classification from structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). FL trains a deep learning model locally at each site, encrypts the local model parameters and sends them to a federation controller that aggregates the local models under homomorphic encryption, the resulting community model is sent back to the sites for further training, and the process repeats for a number of rounds. FL often achieves learning performance (e.g., accuracy) close to centralized training, but no data leaves the sites and model parameters are protected through encryption and other measures. In this paper, we show that federations composed of sites with heterogeneous amounts of data (1 large site plus small sites) perform better than homogeneous (same data per site) federations, particularly in low data regimes, while reaching performance close to centralized training. Having a big site often results in faster convergence and higher final accuracy. Heterogeneous federations better exploit sites with small amounts of data, a common situation in large consortia such as ENIGMA.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Semantic Communications over Multiple Access Channels
papers.abstract: This paper presents a federated learning (FL) framework for semantic communication (SemCom) over the multiple access channel (MAC), where multiple distributed transmitters simultaneously convey semantic information to a common receiver using end-to-end learned semantic representations. Semantic feature extraction, compression, wireless transmission, and semantic inference are jointly optimized through FL-based SemCom. Unlike conventional SemCom systems that train users independently, simultaneous semantic transmissions over the MAC enable concurrent training of multiple transmitters within the same transmission interval, thereby reducing training overhead and channel usage. Federated semantic aggregation is incorporated with shared and personalized encoder components, allowing transmitters with limited local training data to benefit from semantic representations learned from transmitters possessing larger datasets while preserving local adaptation. Evaluated using the CIFAR-10 dataset over fading channels, the proposed approach maintains high semantic inference accuracy under shared wireless access and significantly improves performance under severe data imbalance. In the meantime, simultaneous semantic transmissions can significantly reduce training overhead while preserving robust semantic performance across distributed transmitters with heterogeneous local datasets. These results highlight the potential of combining FL and SemCom to support scalable and communication-efficient edge intelligence in future wireless networks.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Over-the-Air Federated Learning over Cell-Free Massive MIMO System with User-Centric Clustering
papers.abstract: This paper investigates cross-layer design for differentially private federated learning over cell-free massive MIMO networks with over-the-air (OTA) aggregation. Distributed access points (APs) collaboratively serve user equipments (UEs) through user-centric clustering, where clipped local model updates are perturbed with Gaussian noise and simultaneously transmitted over a shared uplink for OTA averaging at a central processing unit. Exploiting channel hardening, we show that thermal noise inherent in wireless reception can act as a privacy-masking resource, reducing or even eliminating the need for artificial noise. Based on this observation, we formulate a joint optimization problem over AP-UE associations, UE transmit powers, and artificial noise variances to minimize aggregation variance subject to per-UE zero-concentrated differential privacy constraints derived from an ergodic privacy accounting framework. Analysis reveals a regime-dependent structure: stringent privacy requirements favor low transmit powers and sparse AP associations to exploit thermal noise for privacy, whereas relaxed requirements favor larger clusters to improve aggregation quality. The resulting mixed-integer nonconvex problem is solved via alternating optimization combining difference-of-convex power allocation and greedy coordinate-descent clustering. Numerical results show up to 89% lower aggregation variance than conventional baselines and enable 97% test accuracy on MNIST with consistent gains on CIFAR-10. Under strict privacy budgets, competing schemes remain near random-chance performance, while under relaxed budgets they continue to lag significantly behind the proposed design.

papers.title: Split Federated Unlearning
papers.abstract: Split federated learning (SFL) combines partitioned model execution with federated aggregation to support collaborative learning across distributed Web and edge environments. However, removing learned contributions in SFL is challenging due to cross-partition coupling and historical influence propagation through dual-side aggregation. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first systematic formulation of Split Federated Unlearning (SFU), encompassing client-wise and class-wise removal, counterfactual retraining, and partition-specific update constraints. We theoretically characterize historical influence propagation and mode-dependent unlearning feasibility, revealing structural limitations of restricted model updates. As an initial solution, we propose SURE, integrating dual-importance estimation, selective parameter perturbation, and importance-guided recovery. Extensive experiments with existing unlearning methods adapted to SFL reveal substantial forgetting-utility trade-offs across model architectures, data distributions, and update modes. SURE achieves competitive agreement with mode-matched retraining at modest additional cost, while further analyses highlight the impact of split position and update constraints on unlearning behavior. These findings establish SFU as a distinct research problem and provide a foundation for unlearning in partitioned federated systems.

papers.title: Pricing Cross-Bank Context in Federated Anti-Money Laundering
papers.abstract: Most graph-based Anti-Money Laundering (AML) methods assume access to a pooled transaction graph containing all accounts and payments, which in reality does not exist. Federated learning offers the necessary privacy guarantees but it remains unclear how money laundering patterns spanning separate graphs can effectively be detected. We exploit transactions already recorded by both endpoint banks to approximate remote account states locally, enabling multi-layer Graph Neural Network (GNN) computation without additional account-specific exchange. Starting from this baseline, we test whether the remaining context is worth sharing, using a disclosure ladder that adds two transaction counts per remote account or the counterparty's own GNN states. On AMLworld HI-Small, across six GNN backbones and up to 32 silos, the observable baseline yields the largest gain and keeps it as fragmentation shrinks the visible slice; counts add a robust correction, while exact remote states help only in specific regimes. In controlled privacy--utility studies, the noise needed to protect shared states erases their detection value before it buys meaningful privacy, whereas counts stay useful even under strong privacy protection. These findings support a practical rule for banks: use what they already record, and formally protect the little that must move.

papers.title: Evaluating Federated Vision-Language and Vision-Only Models for Privacy-Aware Breast Cancer Imaging
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) shows promise for breast imaging, but limited labeled data, institutional data fragmentation, and privacy concerns hinder centralized training. We investigate a privacy-aware federated learning framework combining pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) with client-level differential privacy. We compare general-purpose CLIP models, biomedical BiomedCLIP, and an ImageNet-pretrained ViT-B/16 baseline on two public breast imaging datasets, with and without differential privacy. We also evaluate a CLIP ViT-B/16 ablation that removes the text pathway. Evaluation includes patient-level ROC-AUC with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, baseline comparisons, threshold sensitivity, inter-model agreement, and communication cost. Under federated learning, all five models achieve high normal-versus-sick discrimination (ROC-AUC: 0.940-0.990). However, acquisition year alone achieves 0.974 on the same test partition, raising concerns about confounding rather than genuine pathology recognition. Benign-versus-malignant discrimination remains uncertain (ROC-AUC: 0.504-0.637), with all confidence intervals including 0.50. Removing the text pathway preserves classification accuracy while halving communication cost. Differential privacy reduces ROC-AUC by 0.375, attributable to perturbing the full model state rather than only trainable parameters. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating confounding, predictive reliability, privacy implementation, and deployment efficiency when developing federated AI systems for breast imaging.

papers.title: Information-Theoretic Secure Aggregation With Heterogeneous Client Quantization
papers.abstract: In federated learning (FL), secure aggregation enables a server to compute the sum of local model updates of $N$ clients, without revealing any information on the individual model updates to the server, beyond their sum. Different clients may be subject to heterogeneous bandwidth constraints, and consequently may choose different numbers of quantization levels to represent the information they send. Most secure aggregation works require the clients to project the values of their update parameters to a common finite group (or field), which does not directly accommodate heterogeneous precision constraints on their transmitted masked updates. Existing approaches of secure aggregation with heterogeneous quantization levels reveal partial aggregates of model-updates, and can reveal segments of individual model updates, under certain dropout and client-server collusion patterns. To prevent this privacy breach, we propose an information-theoretic secure aggregation scheme that tolerates client drop-outs, and up to $T$ semi-honest clients that collude with each other and with the server, under heterogeneous quantization at clients. Our protocol utilizes the $(T+1, N)$ threshold black-box secret sharing construction, where secret shares of the client updates, despite belonging to distinct algebraic groups owing to different quantization, are generated from identical linear integer systems.

papers.title: SCAFFOLD under Hessian Similarity: Sharp Convergence Rates
papers.abstract: One of the main challenges of federated learning is heterogeneous data split among the clients, leading to biased local updates called client drift. The SCAFFOLD algorithm (Karimireddy et al., 2020) corrects client drift with control variates, but its relation to the similarity of client data is not yet fully understood: the original similarity-based guarantees cover only quadratics with a stronger second-order similarity assumption, and a follow-up weakly convex analysis (Luo et al., 2025) obtains a $\sqrt{Lδ}$ dependence for $L$-smooth losses with averaged Hessian similarity $δ$. We analyze SCAFFOLD with minibatch-based control variates and establish linear dependence on Hessian similarity beyond quadratics, for both convex and nonconvex objectives. In particular, for convex objectives with exact gradients, $R$ SCAFFOLD rounds with $K$ local steps lead to an objective gap of order $(L/K+δ)D_0^2/R$, where $D_0$ is the initial distance to a minimizer. When $K=Θ(L/δ)$, it improves the minibatch SGD rate by a factor $Θ(L/δ)$. For nonconvex objectives, we prove an analogous stationarity guarantee under uniform Hessian similarity for a client-selection variant. In both settings, we extend these guarantees to stochastic gradients and prove matching lower bounds for the analyzed methods with constant local stepsizes. We also show that, under partial participation, even identical clients need not obtain the full communication benefit of additional local steps.

papers.title: FedAvgIm: Federated Learning for Multi-Site Impedance Identification of Inverter-Based Resources
papers.abstract: With the increasing integration of inverter-based resources (IBRs) into power systems, assessing small-signal interaction stability has become essential. Impedance/admittance models enable frequency-domain characterization of IBR dynamics without requiring access to proprietary internal control details, but measurement-based identification is time-consuming and must be repeated across operating points. This paper proposes FedAvgIm, a privacy-aware federated-learning framework for multi-site dq-admittance identification under severe local data scarcity and raw-data-locality constraints. Each IBR site trains a local feed-forward neural network using a small set of operating-point-frequency samples, while only model parameters are shared with a cloud aggregator that performs sample-size-weighted FedAvg to update a global model and broadcast it back to all sites. To demonstrate effectiveness, EMT measurement-based admittance datasets are constructed for nine grid-following IBRs with different parameters, architectures, measurement-noise levels, and non-IID settings, where each client has only 40-390 training samples. Results show that FedAvgIm achieves performance close to centralized training and consistently outperforms local-only learning and raw-data-locality-preserving transfer-learning baselines. Additional studies show that FedAvgIm maintains stable learning behavior under measurement noise and remains beneficial under moderate non-IID conditions. The estimated dq-admittance models are further applied to generalized Nyquist stability analysis and validated against EMT time-domain simulations under multiple operating points and grid-strength conditions.

papers.title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
papers.abstract: Clinical expertise is inherently distributed: it resides not in any single dataset or institution but in the accumulated reasoning experiences of thousands of clinicians navigating diverse patient populations, resource constraints, and evolving treatment protocols. Yet current approaches to scaling medical AI, from centralized large language models to federated learning, remain anchored to a data-centric paradigm that treats knowledge as static parameters to be aggregated. In this Perspective, we argue for a fundamental shift from data aggregation to experience aggregation. We propose Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS), a framework in which distributed AI agents operating across healthcare institutions synthesize collective clinical intelligence by sharing abstracted reasoning trajectories rather than raw data or model parameters. Unlike federated learning, which averages numerical gradients across homogeneous model architectures, DAS exchanges structured records of clinical reasoning, specifically the sequence of observations, hypotheses, tool invocations, and outcome feedback that constitute diagnostic experience. We examine the architectural principles, deployment considerations, governance requirements, and critical open challenges of this framework, laying the groundwork for a collaborative medical AI ecosystem where distributed expertise autonomously adapts to the complexities of longitudinal patient care.

papers.title: Satellite Intelligence: Distributed Training, Collaborative Inference,and LLM Adaptation in LEO Constellation
papers.abstract: The proliferation of orbital sensing data and the real-time demands of emerging global services are pushing low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks from bent-pipe relays toward intelligent onboard processing. This shift confronts a fundamental tension, where modern artificial intelligence (AI) training paradigms require intensive computation, abundant memory, and stable connectivity, all of which are scarce under the dynamic topologies, intermittent links, and severe size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints of satellite networks. Addressing this tension demands rethinking AI workflows, from training and inference to the emerging deployment of large language models (LLMs), under a constraint-aware design philosophy. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first survey that jointly covers all three, whereas prior surveys examine these aspects in isolation. We begin by identifying the deployment challenge of satellite intelligence (SI) and deriving design principles for SI. We then examine three advancing paradigms: i) distributed training, where federated learning (FL) and split learning (SL) enable satellite-ground co-training under resource limitations; ii) collaborative inference, which exploits single-satellite, multi-satellite, and satellite-ground architectures to meet real-time service demands; and iii) on-orbit LLM adaptation and serving, which tackles the frontier challenge of deploying LLMs under severe orbital constraints and resource-aware serving. Finally, we identify open challenges and future directions. By bridging the AI and satellite networks, this paper provides a research roadmap for the implementation of space-native AI technologies.

papers.title: One-Shot Federated Model Editing for Device Dynamics at the Edge
papers.abstract: Standard federated learning (FL) requires persistent device connectivity across multiple communication rounds, making it unsuitable for dynamic environments such as vehicular networks, where devices frequently join and leave. One-shot FL offers a promising alternative by completing training in a single communication round. However, one-shot FL suffers from model solidification and cannot readily adapt to subsequent client dynamics, including new client contributions and the withdrawal of previous contributions. We therefore consider exact model editing, which removes withdrawn contributions through unlearning or incorporates newly contributed ones through incremental learning without retraining from scratch. We identify that efficient editing fundamentally hinges on learning stability. To this end, we propose F-SOSA, the first stable one-shot FL algorithm that enables rapid and exact model editing. F-SOSA leverages sub-sampling of local models with carefully tuned rate for stable aggregation and performs curvature-aware model fusion to preserve utility. We prove that F-SOSA achieves vanishing training error and reasonably small generalization error bounds. Building on this stability, we further develop two single-round editing algorithms: F-SOSA-U for unlearning and F-SOSA-I for incremental learning. They ensure that the edited model, along with all intermediate algorithmic states, is statistically indistinguishable from retraining while incurring only an expected $O(ρ)$ fraction of its cost, where $ρ$ quantifies stability. Experiments demonstrate that our approach matches retraining performance while reducing cumulative time and communication overhead by at least 36% and 22%, respectively, under realistic urban mobility simulations.

papers.title: Movable-Element Multi-Functional RIS-Assisted Hybrid RSMA-NOMA: A Constrained Hybrid Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.abstract: In this work, we propose a movable-element (ME) multi-functional reconfigurable intelligent surface (MF-RIS) architecture, termed MM-RIS, which integrates element mobility with adaptive signal reflection, transmission, amplification, and energy harvesting (EH) to enhance communication flexibility and energy self-sustainability. A hybrid rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA) and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) transmission scheme is further designed to improve spectral efficiency. We formulate an energy efficiency (EE) maximization problem by jointly optimizing transmit beamforming, power and rate allocation, MM-RIS configurations, panel deployment, and ME positions. To address the resulting non-convex mixed continuous-discrete optimization problem, we propose constrained hybrid deep reinforcement learning with federated transformer and parametrized sharing (CRAFTS). CRAFTS integrates multi-agent proximal policy optimization (MAPPO) and multi-agent deep Q-networks (MADQN) through bi-directional parametrized sharing to handle continuous and discrete actions, respectively. Moreover, a transformer-based architecture and federated learning (FL) are incorporated to enhance state representation and distributed knowledge sharing, whilst a Lagrangian-based adaptive penalty mechanism facilitates the constraint satisfaction. Simulation results have demonstrated that the proposed MM-RIS architecture and CRAFTS framework substantially improve EE and constraint satisfaction compared to the benchmarks in the open literature. Moreover, the results validate the benefits of spatially reconfigurable MM-RIS, hybrid RSMA-NOMA transmissions, and intelligent collaborative learning, highlighting the potential of the proposed framework for energy-efficient and adaptive next-generation wireless networks.

papers.title: Heterogeneity and Subgrouping in Modern Statistics and AI
papers.abstract: Heterogeneity is a defining feature of modern data: individuals, subpopulations, sites, modalities, tasks, and time points may differ in distributions, associations, treatment effects, or decision objectives. This review develops a unified perspective in which heterogeneous analysis is a problem of structured information borrowing: deciding what should be shared, what should remain distinct, and how uncertainty about that structure should enter inference and decisions. We connect classical stratification, interaction models, finite mixtures, mixed-effects models, and empirical Bayes with subgroup discovery, individualized learning, synthetic data generation, large language models, federated learning, privacy, security, and mobile health. Precision medicine provides a central example: subgroup rules offer interpretable approximations to individualized response surfaces, whereas partially pooled models stabilize patient-specific estimation. Across applications, the same tensions recur: population averages can conceal consequential variation, unrestricted personalization is unstable, adaptive subgroup discovery creates selection bias, and borrowing across incompatible sources causes negative transfer. These difficulties are amplified in contemporary AI, where sparse user histories, entangled representations, heterogeneous preferences, feedback loops, distribution shift, and privacy constraints make reliable personalization and evaluation especially challenging. We conclude with an agenda for calibrated personalization that integrates multilevel representations, selective borrowing, subgroup-aware evaluation, and valid uncertainty quantification.

papers.title: Projection-Based Federated Learning on Compact Submanifolds with Geometry-Independent Differential Privacy
papers.abstract: Federated learning trains a shared model across clients without exchanging their data, yet the updates they transmit still leak information about individual records. Enforcing differential privacy is harder still when the model parameters lie on a Riemannian manifold. Existing methods rebuild the noise added for privacy in the geometry of each new iterate, aggregate through intrinsic maps that often lack a closed form, and prove convergence only in restricted regimes. We introduce DP-RFedProj, a record-level differentially private federated learning method for compact submanifolds that aggregates through closed-form projections and privatises gradients in a fixed ambient geometry. Each client may run any stochastic first-order optimiser, take several local steps, and participate only intermittently. An explicit record-level $f$-DP guarantee holds for the entire training transcript, independently of the manifold, the aggregation scheme and the local optimiser. We establish convergence of DP-RFedProj when each client runs Riemannian SGD locally and the server aggregates by projected averaging, and show that privacy enters the rate through a term scaling with the manifold's intrinsic dimension rather than the ambient one. Synthetic experiments on federated PCA over the Grassmann manifold corroborate these findings. On EEG motor-imagery classification with SPDNet, whose weights lie on the Stiefel manifold, the method outperforms a Euclidean baseline at every privacy budget considered. In both experimental settings, our accounting requires five to six times less noise than that of the closest prior method for the same budget, which translates into higher utility.

papers.title: Geodesic-SVDD Latent Mixup for One-Shot Distributed Tabular Learning
papers.abstract: Distributed Learning on structured data is a key and widely adopted approach in privacy-sensitive sectors, ranging from financial fraud prevention to federated healthcare diagnostics. While Gradient Boosted Decision Trees are widely used in centralized settings due to their efficiency, they are incompatible with standard gradient-based federated learning protocols because of their non-differentiability. Conversely, standard deep classifiers that are amenable to federated optimization often suffer from catastrophic forgetting under label distribution skew. In this work, to address these gaps we propose Geodesic-SVDD, a framework for Distributed Spherical Prototype Learning that recasts each client's task as one-class density estimation on the hypersphere, so that local models can be aggregated as probabilistic manifolds in a single round. Specifically, for each client, we employ a Residual Spherical Encoder and Geodesic Latent Mixup that enforces strict hyperspherical constraints ($\|φ(x)\| \equiv 1$), preventing the manifold collapse observed in linear approximations. Furthermore, leveraging this insight, we propose a novel One-Shot "Product of Experts" protocol that enables privacy-preserving aggregation without iterative synchronization. Finally, we mechanistically analyze the trade-off between interpolation strategies, demonstrating that while linear mixup offers an enticing computational shortcut, it destabilizes optimization gradients by orders of magnitude ($10^9\times$). Across five tabular benchmarks and four levels of label skew, Geodesic-SVDD attains the highest mean AUROC among seven federated methods, outperforms federated tree ensembles by up to 21 AUROC points on Covertype, and its One-Shot variant matches centralized Deep SVDD under IID and mild skew with a single communication round.

papers.title: DiffusedSplitFed: Latent Diffusion-based Obfuscation for Reconstruction-Resilient Split Federated Medical Image Segmentation
papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL), Split Learning (SL), and Split Federated Learning (SplitFed) enable collaborative medical image analysis without sharing raw patient data. However, intermediate features and gradients exchanged during SplitFed training may reveal sensitive information through reconstruction attacks. To address this vulnerability, we propose \textbf{DiffusedSplitFed}, a SplitFed framework that integrates Latent Denoising Diffusion Models (LDDMs) at client--server split points to obfuscate transmitted representations while preserving segmentation performance. Three architectural variants (V1--V3) are developed using different combinations of dual conditioning and global feature fusion to investigate trade-offs among reconstruction resistance, segmentation accuracy, and computational complexity. Experiments on three medical imaging datasets (HAM10K, Blastocysts, and FHPsAOPMSB), supported by multiple independent runs and paired statistical analyses, demonstrate improved resistance to the evaluated image reconstruction attacks compared with Baseline SplitFed, while maintaining competitive segmentation performance. Comparisons with existing diffusion-based segmentation methods further demonstrate competitive segmentation accuracy under the evaluated settings. A conditional convergence analysis is also provided to characterize the effects of LDDM-induced gradient perturbations and local optimization on training. These findings highlight the potential of latent diffusion-based representation obfuscation for reconstruction-resilient collaborative medical image segmentation. The implementation is available at https://github.com/ChamaniS/DiffusedSplitFed.

papers.title: When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.

papers.title: Clean-label Poisoning Attack and Defense Game for Federated Learning in Vehicular Networks
papers.abstract: This paper studies interactions between clean-label poisoning attack and defense in vehicular networks using federated learning (FL). Basic Safety Message (BSM) classification for anomaly detection is modeled as a distributed learning problem over a vehicular network with dynamic topology. As a critical threat to FL, a feature-space clean-label attack is introduced, wherein benign samples are perturbed toward malicious feature extremes, degrading class separability while preserving labels. To counter this, a feature-consistency relabeling defense is proposed to detect and relabel suspicious samples. A game-theoretic framework is developed to capture attack-defense interactions and characterize equilibrium strategies based on attack effectiveness and cost parameters. Results show that the attack scales effectively with compromised nodes, while the proposed defense keeps attack success low without degrading clean accuracy and shifts equilibrium regions toward attack-averse regimes.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Loss Exploration for Vision-Based Perception under Non-IID Data
papers.abstract: Vision-based image classification models benefit from Federated Learning (FL) across vehicles, however learning accurate models from distributed vehicular cameras is challenging due to data heterogeneity and privacy concerns. To improve performance on non-IID data, advanced FL optimization approaches have emerged that share auxiliary insights, such as client gradient behaviors. While these gradient-guided optimized FL methods improve the model accuracy, their reliance on sharing additional gradient information introduces a previously unexplored privacy vulnerability. In our empirical privacy-leakage experiment, we show that a malicious server can infer clients' label sets from shared guidance matrices under heterogeneous client label distributions (simulated via Dirichlet-based label partitions), between 50% and 84% accuracy. To address this privacy leakage, we propose PPFLex that replaces the central server with three Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) servers to securely compute the global guidance matrix and perform federated averaging under semi-honest and malicious MPC server assumptions. We evaluate PPFLex on widely used traffic-sign classification datasets (e.g., GTSRB and BTSC) as representative autonomous vehicle perception benchmarks, comparing against baselines. Our results show that PPFLex achieves accuracy comparable to the plain-text FedLEx pipeline while preventing privacy leakage, incurring acceptable MPC overhead.

papers.title: Democratizing LLM Training with the Edge: Challenges, Systems, and the Road Ahead
papers.abstract: The growing computational power of modern GPU data centers has let a few industrial giants train and deploy large language models (LLMs) on massive amounts of data. Yet the sheer scale of these models and their training data makes centralized development increasingly hard to sustain, and at the same time shuts out smaller institutions that hold relevant private data but lack comparable infrastructure. In this paper, we organize our positions on distributed LLM training around the pretraining and fine-tuning paradigms, covering federated learning, split learning, and decentralized approaches, and we assess their readiness for geo-distributed settings with heterogeneous hardware and unreliable connectivity. We then present a {\em unified} system architecture built around a cloud-hosted parameter server that coordinates heterogeneous clients over outbound gRPC connections, reusing one communication, compression, and fault-tolerance stack for both pretraining and a family of fine-tuning methods. We validate the design with real geo-distributed experiments on GPT-2 Medium and Llama3-1B pretraining across multiple university sites, showing stable convergence under realistic conditions. Finally, we chart the road ahead, identifying open problems that span frontier model support, elastic fault tolerance, adaptive compression, federated alignment, privacy and trust, incentive design, and system--algorithm co-design, all of which must be addressed to make democratized LLM training a reality.

papers.title: Evolving Federated Density Peak Clustering with Shuffler-Based Anonymization
papers.abstract: In this paper, we present a novel one-shot federated clustering approach based on evolving fuzzy clustering and shuffler-based anonymization. In federated clustering, each round reveals additional model information to the server and can increase the opportunity to infer properties of local datasets, even when raw samples are never shared. Consequently, fewer client-server exchanges and unlinkability are important, so transmitted information cannot be attributed to any single client. Data-stream clustering algorithms, which learn in a single pass over the data, align well with the one-shot federated learning paradigm, where a single communication round can be sufficient. The proposed Evolving Federated Density Peak Clustering (eFDPC) method combines evolving fuzzy data-stream clustering and density peak clustering in a federated setting. Each client independently evolves micro-clusters from private data mini-batches through cluster addition and merging. To limit communication, density peak clustering is applied to the learned micro-clusters and only the selected peaks are transmitted, rather than the full local models. A shuffler-based layer is introduced between the clients and the server to anonymize contributions prior to reconstruction and global peak selection. We consider a peak-only variant, eFDPC-P, as well as eFDPC-G with server-side label propagation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmark datasets show that eFDPC outperforms recent federated clustering baselines in one-shot settings and scales to higher-dimensional, non-IID data.

papers.title: Is High Local Accuracy Enough? Geometric Consensus with Support-Adaptive Statistical Personalization for Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Real-world deployment of personalized federated learning (PFL) requires adapting to heterogeneous clients while preserving recognition performance beyond local distributions. However, high local accuracy can conceal failures on locally rare or absent classes. Effective personalization should therefore strengthen global recognition while raising the personalization floor. We propose an evaluation protocol that complements local accuracy with global, rare-class, and unseen-class evaluations to reveal generalization obscured by local scores, and assesses personalization floors among the worst-performing clients to expose weaknesses hidden by aggregate performance. To meet these deployment challenges, we propose FedGRC, a unified PFL framework integrating generalization and personalization through (i) Consensus-Guided Representation Learning (CGRL), which learns discriminative representations through shared directional and magnitude guidance; (ii) Multilayer Metric Synthesis (MMS), which constructs a shared covariance metric from these multilayer representations for statistical classification; and (iii) Support-Adaptive Shrinkage Personalization (SASP), which adapts class means within this metric by shrinking local estimates toward shared means according to local sample support, enabling adaptation while retaining shared knowledge. Extensive experiments, including benchmarking against 21 methods across 5 heterogeneity settings on 3 datasets and comprehensive ablation studies, validate the effectiveness of FedGRC. On CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, FedGRC surpasses state-of-the-art (SOTA) baselines in global recognition and personalization floors by at least 2.17% and 2.13%, respectively. On the real-world heterogeneous FedRS dataset, it outperforms the respective best baselines by 2.15%, 3.30%, and 4.61% in local adaptation, global recognition, and the personalization floor.

papers.title: FedBST: Bilateral Self-Training for Unsupervised Federated Classification
